## **Instructions for companies** 

This is the template for submission of evidence to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) as part of the single technology appraisal (STA) process. Please note that the information requirements for submissions are summarised in this template; full details of the requirements for pharmaceuticals and devices are in the user guide. 

This submission must not be longer than 150 pages, excluding appendices and the pages covered by this template. If it is too long it will not be accepted. 

Companies making evidence submissions to NICE should also refer to the NICE health technology evaluation guidance development manual. 

In this template any information that should be provided in an appendix is listed in a box. 

## **Highlighting in the template (excluding the contents list)** 

Square brackets and grey highlighting are used in this template to indicate text that should be replaced with your own text or deleted. ## **B.1 Decision problem, description of the technology and clinical care pathway** 

- Haemophilia is a rare, lifelong, genetic disease that results in repeating bleeding episodes that can lead to long-term, progressive joint damage, pain and impaired mobility, with many patients reporting substantial impacts on anxiety and their ability to participate in activities of daily living[1] 

- There are two types of haemophilia, A and B, which are characterised by deficiencies in clotting factor levels; factor VIII (FVIII) for haemophilia A and factor IX (FIX) for haemophilia B. Although caused by different mutations the two types of haemophilia are largely indistinguishable with regards to clinical outcomes[2] 

- Severe haemophilia is defined as having <1% of normal factor activity and is primarily managed by life-long regular intravenous (IV) infusions of factor prophylaxis, with extended half-life (EHL) products favoured in the UK over standard half-life (SHL) given the reduced frequency of administration.[3, 4] In haemophilia A, emicizumab, a chimeric bispecific antibody that replaces the function of FVIII, is an increasingly common treatment option[5] 

- However, there are limitations to the current treatment options; factor prophylaxis products require regular IV infusions which can be strenuous and time consuming, and emicizumab, although a subcutaneous (SC) therapy, is not an available treatment option for patients with haemophilia B.[6, 7] 

- There remains an unmet need for a convenient prophylaxis therapy, particularly in haemophilia B where there are no SC administration options, to reduce the burden of IV administration of factor replacement products. 

- Marstacimab is a novel monoclonal antibody directed against the tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI), the primary inhibitor of the extrinsic coagulation cascade. Marstacimab is delivered SC on a weekly basis, and offers patients a simpler self-administration treatment, via a pre-filled pen, removing the burden of IV factor infusions. Marstacimab is administered as a flat dose, further reducing the complexity of administration.

## **B.1.3.1 Overview of the disease** 

_**Haemophilia is a rare, lifelong, genetic disease that results in repeated bleeding episodes that can lead to long-term, progressive joint damage, pain and impaired mobility, with many patients reporting substantial impacts on anxiety and their ability to participate in activities of daily living and live spontaneously**_ 

- Haemophilia is characterised by the impaired production of coagulation factors, which are required for proper blood clotting.[1] As an X-linked, recessive condition, haemophilia predominantly presents in males, however, females can also be affected and de novo, noninherited, cases can arise.[15] 

- The two primary forms of haemophilia, haemophilia A and B, are distinguished by the affected clotting factor. Individuals with haemophilia A have reduced activity of FVIII, while individuals with haemophilia B have reduced activity of FIX.[16] FVIII and FIX are important constituents of the blood coagulation cascade; absence or deficiency of these proteins impairs fibrin production which delays clot formation once bleeding has occurred.[17, 18] 

- While haemophilia A and B are distinct diseases, caused by mutations in genes encoding different proteins, their clinical outcomes are largely indistinguishable, and both diseases are considered clinically similar.[2,19] 

- People with haemophilia present with prolonged and spontaneous bleeding episodes, the severity of which is related to the percentage of normal factor (FVIII or FIX) activity in an individual; severe haemophilia is defined as having <1% of normal factor activity.[2, 13, 20] 

- Haemophilia B is rarer than its counterpart, haemophilia A, accounting for 20% of all haemophilia cases.[21] It has been estimated that there were 2,128 patients treated for severe haemophilia A and 329 treated for severe haemophilia B in the UK in 2022/2023.[4] 

- Those with haemophilia experience repeat bleeding episodes into muscles, soft tissue and joints; long-term, progressive joint damage (arthropathy) can result following continued joint bleeds, resulting in substantial pain, reduced range of motion and poor mobility all of which contribute negatively to quality of life.[13, 22-24] 

- The physical impairment brought about by recurrent bleed episodes can limit individuals in their ability to participate in activities of daily living or the ability to live spontaneously.[24-27] 

- A substantial psychological burden is associated with haemophilia; anxiety and depression are commonly reported due to the unpredictability of bleeding events, frustration with treatment and issues with venous access.[6, 24, 27] 

## **B.1.3.1.1 Haemophilia background and pathophysiology** 

## _**Haemophilia is a rare, X-linked genetic disorder caused by a deficiency or absence of coagulation factors (FVIII or FIX), with disease severity that is defined by circulating levels of these factors**_ 

Haemophilia is a rare, lifelong genetic condition that affects blood clotting.[1] The reduced ability of the body to produce coagulation factors (referred to as factor[s] from here on), proteins that are essential for normal blood clotting, results in prolonged and spontaneous bleeding episodes.[16] There are two primary forms of haemophilia: haemophilia A and the less common haemophilia B.[19] The form of haemophilia that presents is dependent on the affected factor, with haemophilia A and haemophilia B characterised by an absence or deficiency of FVIII and FIX, respectively.[19] 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 21 -->

FVIII deficiency is the result of mutation of the factor gene, _F8_ , located on the X-chromosome at position Xq28, while FIX deficiency is the result of mutation of the factor gene, _F9_ , located on the X-chromosome at position Xq27.1. As an X-chromosome-linked, recessive condition, haemophilia predominantly affects males. Although instances of more severe forms of haemophilia in females are rare, those carrying two mutated copies of the X chromosome present with symptomatic disease, while female carriers are largely asymptomatic.[28] Haemophilia can occur without family history of the disease; approximately one third of all haemophilia cases are not inherited, instead occurring _de novo_ . 

The stopping of bleeding (haemostasis) is a complex process involving the interaction of blood vessels, platelets (specialised human blood cells) which adhere to each other, and clotting factors. Primary haemostasis, the body’s initial response to vascular injury, involves the build-up of platelet aggregates at the site of the damaged blood vessel to form a haemostatic plug; this temporarily blocks the disrupted vasculature.[29, 30] Secondary haemostasis, the formation and deposition of insoluble fibrin (a clot forming protein) through the blood coagulation cascade, is required to form blood clots and permanently stop bleeding episodes.[31] 

FVIII and FIX are key components in the intrinsic pathway of the blood coagulation cascade.[32] Specifically, FIX works in the presence of its cofactor, FVIII, to activate factor X (FX), an important step in the activation cascade of several plasma factors which results in fibrin formation, ultimately contributing to the cessation of bleeding (Figure 1).[17, 18] 

TFPI is an early inhibitor of the extrinsic coagulation system, blocking FXa via the K2 domain and the tissue factor-FVIIa complex via the K1 domain.[33] Marstacimab acts by preventing this early inhibition of blood clotting by binding to TFPI, blocking its inhibitory effects (Figure 2).

In haemophilia, the formation of the haemostatic plug is unaffected, but reduced fibrin production due to factor deficiency causes impaired secondary haemostasis; this results in delayed clot formation and susceptibility to continued bleeding.[35] Consequently, people with haemophilia experience frequent and prolonged bleeding episodes. Depending on disease severity, these bleeding episodes can occur either spontaneously or following minor trauma; this can be acutely life-threatening and lead to debilitating long-term complications.[36, 37] 

## **B.1.3.1.2 Disease severity** 

The severity of haemophilia can be classified according to the plasma level of FVIII or FIX relative to normal plasma levels (Table 3). Factor activity in plasma is usually expressed either as a percentage (relative to normal human plasma) or in international units (IU) (relative to an international standard for FVIII or FIX in plasma). The normal factor activity in blood plasma is defined as 100 IU/decilitre (dL) (equivalent to 1 IU/mL [i.e.,100% of normal factor activity]). Factor activity levels lower than this usually correlate with an increased likelihood of bleeding events and injury. For patients with severe haemophilia (i.e. factor activity below 1% of normal [<1 IU/dL]), bleeding often presents spontaneously.[2, 13, 20]

## **B.1.3.1.3 Epidemiology** 

## _**Severe haemophilia is a rare condition, with recent epidemiological data indicating that there were an estimated 2,457 adults treated in the UK in 2022/2023**_ 

Haemophilia A is more common than haemophilia B, with the former occurring in one in 5,000 live male births and the latter occurring in one in 30,000 live male births.[15] Some global estimates have calculated the prevalence of haemophilia A to be 12.8 per 100,000 men and haemophilia B to be 2.69 per 100,000 men (based on data from Western European countries, the United States, and Canada).[38, 39] 

A key source of epidemiological information for people with severe haemophilia in the UK is derived from the United Kingdom Haemophilia Centre Doctors’ Organisation (UKHCDO) National Haemophilia Database (NHD). The UKHCDO is an association of medical practitioners working within haemophilia centres in the UK. They manage the UK NHD which prospectively collects data for all people registered with a bleeding disorder in the UK, as well as the Haemtrack home therapy reporting system which allows individuals with haemophilia to report their treatments in real-time. The most recently available data from the NHD indicated that there were 2,128 patients treated for severe haemophilia A and 329 people treated for severe haemophilia B in the UK.[4] The full breakdown of patients with haemophilia by severity is provided in Table 4.

## **B.1.3.1.4 Overview of symptoms and clinical features** 

_**The primary clinical features of haemophilia are repeated episodes of bleeding into the muscles, soft tissue and joints. Patients with haemophilia have reduced life expectancy compared with the general population, and persistent bleeding into the joints can result in the development of long-term joint damage that is associated with joint pain, reduced range of movement and impaired mobility**_ 

Individuals with haemophilia A and B display comparable symptoms, of which the defining clinical feature is the repeated and prolonged bleeding events into muscles and soft tissue which can occur spontaneously (without an identifiable cause) or in response to trauma (e.g., following injury or surgery).[13][22, 41, 42] Recurrent bleeding events can lead to inflammation, joint pain, diminished range of movement and poor mobility.[23] 

Approximately 70–80% of all bleeds occur into joints (haemarthrosis) which can lead to progressive haemophilic joint damage (arthropathy), an important long-term complication of bleeding.[43] Recurrent spontaneous and/or traumatic haemarthrosis aggravates joints, resulting in the development of chronic synovial inflammation (synovitis) – a joint that experiences chronic synovitis is known as a “target joint” – and joint arthropathy.[44, 45] The severity of joint arthropathy, is proportional to the number of joint bleeds experienced by an individual, with permanent damage observed following three episodes of haemarthrosis into the same joint. Long term, irreversible, progressive joint destruction follows, ultimately causing substantial physical dysfunction and impairment in individuals with severe haemophilia.[13] 

Asymptomatic (sub-clinical) microbleeds into joints have also been observed in individuals with haemophilia that do not present with clinically evident joint bleeds.[46] Studies have reported on individuals who, despite maintaining excellent bleed outcomes, report abnormalities consistent with microbleeds following magnetic resonance imaging.[47, 48] Such asymptomatic leakage of small amounts of blood into a joint can contribute to joint arthropathy and damage over an individual’s lifetime.[46] 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 25 -->

Those with haemophilia may also experience bleeding into muscles and abdominal organs, which can lead to organ rupture and further severe blood loss.[49] Long-term internal bleeding can also lead to the development of osteoporosis, the most common comorbidity of haemophilia. Reductions in bone mineral density are often observed in those with moderately severe to severe haemophilia, resulting in further chronic pain and an increased propensity for fractures in older individuals.[50, 51] 

Evidence suggests that people with haemophilia may have a higher mortality risk than the general population, with the risk of mortality linked to severity.[52, 53] In the UKHCDO 2023 report, the median life expectancy of individuals with severe haemophilia A and B, who were actively registered between 1996 and 2023, was reported as 77 and 79 years, respectively, compared with a median life expectancy of 84 and 85 for individuals with mild haemophilia.[4] Approximately 20% of deaths in people with haemophilia are caused by spontaneous intracranial bleeding,[54] which can additionally lead to seizures or impaired motor functioning in those surviving these debilitating incidents.[13, 37] 

## **B.1.3.1.5 Impacts of severe haemophilia on people living with the condition** 

## _**Severe haemophilia has a substantial and wide-ranging physical and psychological impact on people living with the condition and their daily activities**_ 

Given the increased prevalence of haemophilia A compared with haemophilia B, there is a greater body of evidence describing the impacts of the condition on people with haemophilia A. Therefore, given the comparable disease profiles between haemophilia A and B, applicable data from those with haemophilia A are presented where appropriate, and where possible evidence from people with haemophilia B will also be discussed. 

## **Impact of physical symptoms on quality of life** 

## _**The recurrent bleeding episodes that characterise severe haemophilia can lead to progressive joint damage (arthropathy) and pain, resulting in physical impairment and negative impacts on quality of life**_ 

As described in B.1.3.1.4, repeated episodes of bleeding into muscle, soft tissue and joints are a central clinical feature of haemophilia.[22] Bleeding into joints can result in the development of joint arthropathy,[44, 45] in turn leading to joint pain, reduced range of movement and impaired mobility.[23] High bleeding rates, joint arthropathy and associated joint pain have each been shown to be key drivers of negative impacts on health related quality of life (HRQoL) in people with haemophilia and have been considered in turn below.[25] 

## _**Bleeding as a driver of impacted HRQoL**_ 

The Cost of Haemophilia across Europe – a Socioeconomic Survey (CHESS) study has been used as a dataset to determine the impact of bleeds on the HRQoL of people with haemophilia. CHESS was a real-world study in which individuals with haemophilia (n=996 with severe haemophilia A [78%]; n=289 with severe haemophilia B [22%]) and physicians from five European countries (including the UK) completed questionnaires between 2014 and 2015 on bleeding, joint status, QoL and haemophilia-related direct and indirect costs.[45] 

One study utilising a subset of data from CHESS (n=400 with haemophilia A; n=115 with haemophilia B) evaluated the relationship between bleeding rates (as assessed by ABR) and HRQoL (as measured using the EQ-5D-3L instrument).[55] Notably, individuals with zero bleeds

## _**Joint bleeds as a driver of impacted HRQoL**_ 

The development of joint arthropathy resulting from repeated bleeding episodes represents one of the most debilitating consequences of severe haemophilia and has been shown to be a key driver of quality-of-life impacts for people with the condition. A strong association between musculoskeletal complications caused by haemophilia and negative impacts on HRQoL has been observed in a further analysis of data from the CHESS study (n=551 with severe haemophilia A and B).[26] In this study, participants with one or more target joints reported significantly worse HRQoL when compared with those with no recorded target joints (mean EQ5D index score: 0.73 [Standard deviation (SD): 0.285] versus 0.87; SD: 0.179]), with scores worsening as the number of target joints increased.[26] Furthermore, participants with severe haemophilia B interviewed in the Haemnet study raised the issue of joint health and the frustrations this causes on multiple occasions, demonstrating that the development of long-term joint damage and associated physical impairments also result in negative impacts on HRQoL:[24]

I want to be able to do the things, I can’t go on hikes with them, I can’t go cycling with them because I don’t have the range in my ankles. I’m not as fit as I used to be, I used to work out five times a week, I can’t lift stuff now.” “Speaking as somebody who has long-term joint damage and, you know, really painful long-term joint damage, it really affects my mobility and so I can’t be as spontaneous as I would like to be.”_ 

## _**Pain as a driver of impacted HRQoL**_ 

Finally, pain associated with bleeding is another factor that can have a substantial impact on individuals with severe haemophilia. The CHESS II real-world burden of illness study was conducted across five European countries between 2019–2020 and aimed to describe the burden of haemophilia following advances in the management and treatments of the disease since the original CHESS study five years prior.[57, 58] One analysis of the CHESS II study focused on individuals with haemophilia A (moderate haemophilia A: n=190; severe haemophilia A: n=278) with problem joints, defined as joint damage presenting with chronic joint pain and/or limited range of movement due to compromised joint integrity. Patients with problem joints reported markedly lower EQ-5D scores, which decreased in patients with a greater number of problem joints.[59] An additional analysis of the CHESS II study specifically focussed on people with severe haemophilia B receiving prophylaxis (n=75, with 29% from the UK). In this study, it was reported that 76% of participants had mild or moderate chronic pain and 5% endured severe chronic pain, with low EQ-5D scores (mean 0.67) measured across this cohort of individuals as a result.[58] 

Further insight into the prevalence and severity of pain experienced by people with haemophilia is provided by the pain, functional impairment and quality of life (P-FiQ) study, an observational cross-sectional assessment of adults in the United States with haemophilia (n=381) presenting for routine care.[25] This study assessed pain and functional impairment via the EQ-5D-5L overall Brief Pain Inventory (BPI; a validated and widely used means to assess pain). Severity scores for adult participants indicated substantial levels of pain, and as shown in Figure 4, pain due to haemophilia caused substantial interference across many aspects of the cohort’s life, including the ability to enjoy life, work normally, sleep and walk, all of which are areas that individuals without the disease may take for granted.[25] Additionally, over three-quarters of participants in this study reported a history of pain and discomfort as measured by EQ-5D-5L, with higher median pain interference scores (indicating increased pain interference) for general activity, mood, walking and work, providing further evidence to show that the effects and causes of pain in those with haemophilia is multifaceted.[60]

## **Impact on daily living** 

_**The downstream physical impairment brought about by recurrent bleeding episodes can limit individuals in their ability to participate in activities of daily living that those not living with haemophilia may take for granted**_ 

The physical impairments that can develop as a result of bleeding are closely linked with challenges in performing routine activities of daily living, including physical activity and household tasks.[25] The aforementioned study analysing CHESS II highlighted that 63% of participants reported an impact of haemophilia on their daily lives.[58] Personal care, work-related issues and leisure activities are also all detrimentally impacted by the functional impairment caused by haemophilia.[25] Fatigue, loss of enjoyment, and reduced leisure pursuits also correlate positively with the presence of target joints.[26] 

Similar themes were discussed in the Haemnet workshop and interviews with people with severe haemophilia B.[24] While haemophilia had affected the lives of participants to different degrees, all stated an impact of the disease on their family and relationships, education, employment and physical activities. Additionally, the participating individuals felt limited in their ability to travel, particularly due to the need to take medical products like liquids and syringes with them. The

individuals noted travel was “frustrating” due to the requirement of travelling with liquids and syringes, with one stating:[24] 

_“I hadn’t been out of the country until this year for nine years. Going out of a UK airport I feel like a criminal every time. Even though I’ve got the hospital letters, etc.”_ 

Physical leisure activities were also significantly curtailed in individuals with haemophilia, despite a desire to be able to participate. One patient noted:[24] 

_“My earliest memory of a consultant was [them saying] ‘you will not play football, you will not play cricket, you will not play rugby, you will not play basketball, you will not do PE at school’ and I was bored and I got fed up.”_ 

Further evidence for the impact on daily living due to bleeds and subsequent physical burden is provided in a qualitative study involving nine members of The Haemophilia Society.[27] All participants reported that joint bleeds had a substantial impact on their physical well-being, with bleeds and associated comorbidities limiting mobility and independence, along with the inability to partake in activities of daily living, as emphasised by one participant:[27] 

_“I’ve had a fair number of bleeding episodes, like knees, ankles, elbows, shoulders and hips and, later on, I’ve begun to suffer with arthritis which has obviously had a major impact on my mobility which effects all aspects of my life... especially doing things for myself.”_ 

## **Psychological impacts** 

_**Beyond the physical aspects of the condition, anxiety and depression are commonly reported in people with severe haemophilia, highlighting how aspects of living with the condition can result in an additional psychological burden**_ 

Across the cohort of individuals with haemophilia A and B (n=515) in one secondary analysis of the CHESS study, anxiety and depression were two of the most common dimensions in which ‘extreme’ problems were reported on the EQ-5D-3L instrument.[26] In a separate analysis of the CHESS dataset (n=404 with severe haemophilia A), the relationship between bleeding and psychological impact was also stronger when considering the pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression domains of the EQ-5D-3L instrument, indicating that physical and psychological dimensions of bleeding also contribute to reductions in HRQoL.[56] 

Further evidence for the psychological impact of haemophilia can be drawn from the MIND study, an 11-year Nordic registry study that analysed longitudinal national data from 2007–2017 of people with haemophilia (n=3,246), which showed a higher use of antidepressants amongst those with the condition compared with those without the disorder.[61] 

Additionally, during the Haemophilia Treatment Experience Measure (Hemo-TEM) study, which aimed to capture the broad range of treatment burden issues experienced by individuals with haemophilia (n=28 [93.3%] with severe haemophilia), individuals stated they felt worried, anxious and frustrated, with feelings of stress and being overwhelmed also reported.[6] The cause for these psychological impacts was multifactorial, with participants noting venous access, the

The psychological well-being of all participants as a result of their haemophilia was also noted by participants in the qualitative study involving members of The Haemophilia Society; anxiety was common due to the unpredictable nature of the disease, with strong feelings of uncertainty for the future also reported.[27] The inability to participate in activities that individuals valued, along with a lack of independence, were also cited as reasons for depression, with the inability to partake in activities independently also leading to a feeling of _“disempowerment”_ .[27] Feelings of anger and frustration were further reiterated due to restrictions in activities of daily living and the lifelong nature of the disease: 

_“I think there are a lot of us who are angry and haemophilia is definitely frustrating, it can bring on an awful lot of anxiety”; “I sometimes feel ... why me and I do get angry because it’s not my fault that I’ve got this thing which now I have to live with every day because I know it’s not going to ever go away.”_ 

Restrictions in social engagements and dependency on others were also cited to exacerbate feelings of depression, with participants also forced to stay home due to the physical impact of their disease, as reported by one participant:[27] 

_“I’ve had all sorts of depression on and off for the last eight years. I felt so disempowered, a lot of the time couldn’t do anything for myself, have a shower, get dressed; I was in pain, bleeding, in a mess and couldn’t leave the house.”_ 

## **Socioeconomic burden** 

## _**Severe haemophilia is associated with a substantial socioeconomic burden resulting from reduced work opportunities and productivity**_ 

Haemophilia also represents a major economic burden to society and has a substantial impact on an individual’s employment status and productivity.[62-64] People with haemophilia are up to four times more likely to be unemployed compared with non-haemophilia controls among people of working age.[62] Those with the disease also participate less in full-time work compared with the general population, as reported in a study conducted in the Netherlands.[63] A substantial number of employed individuals with severe haemophilia (39%) were also reported to experience restrictions in performing their job due to pain and frequent absenteeism. This effect was reported in 19% of individuals with mild or moderate haemophilia.[63] 

Many participants in the qualitative study with members of The Haemophilia Society also mentioned the impact that bleeding had on their education, work and social life. Five individuals included in the study reported that their working lives were notably impacted, with three participants having to retire early due to their haemophilia.[27] One participant also mentioned:[27] 

_“… you have no social life, you can’t leave the house, you can’t do anything by yourself.”_

Education and employment were also key themes of the workshop and interviews conducted by Haemnet on behalf of Pfizer. Participants stated that having haemophilia influenced their hopes and goals regarding employment and caused them to miss out on educational opportunities. Participants discussed the negative impacts on schooling and work:[24] 

_“I was hardly ever at school; I was mainly in hospital and when I was at school I was bullied and if I wasn’t bullied, I was in detention… So my teachers didn’t really take much notice of me.”_ 

_“It [bleeding] was basically every month and I was having to have, like, a week off work and then come in in a wheelchair the next week, and it was just like … it was crap.”_ 

Furthermore, direct and indirect costs due to disease-related complications such as orthopaedic complications, transfusion-related infections (e.g. human immunodeficiency virus [HIV], Hepatitis C) and development of inhibitors can be substantial.[65] This is due to greater use of clotting factors, more frequent hospitalisations for bleeding, a greater need for surgical intervention (e.g., joint replacements) and the high cost of treating individuals with inhibitors to factor prophylaxis.[65, ] 66 From an economic perspective, while the lifetime medical costs incurred to prevent and manage bleeding risk and the long-term consequences of joint damage are most notable for the NHS (as discussed in Section B.1.3.2), it is important to not overlook the negative impact of severe haemophilia on employment and the lives of those with the disease.[6, 65] 

## **B.1.3.2 Description of the clinical care pathway** 

_**Severe haemophilia A is primarily managed with emicizumab, a prophylactic monoclonal antibody treatment, while life-long IV infusions of FIX prophylaxis remains standard of care in haemophilia B**_ 

- Following its introduction in 2019, emicizumab self-administered as a once weekly SC injection has become the primary treatment for haemophilia A in NHS clinical practice.[67] This was confirmed by clinical experts participating in consultancy interviews who noted that emicizumab is now considered standard of care for haemophilia A.[68] 

- Whilst their use has declined following the introduction of emicizumab, prophylactic replacement therapies given as regular IV infusions remain an important treatment option in haemophilia A 

- In the absence of newly recommended alternatives, standard of care in haemophilia B remains life-long regular IV administration of factor prophylaxis infusions to transiently raise circulating factor activity levels to prevent bleeding and preserve musculoskeletal function.[14] 

- On-demand factor therapy is also available to resolve individual bleeds, for example following surgery or injury, and can be used in addition to prophylaxis or, rarely, on its own.[13] 

- Factor prophylaxis therapies are available in two forms: SHL and EHL products. Haemophilia A SHL products require administration 3 to 4 times a week, while EHL products are typically administered twice weekly.[69-75] In haemophilia B, SHL products can require administration twice per week, whilst EHL products are typically administered at frequencies from once a week to once every two weeks for those whose bleeding is well controlled.[76-79] 

- In patients with haemophilia A, EHL and SHL products have similar market share, while in patients with haemophilia B, EHL products are favoured given they reduce the frequency of administration and the subsequent treatment burden, with their use increasing substantially over time.[4, 80]

## **B.1.3.2.1 Overview of clinical care** 

_**Current clinical management of severe haemophilia primarily consists of life-long prophylaxis to prevent bleeding and preserve musculoskeletal function. Factor replacement remains a common form of prophylaxis, however prophylaxis with emicizumab is becoming more commonly used to treat patients with haemophilia A**_ 

Given that haemophilia is a life-long condition characterised by recurrent bleeding episodes that can lead to irreversible joint damage, the primary goals of current treatments are to reduce or prevent bleeding while allowing patients to lead active lives and achieve a quality of life comparable to individuals not affected by this condition.[14] 

## **B.1.3.2.2 Factor replacement therapy** 

Routine factor replacement prophylaxis remains a mainstay of treatment for people with severe haemophilia, as recommended by the World Federation of Hemophilia (WFH).[13] Prophylaxis treatment can significantly reduce joint bleeding and improve joint health as compared with ondemand therapy. 

In the UK, there are currently no available NICE-recommended treatments for haemophilia. However, guidelines published by the BSH in 2020 recommend that factor replacement prophylaxis should be started before or immediately after the first joint bleed in a person with severe or moderate haemophilia with a baseline level 1–3 IU/dL; this will usually be early in life, prior to the age of three.[14] UK clinical experts have confirmed that the BSH guidelines represent commonly followed clinical practice in the UK.[68] 

Currently available recombinant factor therapies include SHL and EHL products.[13, 14] In haemophilia A, SHL products require administration 3 to 4 times a week, while EHL products are typically administered twice weekly.[69-75] In haemophilia B, SHL products can require administration twice per week, whilst EHL products are typically administered at frequencies from once a week to once every two weeks for those whose bleeding is well controlled.[76-79] 

Given EHL factor prophylaxis reduces the frequency of administration and the subsequent treatment burden compared with SHL products (see Section B.1.3.3.1), EHL products are favoured, especially in haemophilia B, as evidenced by their greater market share in the UK.[4] In haemophilia A there is a greater balance between the use of EHL and SHL products, likely due to the reduced extension of effect for EHL products. FVIII EHL products have a half-life of approximately 19 hours (1.4 to 1.6 fold extension compared to FVIII SHL products), whereas FIX EHL products have a half-life of approximately 82 to 89 hours (3 to 5 fold extension compared to FIX SHL products).[13] 

## **B.1.3.2.3 On-demand treatment** 

Management of haemophilia in the UK may also involve on-demand administration of factor replacement products, either on its own or in addition to emicizumab (for patients with haemophilia A only) or factor prophylaxis, with the aim of stopping bleeding once it has occurred, as may be required following trauma or surgery.[81] However, administration of on-demand factor replacement without prophylaxis is rarely used as a treatment strategy in haemophilia, especially in patients with severe haemophilia. While on demand treatment is essential for reducing the pain and debilitating impact of individual bleeds, it does not significantly alter the bleeding profile and does not subsequently change the natural history of haemophilia leading to musculoskeletal 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 33 -->

damage and other complications from bleeding. On-demand therapy on its own has been demonstrated to be significantly less effective compared with factor prophylaxis at reducing ABR.[82, 83] On-demand treatment on its own is therefore not recommended for use in severe haemophilia, as per WFH and BSH guidelines.[13, 14] 

As previously outlined in Section B.1.1, five UK clinical experts in haemophilia confirmed that ondemand use of factor replacement products alone are rarely used to treat severe haemophilia in the UK. One clinician estimated that 96% of patients with severe haemophilia are on prophylaxis, with patients only very rarely choosing on-demand therapy.[68] On-demand factor replacement treatment as standalone therapy has therefore not been considered relevant in this appraisal, in line with other recent NICE appraisals for severe haemophilia.[10, 84] 

## **B.1.3.2.4 Emicizumab** 

For decades, the standard of care for haemophilia was to use clotting factor replacements as prophylaxis to enhance homeostasis. However, non-factor replacement treatments have also been in development, with emicizumab being available in the UK for people with severe haemophilia A without inhibitors since 2019.[85] Since then, emicizumab has become the primary treatment option for patients with severe haemophilia A, with over half of UK patients estimated to have received emicizumab in 2023.[80] Emicizumab is a monoclonal immunoglobin G4 (IgG4) antibody with a bispecific structure enabling it to bridge activated FIX and factor X, restoring the function of the missing FVIIIa and thus promoting the intrinsic pathway of blood clotting.[67] 

Like factor replacement therapies, emicizumab is given as prophylaxis, however is selfadministered by SC injections instead of IV infusion. The recommended dose is 3 mg/kg once weekly for the first four weeks (loading dose), followed by a maintenance dose from Week 5, of either 1.5 mg/kg once weekly, 3 mg/kg every two weeks, or 6 mg/kg every four weeks.[67] Patients or caregivers may self-administer emicizumab after appropriate training from a healthcare provider.[86] Self-administration of emicizumab requires the individual to first determine their correct weight-based-dose and then draw this up into the SC syringe from the vials of product provided.[67] 

## **B.1.3.2.5 Current clinical management of haemophilia in the UK** 

Based on UK clinical recommendations developed by the BSH, and expert clinical opinion, prophylaxis is considered to represent the primary treatment option for adults with severe haemophilia in the UK.[14, 68] For haemophilia A specifically, the monoclonal antibody emicizumab is an alternative prophylactic treatment to FVIII replacement. The products used to treat haemophilia in the UK and considered in this submission are presented in Figure 5.

## **B.1.3.3 Unmet need** 

_**A substantial unmet need exists for an efficacious therapy with a novel mechanism of action and a convenient and simple method of administration**_ 

- Factor prophylaxis treatment is associated with substantial administration burden; the need for frequent self-administered IV infusions greatly interferes with an individual’s ability to take part in day-to-day activities that others without the condition may take for granted.[6,84] This is particularly true for people with haemophilia B for whom there is no SC treatment option currently available.[6, 13, 87] 

- The high costs of the lifetime use of factor products that require regular IV administration means that disease management is associated with substantial direct treatment costs for the NHS.[45, 58] 

- People with severe forms of haemophilia remain at risk of spontaneous, prolonged bleeding, particularly into the joints, despite regular use of factor prophylaxis. 

- While emicizumab offers an effective treatment option with a different mechanism of action to factor replacement therapies, issues around complicated dosing and administration practices remain. Furthermore, emicizumab is not available to patients with haemophilia B 

- The administration of both emicizumab and factor prophylaxis requires prescribing clinicians to perform weight-based dosing calculations. Patients taking emicizumab must then draw up the solution into a syringe from vials themselves. Additionally, regular factor replacement therapy is challenging for older adults with limited venous access, who have already endured many years of injections. Treatment administration difficulties can additionally lead to issues with treatment adherence.[13, 88, 89 ] 

- There is an unmet need for an easy-to-use and conveniently self-administered prophylactic for all individuals with severe haemophilia. 

## **B.1.3.3.1 Treatment burden associated with current SOC** 

## _**The current approach to clinical management of lifelong, regular IV infusions of factor products results in a substantial treatment burden**_ 

Beyond the physical and psychological burden and impacts on activities of daily living experienced by many people with severe haemophilia, current clinical management with factor prophylaxis (discussed in detail in Section B.1.3.2) imposes a substantial treatment burden for people with the condition. Factor prophylaxis for both haemophilia A and B requires frequent IV infusions of FVIII or FIX over the lifetime of an individual to maintain sufficient circulating levels and prevent bleeds.[13] As individuals are primarily responsible for their administration of factor prophylaxis, such frequent and time consuming infusions can substantially interfere with opportunities to take part in day-to-day activities that others without the condition may take for granted.[13] The effect of treatment burden interfering with daily life was identified in the HemoTEM study; participants reported that travel and social activities were often impacted and that they had to stop activities to treat bleeds.[6] Consequently, people with more severe haemophilia requiring regular IV infusions (every 1 to 3 days) are unable to easily plan their lives, especially when travelling, and they are not afforded the opportunity to live as spontaneously in their day-today lives.[24] Treatment also affected participant’s employment as it caused them to arrive at work late or leave work early. These impacts were also identified by five clinical experts in the HemoTEM study who confirmed treatment regimens may negatively impact a patient’s ability to travel and participate in social activities.[6] 

Self-administration of factor therapies is a complicated and time-consuming process, requiring dexterity and phlebotomy capabilities and the need to regularly endure painful injections.[6] Venous access has been identified as a key barrier to the administration of prophylaxis for people with haemophilia, given the requirement for frequent venous infusion with factor 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 37 -->

replacement products.[13] In a multicentre prospective study conducted in France (n=450) venous access was judged to be difficult in 37% of haemophilia patients, most commonly due to poor vein condition (33%), young patient age (25%), patients being overweight (19%), and difficulty in locating veins (16%).[90] Regular factor prophylaxis thus inflicts further burden on those with limited venous access, a significant challenge for older adults with haemophilia who have endured many years of injections.[13, 88] 

These challenges compound the emotional impacts of haemophilia on individuals, resulting in experiences of frustration and anger in relation to their treatment regimen, particularly due to the interference it has on daily life and the ability to travel (see Section B.1.3.1 for further detail on the impact current treatments have on patients’ daily living).[6] 

Whilst the development of long-acting EHL FIX prophylaxis has reduced treatment burden in patients with haemophilia B to an extent, the more modest half-life extension seen with EHL FVIII treatments means this remains an issue in haemophilia A. IV administration of factor prophylaxis can take from 2 to >50 minutes depending on the product and preparation required, which creates a significant time burden and can be hard to fit around daily life.[91] Additionally, the processes associated with factor product storage and administration can be time consuming, with 33% of patients in a survey of 200 individuals with haemophilia A considering the process of storing, preparing, and mixing FVIII product to be disruptive to their daily routine.[92] A confounding effect from the burdensome treatment schedules of EHL and SHL factor prophylaxes is a potential impact on patients’ ability to adhere to the treatment regimen.[89] Poor adherence has in turn been associated with negative impacts on clinical outcomes, including an increased risk of breakthrough bleeding episodes and target joint bleeds, which may then lead to subsequent worsening of joint damage and HRQoL.[13, 93] 

As a more convenient subcutaneous administration, emicizumab is becoming the treatment of choice for patients with severe haemophilia A. However, the by-weight dosing of emicizumab adds complexity to the administration process.[7] While prescribing clinicians make the calculation regarding the dose required, it is up to the patient to draw this exact dose up into the SC syringe from the vials of product provided.[67] Given that emicizumab is only available in four vial sizes with differing concentrations, producing the correct dose for injection can lead to wastage of product if the exact dose does not meet the vial size.[7] 

## **B.1.3.3.2 Limited treatment outcomes with current prophylaxis** 

## _**A need exists for a new and effective therapy that can address limitations associated with current management of severe haemophilia with factor prophylaxis, including sub-optimal treatment outcomes**_ 

Despite regular use of factor prophylaxis, people with severe forms of haemophilia remain at risk of spontaneous, prolonged bleeding, particularly into the joints.[13] A retrospective analysis of the UK NHD (n=36 with severe haemophilia B) has highlighted that 70% of individuals with haemophilia B do not remain haemarthrosis-free annually.[94] The risk of spontaneous or breakthrough bleeding remains, and suboptimal outcomes are evident, further reinforcing that current clinical prophylactic management of haemophilia is inadequate and fails to fully address the needs of individuals.[13, 95-97] Taken together, this evidence highlights that an unmet need exists for a therapy that can provide greater reductions in bleeding rates, therefore increasing protection from the development of long-term joint damage and associated negative impacts on HRQoL.[13]

## **B.1.3.4 Proposed positioning of marstacimab** 

_**Marstacimab is an innovative monoclonal antibody therapy that offers a practical prefilled SC, self-administered, prophylactic therapy for individuals with severe haemophilia A and B**_ 

Marstacimab is anticipated to be indicated for ******* *********** ** ****** *** ********** ******** ** ***** ** *** *** ***** **** ****** ** ** ****** ********* *********** * *********** ***** *********** ******* ***** ********** ** ****** *********** * *********** *** *********** ******* *** *********** 

With a once weekly, pre-filled SC, fixed-dose regimen, marstacimab prophylaxis offers a more manageable therapy compared with currently available invasive IV factor replacement products. A switch from IV to SC administration for haemophilia treatment products has been shown to improve patient quality of life. Results of a web based survey administered to male adults and their caregivers in the US indicated that both groups preferred treatments administered via SC injection rather than IV infusion.[98] Additionally, as marstacimab is given as a single injection from a pre-filled syringe, it would eliminate the need for complicated weight-based dosing calculations and the requirement for patients to prepare and draw up their own dose of factor therapy or emicizumab. Lessening the burden of administration with routine marstacimab prophylaxis could therefore improve confidence in self-administration, as well as adherence, thereby having a positive effect on patient outcomes. 

As described in detail in Section B.2, in a Phase 3 clinical study, marstacimab has been demonstrated to be superior to routine prophylactic treatment in an intra-patient comparison, as measured by ABR of treated bleeds. This efficacy was maintained long-term (up to 16 months post treatment initiation [based on currently available open-label trial data]), with numerical improvement in participant quality of life compared with those on prophylactic factor replacement therapy. In addition to durable efficacy, the overall safety profile continues to be acceptable. 

The mechanism of action of marstacimab enables it to provide all people with severe haemophilia, regardless of whether they have haemophilia A or B, access to a conveniently administered prophylactic therapy. Its novel mechanism of action, combined with its simple, fixed-dose, pre-filled SC method of administration, separates marstacimab from current products on the market. Ultimately, the introduction of marstacimab would fulfil an important unmet need for a simple and effective treatment option able to improve bleeding rates for patients, reduce the physical and psychological impacts of the treatment-associated and economic burdens of current management, and widen the range of treatment options available. 

## **B.1.4** _**Equality considerations**_ 

Whilst the BASIS trial only recruited male participants, a very small number of females may also be living with severe haemophilia. It is expected that this appraisal will not exclude any people protected by equality legislation, or lead to recommendations that have any adverse impact on people with a particular disability or disabilities. 

Separately, it is worth noting that individuals with active hepatitis B or C, or HIV uncontrolled by antiretroviral drugs (evidenced by CD4+ cell count of ≤200 mm[3] or viral load >20 copies/mL) at the time of enrolment were ineligible for the marstacimab trials, which may present an equality consideration for the Committee.

## **B.2 Clinical effectiveness** 

- A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted to identify evidence on clinical efficacy, including safety, of current therapies for people with severe haemophilia A or B, without a history of factor (FVIII or FIX) inhibitors 

- The Phase 3 BASIS study represents the pivotal clinical trial demonstrating the efficacy and safety of marstacimab prophylaxis compared to factor prophylaxis in patients with severe haemophilia A and B 

- Weekly marstacimab prophylaxis was demonstrated in BASIS to be an effective treatment option, providing a statistically significant, 35.2% (95% CI: 5.6%, 55.6%; p= 0.0376) reduction in the primary endpoint, ABRtreat, compared with the observational period of the trial where patients received SOC factor prophylaxis. 

- The mean ABR reductions observed with marstacimab were generally consistent across haemophillia A and B and age groups for those with prior routine prophylaxis, with all point estimates for a difference <2.5 (non-inferiority margin for the ABR of treated bleeds). 

- Data from BASIS are supported by its open label extension (OLE) which is following trial participants for up to an additional 7 years of participation; currently up to an additional 16 month of data are available from the OLE. Data presented from an average of 6 months of follow up indicate a further numerical reduction in ABRtreat for patients receiving long-term marstacimab prophylaxis in the OLE, compared to patients from the BASIS trial active treatment phase (ATP) 

- In the absence of direct comparative efficacy versus emicizumab, an unanchored simulated treatment comparison (STC) was conducted using data from the BASIS and HAVEN 3 trials. Results from this indirect treatment comparison (ITC) showed that the efficacy of marstacimab is comparable to that of emicizumab with respect to the control of total and treated bleeding rates, however no results reached statistical significance 

- BASIS demonstrated that marstacimab is well tolerated with no notable safety findings. Marstacimab exhibited an acceptable safety profile when compared with factor prophylaxis 

- Overall, weekly marstacimab prophylaxis offers patients with severe haemophilia A or B the option of a convenient and effective treatment able to reduce bleeds and improve quality of life compared to currently available factor prophylaxis 

## **B.2.1** _**Identification and selection of relevant studies**_ 

A _de novo_ SLR of the published literature was conducted. The SLR aimed to identify evidence on the burden of illness and the clinical efficacy and safety of current therapies for adults and adolescents with severe haemophilia A and moderately severe to severe haemophilia B without a history of factor VIII or IX inhibitors. The SLR was wider in scope than the proposed indication in this submission, as it additionally included patients with moderately severe haemophilia B. This reflects the enrolment protocol for the BASIS trial, which ultimately did not enrol any patients with moderately severe haemophilia B. 

The review focused on clinical outcomes data derived from Phase 2/3 and single-arm randomised clinical trials (RCTs), non-RCTs and observational studies (including prospective and retrospective cohort studies and cross-sectional analyses). 

The SLR was conducted in accordance with the high-quality standards required by NICE, as well as standards set forth in other established guidelines (i.e. Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses [PRISMA] and the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions).[99, 100]

The SLR was conducted on the 4[th] August 2020 (original SLR) and subsequently updated on the 21[st] August 2023 and 17[th] May 2024, with a similar review methodology utilised in each iteration. A total of 79 unique trials reported in 333 records were included in the SLR. 46 trials included patients with haemophilia A, 27 included patients with haemophilia B, and 6 included patients with haemophilia A and patients with haemophilia B. Sample size ranged from 2 patients to 216 patients, with the majority reporting on populations under 100 patients. 

Full details of the SLR search strategy, study selection process and results are presented in Appendix D.1. 

## **B.2.2** _**List of relevant clinical effectiveness evidence**_ 

Two unique trials were found in the SLR that reported clinical evidence for marstacimab: one Phase 3 trial, BASIS, and a Phase 2, dose-investigation trial.[101, 102] 

The primary evidence source for the efficacy and safety of marstacimab is the Phase 3 BASIS trial (NCT03938792).[101] BASIS is an ongoing Phase 3, one-way, cross-over, open-label, multicentre study in adolescent and adult patients with severe haemophilia A or moderately severe to severe haemophilia B with or without inhibitors comparing marstacimab versus routine factor prophylaxis. The study compared treatment with patients prescribed on-demand or prophylaxis factor replacement therapy during a 6 month, lead-in, observational phase (OP) with a 12 month ATP, during which patients received prophylactic marstacimab. 

An OLE study (NCT05145127) of the BASIS trial provides further supportive data for the clinical evidence base of marstacimab. The OLE is assessing the long-term safety, tolerability, and efficacy of prophylaxis treatment with marstacimab in patients who successfully completed participation in the BASIS trial.[103] 

This submission focuses on the marstacimab Phase 3 clinical programme (consisting of the BASIS trial and the OLE). An overview of the key clinical evidence from the BASIS trial and OLE is presented in Table 7. The methodology and results of the BASIS trial are presented in Section B.2.3 onwards.

## **B.2.3.1 Summary of methodology of the relevant clinical effectiveness** 

## **evidence** 

_**BASIS, and its OLE study, represent the pivotal clinical trials demonstrating the efficacy and safety of patients receiving weekly marstacimab prophylaxis compared with factor prophylaxis**_ 

- In BASIS, a Phase 3, one-way, crossover, open-label, multicentre study, adult male patients with severe haemophilia A or B received their SOC factor prophylaxis treatment (N=91) during a 6 month OP; 83 patients subsequently progressed to the 12 month ATP where they received weekly SC marstacimab prophylaxis 

- Trial outcomes in the modified intention to treat (mITT) population, those who completed OP and received at least one dose of marstacimab in ATP, were measured at the end of the 12 month ATP 

- The primary outcome measure for BASIS was ABRtreat, the number of treated bleeding episodes experienced by patients during the 12 month ATP compared to during the 6 month OP. - Trial patients had a mean age of 33 years, with 78% (N=65) diagnosed with severe haemophilia A and 22% (N=18) diagnosed with severe haemophilia B. Additionally, the trial included 17 (21%) adolescent patients aged 12 to 17 years 

- UK clinicians consulted as part of this submission considered that the BASIS trial had enrolled a more severe patient population than other haemophilia trials, with patients also slightly younger and lower weight than the average patient in UK practice[68] 

## **B.2.3.1.1 Trial design and methodology** 

The BASIS trial provides the primary clinical evidence base for marstacimab. BASIS is a Phase 3, one-way, crossover, open-label, multi-centre study in adolescent and adult patients that has 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 43 -->

demonstrated the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of marstacimab for routine prophylaxis in male patients aged 12 to 74 years with severe haemophilia A (coagulation FVIII activity < 1%) or severe haemophilia B (coagulation FIX activity < 1%) without inhibitors. The BASIS trial enrolment protocol included patients with moderately severe haemophilia B, but ultimately only enrolled patients with severe disease. 

The BASIS trial included two cohorts which were split based on whether they received on demand factor therapy (N=37 at OP entry) or factor prophylaxis (N=91 at OP entry), during the 6 month OP. As patients with severe haemophilia A or B primarily use factor prophylaxis to manage their condition (Section B.1.3.2.5), this submission will present BASIS trial data for the pre-specified cohort of patients who received factor prophylaxis during the OP only. Additionally, a subset of patients with haemophilia develop neutralising antibodies (nAb), also known as inhibitors, directed against FVIII or FIX. Those with inhibitors are likely to have a reduced effectiveness of factor replacement therapy. The BASIS trial inclusion criteria specified that patients with severe haemophilia A or B both with or without inhibitors were eligible for the trial. However, the marketing authorisation for marstacimab is anticipated to specify that marstacimab is indicated for patients without FVIII or FIX inhibitors. In the cohort of patients receiving prophylactic factor therapy during the OP, which is the focus of this submission, no patients had inhibitors. 

In BASIS, individuals received their current standard of care treatment, prophylactic factor replacement therapy, during a 6-month lead-in OP. Eligible patients then progressed to the ATP where they received a 300 mg loading dose followed by a 150 mg once weekly SC injection of marstacimab prophylaxis. Patients were followed for 12 months in the ATP to evaluate efficacy and safety endpoints. A schematic of the BASIS trial design is presented in Figure 6.

## **Definitions and clinical relevance of trial outcomes** 

## **Overview of efficacy measures: ABR and HJHS** 

In the BASIS trial, ABR was measured according to two definitions, ABRtreat and ABRtotal. The primary endpoint, ABRtreat, involved counting of all treated bleeds experienced by patients and was defined as the number of treated bleeding episodes during the 12-month ATP. Furthermore, ABRtreat was also assessed for specific bleed types, including for spontaneous, joint, and target joint bleeds. 

ABRtotal during the 12-month ATP, a key secondary endpoint, was defined similarly to ABRtreat except that both treated and untreated bleeding was counted. 

As the primary aim of haemophilia treatment is to reduce bleeding and given that acute bleeds have a significant impact on quality of life and also contribute to deterioration of joint health and 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 47 -->

future complications, measurements of ABR are directly relevant as key benefits for patients. ABRtreat quantifies the proportion of bleeds that are most severe and thus require treatment with on-demand factor replacement therapies, whilst ABRtotal additionally reflects those bleeds which, whilst not requiring treatment, still prove burdensome for patients. 

An additional efficacy endpoint in the BASIS trial was the HJHS. The HJHS provides a measure of joint health for the joints most commonly affected in haemophilia, namely the knees, ankles and elbows, and enables tracking of joint health over time. Different aspects of joint health are evaluated, and for each of the six joints, the following items are scored: swelling (scored from 0−3), duration of swelling (0−1), muscle atrophy (0−2), crepitus on motion (0−2), flexion loss (0−3), extension loss (0−3), joint pain (0−2), and strength (0−4). The maximum score for each individual joint is 20, with gait also scored from 0−4, resulting in a maximum total score of 124; higher scores indicate worse joint health. The HJHS was not included in the BASIS trial’s testing hierarchy. 

## **Overview of PRO and HRQoL measures used in BASIS** 

Data from a number of HRQoL instruments and PROs were collected in BASIS: 

- **EQ-5D-5L** is a generic HRQoL measure used in the assessment of QALYs. The EQ-5D measurement is NICE’s preferred method for measuring HRQoL.[12] 

   - The EQ-5D-5L instrument measures 5 dimensions of health on a 5-point scale including Mobility, Self-care, Usual activities, Pain/discomfort and Anxiety/depression. 

   - Also included is a visual analogue scale (VAS) anchored by worst and best imaginable health on a 0 to 100 scale where patients are asked to indicate where on the scale they rate their current health. 

   - EQ-5D results can be used to generate utility values, where 1.0 represents perfect health and 0.0 represents death, which can then be applied in an economic analysis to calculate the QALYs associated with an intervention (see Section B.3.3). 

- **Haemophilia Quality of Life Questionnaire for Adults (Haem-A-QoL)** and **Haemophilia Quality of Life Questionnaire for Adolescents (Haemo-QoL)** are disease specific measures of HRQoL intended for adults and adolescents with haemophilia, respectively. 

   - The instruments use a 4-week recall period to assess health across 10 domains consisting of 46 items in the adult version and 12 domains consisting of 77 items in the adolescent version. The 10 domains and the number of items within each domain of the adult version are as follows: Physical Health (5); Feelings (4); View of Self (5); Sport/Leisure (5); Work/school (4); Dealing with Haemophilia (3); Treatment (8); Future (5); Family Planning (4); and Partnership and Sexuality (3). The 12 domains and the number of items within each domain of the adolescent version are as follows: Physical Health (7); Feelings (8); Attitude/View (10); Family (8); Friends (4); Other people (6) Sport and School (9); Coping/Dealing (7); Treatment (8); Perceived Support (4); Future (4); Relationship (2). 

   - These items are rated by the patients as either ‘never’, ‘seldom’, ‘sometimes’, ‘often’ or ‘always’; for other items, ‘not applicable’ is also an option. Scores are calculated by domain and a single total score is determined, ranging from 0 to 100, with higher scored reflecting lower quality of life.

<!-- page 48 -->

- **Haemophilia Activities List 2.0 (HAL2)** and **Pediatric Hemophilia Activities List (pedHAL)** are multiple domain measures of the impact of haemophilia on functional abilities in adults and children, respectively. 

   - The seven domains of the adult instrument contain 42 items in total, as follows: Lying/sitting/kneeling/standing (8); Lower (leg) functioning (9); Upper (arm) functioning (4); Transportation (3); Self-care (5); Household tasks (6); and Sports/Leisure (7). 

   - The seven domains of the paediatric instrument contain 53 items in total, as follows: Sitting/Kneeling/Standing (10); Functions of the Legs (11); Functions of the Arms (6); Use of Transportation (3); Self-Care (9); Household Task (3); Leisure Activities and Sports (11). 

   - Scoring can be done by domain, components (Activities involving the Upper Extremities, Basic activities involving the Lower Extremities and Complex activities involving the Lower Extremities) or a standardised total score. 

**Patient Global Impression of Change – Hemophilia (PGIC-H)** is a single-item assessment of an individual’s overall impression of the change in their life due to haemophilia. The assessment can be taken by adults and adolescents. 

- The PGIC-H measures the patient’s overall impression of change in their life with haemophilia in a 7-point ordinal scale with lower scores indicating better change; 1: greatly improved, 2: moderately improved, 3: slightly improved, 4: no change, 5: slightly worsened, 6: moderately worsened, and 7: greatly worsened. 

## **Baseline characteristics** 

A total of 128 patients were enrolled in the OP. 91 patients with prior prophylactic treatment using factor replacement entered the study, and were included in the All Analysis Set (AAS) (see Section B.2.4). Of the 91 patients treated with factor replacement prophylaxis, 84 (92.3%) completed the 6 month OP and 7 (7.7%) discontinued during the OP (5 patients no longer met eligibility criteria and 2 patients due to protocol deviations). 

Of the 84 patients who completed the OP, 83 patients entered the ATP, of whom 78 (94.0%) completed the 12 month ATP and 5 (6.0%) discontinued (4 patients withdrew by subject [subject initiated withdrawal unrelated to AEs] and 1 patient due to AE [not treatment related]). 

Baseline characteristics for patients treated with prior factor prophylaxis in the OP of the trial who continued to the ATP of the trial are provided in Table 9. Baseline disease characteristics for this mITT BASIS factor prophylaxis cohort are presented in Table 10. 

The proportion of patients with haemophilia A and B were comparable to UKHCDO data for 2022/23, with haemophilia B patients making up 21.7% of individuals in the BASIS trial and 14.3% of individuals in UK clinical practice.[4] Clinical experts consulted as part of this appraisal noted however that the age (**** years) and weight (**** kg) of patients from the UKHCDO dataset were more reflective of patients in the UK, with the population in the BASIS trial being younger and lower weight. The advisors additionally noted that the BASIS trial may have enrolled a more phenotypically severe group of patients and included an overrepresentation of Asian patients compared with the UK, but did not consider this difference to be a prognostic variable or treatment effect modifier.[68]

## **Statistical analysis** 

The primary efficacy hypothesis in BASIS was to demonstrate non-inferiority in ABRtreat following 12 months of treatment with marstacimab in the ATP compared with routine factor prophylaxis in the OP. Details on the statistical analysis of the primary efficacy endpoint are presented in Table 12. 

**Table 12: Statistical methods for the primary analysis of ABRtreat in BASIS** 

• Marstacimab was considered non-inferior to prior prophylaxis treatment if the upper bound of the 2-sided 95% confidence interval for the difference (ATP **Hypothesis** minus OP) in ABR was less than the non-inferiority boundary of 2.5 **objective** • The primary objective for ABR was considered to have been met if non-inferiority was demonstrated. • Marstacimab was compared with prior routine prophylaxis for various bleeding count endpoints (treated, spontaneous, joint, target joint[s], and all bleeds), using a repeated measure negative binomial regression model via generalised estimating equation (GEE) approach with identity link function. If the non- **Statistical** inferiority on ABRtreat was established, subsequent testing for superiority was **analysis** conducted. • The estimated mean ABRtreat difference and its 2-sided 95% CI obtained from the analysis model are presented along with the conventional p-value (for the null hypothesis that the difference is 0). ## **B.2.6** _**Clinical effectiveness results of the relevant studies**_ 

## _**Marstacimab was demonstrated in BASIS to be an effective treatment option, providing significant reductions in ABRtreat, the primary endpoint**_ 

- Marstacimab prophylaxis demonstrated non-inferiority and superiority over routine prophylaxis as measured by ABRtreat. A statistically significant reduction of 35.2% (95% CI: 5.6%, 55.6%; p= 0.0376) in the primary outcome of ABRtreat was achieved following 12 months of marstacimab prophylaxis in the ATP compared with 6 months of factor prophylaxis in the OP 

- Marstacimab also demonstrated non-inferiority to factor prophylaxis in all bleed-related secondary efficacy outcomes, reducing the rates of annualised joint bleeding rate (AJBRtreat), ABRtarget joint, ABRspontaneous and ABRtotal from the OP to the ATP 

- A comparable HJHS total score was reported in patients receiving marstacimab prophylaxis or factor prophylaxis, with a –2.0 and –2.2 estimated median difference measured for marstacimab prophylaxis compared with the 6 month OP value at 6 months and 12 months of the ATP, respectively 

- Marstacimab demonstrated non-inferiority to factor prophylaxis in Haem-A-QoL for both total score and physical health score. Additionally, results from the BASIS trial indicate that marstacimab demonstrated non-inferiority in both the EQ-5D-5L index score and EQ-VAS score as compared to prior routine prophylaxis, indicating preservation of patient health status 

The BASIS trial provides the primary clinical evidence base for marstacimab and details the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of marstacimab for routine prophylaxis in male patients aged 12 and over with severe haemophilia A (coagulation FVIII activity < 1%) or severe haemophilia B (coagulation FIX activity < 1%) without inhibitors. During the 6 month BASIS trial OP, participants received their SOC factor treatment either on-demand or as prophylaxis, followed by treatment with marstacimab in the 12 month ATP. As explained in Section B.1.3.2.3, on-demand factor treatment is very rarely prescribed in isolation to treat severe haemophilia, whilst factor prophylaxis represents an important treatment option. As such, the section below focuses on the outcomes reported by patients who received factor prophylaxis in the OP. 

As noted in Table 8, Section B.2.3.1.1, patients meeting prespecified dose escalation criteria were permitted to receive a maintenance dose of 300 mg marstacimab administered weekly. All efficacy analyses prespecified in the BASIS trial protocol censored the bleeding records on or after a dose escalation to 300 mg for the eleven patients in the trial who received a dose escalation. The data presented in Section B.2.6 are aligned with this prespecified trial analyses. 

However, for the purposes of the cost-effectiveness analysis presented in Section B.3 of this submission, it was considered that costs and efficacy estimates should include bleeding data for those patients who received dose escalation, as specified in the draft marstacimab SmPC, to align with the possibility of dose escalation in NHS clinical practice. Additionally, given the model structure (detailed in Section B.3.1.2) considers both a bleed and a non-bleed health state, ABRtreat and AJBRtreat were analysed post-hoc to reflect the rates amongst those who experienced at least one bleeding event (i.e. excluding those patients with zero treated bleeds). Outputs from these post-hoc analyses that inform the economic model are presented in Section B.2.9 and Appendix N. 

## **B.2.6.1 Primary endpoint** 

As described in Section B.1.3.1.4, the primary clinical manifestation of haemophilia is bleeding with the most severe bleeding events requiring treatment. Therefore, the annualised bleeding rate of treated bleeds, the primary endpoint of the BASIS trial, is a clinically meaningful outcome

to determine the efficacy of marstacimab at reducing the number of bleeding episodes, compared with factor prophylaxis. 

## **Annualised bleeding rate for treated bleeds (ABRtreat)** 

In the mITT set, marstacimab demonstrated non-inferiority and superiority over factor prophylaxis as measured by ABRtreat. The mean model-derived ABRtreat was 5.08 (95% CI: 3.40, 6.77) for marstacimab prophylaxis during the 12 month ATP compared with 7.85 (95% CI: 5.09, 10.61) for routine prophylaxis during the 6 month OP. This represented a reduction in estimated ABRtreat of – – – 2.77 (95% CI: 5.37, 0.16), equating to a 35.2% (95% CI: 5.6, 55.6) decrease. ABRtreat data are presented in Figure 7 and Table 14.

## **Assessment of ABRtreat in patients who had their marstacimab dose increased during the ATP** 

Eleven patients (13%) in the BASIS trial who received prior prophylaxis during the OP had their weekly marstacimab dose increased from 150 mg to 300 mg during the ATP due to insufficient clinical response, based on clinician judgement of the dose escalation criteria. The median durations for 150 mg treatment was 251.0 days, with a subsequent median duration of 108.0 days on the increased dose 300 mg treatment. The mean ABRtreat were 14.03 (before dose increase) and 3.42 (on or after dose increase) with additional data presented in Appendix M.2. 

Separate post-hoc analyses used to inform the model, based on ABRtreat for all patients who received marstacimab during the ATP, including dose escalated patients, and who experienced at least one bleeding event, are presented in Section B.2.9. 

## **B.2.6.2 Secondary endpoints** 

## **Incidence of joint bleeds** 

Results from the BASIS trial indicate that the incidence of joint bleeds (treated) with marstacimab treatment was non-inferior to that observed during the OP with prior routine prophylaxis. The model derived treated AJBRtreat was 4.13 (95% CI: 2.59, 5.67) for marstacimab prophylaxis during the ATP compared with 5.66 (95% CI: 3.33, 7.98) for prior routine prophylaxis during the – OP, with a resulting estimated reduction in AJBRtreat of 1.53 (95% CI: –3.70, 0.64; Table 15). Additionally, 39.8% of patients (33 out of 83) did not have any treated joint bleeds.

## **Haemophilia Joint Health Score (HJHS)** 

As detailed in section B.2.3.1, the HJHS provides a measure of joint health for the joints most commonly affected in haemophilia, namely the knees, ankles and elbows, and enables tracking of joint health over time. HJHS was assessed at both Month 6 and Month 12 in the ATP. Given that the reference treatment duration in the OP was 6 months, while marstacimab prophylaxis was administered for 12 months during the ATP, the main comparison timepoint between the OP and ATP is at 6 months. Where 12 month data from the ATP is presented it is compared to 6 month results from the OP. It should also be noted that for HJHS, data from marstacimab dose escalated patients in the ATP are not censored. 

The median change from baseline in HJHS total score at 6 months was –0.6 (95% CI: –2.2, 1.0) for marstacimab prophylaxis during the ATP compared with 1.3 (95% CI: –0.7, 3.3) for routine prophylaxis during the OP, representing a median difference in decrease between treatments of –2.0 (95% CI: –4.3, 0.3). This difference corresponds to an observed effect size of 0.11 SD units, indicating a similar effect of marstacimab compared to routine prophylactic treatment. Results are presented in Table 19.

## **Number of target joints (exploratory endpoint)** 

As discussed in Section B.1.3.1.4, one of the defining clinical features of haemophilia is recurrent haemarthrosis, which aggravates joints and can result in the development of chronic synovitis. Any joint with chronic synovitis is known as a target joint; as these are common in people with severe haemophilia, the BASIS trial investigated the number of target joints following marstacimab prophylaxis compared with factor prophylaxis baseline.[44, 45] A target joint is defined as a major joint (eg, hip, elbow, wrist, shoulder, knee, and ankle) into which repeated bleeds occur (three or more spontaneous bleeds into a single joint within a consecutive 6 month period). The number of target joints is derived from the eDiary via counting joints that meet the definition of a target joint during the treatment period. 

At baseline, the mean number of target joints was 1.2 with this decreasing to 0.3 after 6 months of routine prophylaxis in the OP and remaining at 0.3 after 12 months of marstacimab prophylaxis in the ATP (Table 20).

## **B.2.6.3 Health-related quality of life and other PROs** 

A secondary objective of the BASIS trial was to evaluate the effect of marstacimab on healthrelated quality of life (HRQoL) as measured by both disease specific and patient reported outcome (PRO) measures. PRO measures were completed at scheduled office visits via an electronic tablet.[105] Overall, marstacimab is comparable or non-inferior to routine prophylactic factor treatment with respect to disease specific and general patient reported health related quality of life (HRQoL) outcomes. 

PRO measures were assessed at Month 6 and Month 12 in the ATP. Given that the reference treatment duration in the OP was 6 months, while marstacimab prophylaxis was administered for 12 months during the ATP, the main comparison timepoint between the OP and ATP is at 6 months. Where 12 month data from the ATP is presented it is compared to 6 month results from the OP. It should also be noted that for all PROs, data from marstacimab dose escalated patients in the ATP are not censored.

## **Haem-A-QoL and Haemo-QoL** 

The Haem-A-QoL and Haemo-QoL surveys are disease-specific measures of HRQoL in individuals with haemophilia. Each of the total or domain scores of Haem-A-QoL and HaemoQoL range from 0 to 100, with lower scores indicating better haemophilia QoL.
