## **EQ-5D-5L and EQ-Visual Analogue Scale** 

Results from the BASIS trial indicate that change from baseline at 6 months with marstacimab prophylaxis was non-inferior to that with prior routine prophylaxis, with respect to EQ-5D-5L and EQ-visual analogue scale (VAS) index scores. In both patient questionnaires, a higher score indicates better health states. 

The estimated change in EQ-5D-5L index score from baseline to 6 months was 0.0752 (95% CI: 0.0178, 0.1325) for marstacimab prophylaxis during the ATP and 0.0300 (95% CI: –0.0140, 0.0740) for prior routine prophylaxis during the OP, a difference between treatments of 0.0223 (95% CI: –0.0432, 0.0877; Table 25). These results demonstrated the non-inferiority of marstacimab compared to prior routine prophylaxis. The difference of 0.0223 corresponds to the observed effect size of 0.12 SD units, indicating a similar effect of marstacimab compared to routine prophylaxis.

## **Patient Global Impression of Change-Haemophilia** 

The patient global impression of change-haemophilia (PGIC-H) is a single item assessment of an individual’s overall impression of the change in their life due to haemophilia. The PGIC-H was assessed at two timepoints during the BASIS trial; after 6 months of routine prophylaxis in the OP and after 6 months of receiving marstacimab during the ATP. 

After 6 months of routine prophylaxis in the OP the median PGIC-H was 3.5 (95% CI: 3.0, 3.9) compared with 1.8 (95% CI: 1.4, 2.3) after 6 months of marstacimab prophylaxis in the ATP. The median difference of –1.8 (95% CI: –2.2, –1.4) indicates marstacimab prophylaxis improved PGIC-H compared with prior routine prophylaxis.[104] 

## **Haemophilia Activities List** 

Marstacimab prophylaxis was comparable to prior routine prophylaxis for self-perceived functional abilities as assessed by the HAL2 and the PedHAL. For both instruments, scores range from 0 to 100 with higher scores indicating a better functional status.

For HAL2 (adults ≥17 years; N=63) total score, the estimated median change from baseline at 6 months was 2.1 (95% CI: –1.0, 5.1) for marstacimab prophylaxis during the ATP compared with –0.6 (95% CI: –3.0, 1.8) for prior routine prophylaxis during the OP, with a resulting estimated median difference in change from baseline scores of 2.0 (95% CI: –1.8, 5.7) between treatments.[104] 

For the pedHAL (adolescents 12 to <17 years; N=20) total score, the estimated median change from baseline at 6 months was 5.3 (95% CI: –4.7, 15.3) for marstacimab prophylaxis during the ATP compared with –1.7 (95% CI: –9.8, 6.3) for prior routine prophylaxis during the OP, with the resulting estimated median difference in change from baseline scores of 6.7 (95% CI: –9.3, 22.7) between treatments.[104] 

## **Haemophilia Life Impacts Questionnaire (Exploratory Endpoint)** 

Improvements in most haemophilia life impacts questionnaire (HLIQ) domains related to life impacts associated with living with and receiving treatment for haemophilia were also observed. For example, from baseline to Year 1, the proportion of patients reporting that haemophilia was not on their mind at all increased from 16.0% to 26.7%. Detailed results of the HLIQ are presented in Appendix M.2.3. 

## **B.2.7** _**Supportive clinical efficacy results – Phase 3 Open Label**_ 

## _**Extension Study**_ 

_**Data from BASIS are supported by evidence from its OLE study, demonstrating continued durability of efficacy March 2023 data-cut:**_ 

- Fifty-nine patients who had received prophylaxis in the BASIS trial OP and completed the ATP without early termination were enrolled in the Phase 3 OLE where they continued to receive weekly SC marstacimab prophylaxis up to an additional 16 months. One patient withdrew from the OLE 

- Of the 58 OLE patients analysed, 77.6% had haemophilia A and 22.4% had haemophilia B 

- In terms of the primary endpoint, model derived ABRtreat further decreased from 5.08 (95% CI: 3.40, 6.77) in the BASIS ATP to 2.27 (95% CI: 1.40, 3.67) in the OLE, although the OLE was not powered to detect differences between outcomes in the ATP and OLE 

- Further reductions in AJBRtreat, ABRtarget joint, ABRspontaneous and ABRtotal were also detected for patients receiving marstacimab prophylaxis during the OLE 

- Additionally, marstacimab prophylaxis preserved joint health as assessed by HJHS at Day 180, with a –2.7 mean change from OLE baseline in the prior prophylaxis group (n=24) 

- **October 2023 interim data-cut:** 

- Seventy-five patients who had received prophylaxis in the BASIS trial OP and completed the ATP without early termination were enrolled in the Phase 3 OLE where they continued to receive weekly SC marstacimab prophylaxis up to an additional 23 months. 

- Of the 75 OLE patients, 77.3% had haemophilia A and 22.7% had haemophilia B 

- In terms of the primary endpoint, model derived ABRtreat further decreased from 5.08 (95% CI: 3.40, 6.77) in the BASIS ATP to 2.79 (95% CI: 1.95, 3.98) in the OLE, although the OLE was not powered to detect differences between outcomes in the ATP and OLE. 

- There were no new safety signals and no reports of thromboembolic events 

The clinical results from the OLE support the Phase 3 BASIS trial data in demonstrating that marstacimab is noninferior and superior in the primary endpoint of ABRtreat for patients with prior prophylactic treatment of severe haemophilia. In the OLE, long term efficacy of marstacimab was

## **B.2.7.1 Study overview** 

The Phase 3 OLE study was an extension of the BASIS trial designed to evaluate the long-term safety, tolerability, and efficacy of marstacimab prophylaxis in patients with severe haemophilia. The OLE recruited patients from the BASIS trial who did not require early termination. Patients would remain on their 150 mg weekly SC dose of marstacimab, with potential dosage escalation to 300 mg SC weekly prescribed to patients meeting dose escalation criteria (as detailed in Table 8). Patient inclusion and exclusion criteria remained the same as the BASIS trial. 

As of the interim data analysis cut-off of 10[th] March 2023, 88 patients had enrolled in the OLE. 29 patients had prior on-demand treatment and 59 patients had prior prophylaxis treatment during the OP. Two patients, one receiving prior on demand factor therapy and one receiving prophylaxis, discontinued from the OLE study due to patient withdrawal. One patient who received prior prophylaxis was not included in the safety analysis set reported herein, as their data was not available by the 10[th] March 2023 interim data cut-off. Of the 58 OLE patients who received prophylaxis in the BASIS trial OP and included in the OLE safety analysis set, 45 (77.6%) had haemophilia A and 13 (22.4%) had haemophilia B. 

A more recent analysis comprising of a 4-month safety update was conducted in October 2023. This was a limited data cut primarily assessing safety. Data for the main trial endpoints were analysed but data on all trial endpoints were not assessed as part of this data-cut. Results have recently presented at the European Haematology Association meeting (June 13-16 2024). 

At the time of the October 2023 data cut-off, 107 of 116 (92.2%) of non-inhibitor participants from the pivotal study had enrolled in the OLE study (32 from the prior on-demand group and 75 from the prior prophylaxis group).  Of the 75 OLE patients who received prophylaxis in the BASIS trial OP, 58 (77.3%) had haemophilia A and 17 (22.7%) had haemophilia B.[110] 

Further demographics and baseline characteristics for the OLE patients with prior prophylaxis at OP are presented in Appendix M.1.2. 

## **B.2.7.2 Efficacy endpoints** 

## _**Original Submission – March 2023 OLE data cut**_ 

At the interim analysis data cut-off of 10[th] March 2023, 58 patients with haemophilia A or B, previously treated with prophylaxis in the BASIS trial OP, were treated with marstacimab, with a median treatment duration of 180.0 days (34.0 to 483.0 days) beyond the 12 month BASIS trial ATP. The mean percentage of missed doses was 1.2% indicating good adherence with study medication administration. As of the interim analysis data cut-off, four participants had their dose escalated from 150 mg weekly (QW) to 300 mg QW during the OLE; this is in addition to 10 participants in the BASIS trial who had their dose escalated to 300 mg QW and continued on this dose during the OLE (all eleven BASIS trial participants who had dose escalation of marstacimab continued to the OLE, however for one patient, their data were not available at the time of the interim analysis). The median exposure on the 300 mg QW dose of marstacimab was 98.0 days. All efficacy endpoints reported from the OLE includes data from individuals who received a dose escalation of marstacimab during the BASIS trial ATP or the OLE.

## **B.2.8** _**Subgroup analysis**_ 

Due to the targeting of marstacimab as a treatment for both haemophillia A and B, the BASIS study was not powered to detect differences within subgroups. Despite this, data are presented for the primary endpoint, ABRtreat, split by haemophilia A and B as well as adult and adolescent patients (Figure 10). The efficacy of marstacimab was consistent across subgroups and all point estimates of differences were consistently under 2.5, the non-inferiority margin for the primary analysis. 

Mean ABRtreat in patients with haemophilia A was 5.30 for marstacimab prophylaxis during the 12 month ATP compared with 9.16 for routine prophylaxis during the 6 month OP. For haemophilia B, mean ABRtreat was 4.71 for marstacimab prophylaxis during the 12 month ATP compared with 3.26 for routine prophylaxis during the 6 month OP. Six patients with haemophilia B increased their dose of marstacimab during the ATP; the mean ABRtreat for all 18 patients with haemophilia B during the entire ATP including the data following the dose increase was 3.88 indicating similar bleed control compared to routine prophylaxis. 

Given the lack of powering and small sample sizes associated with the subgroup analyses by haemophilia type (A or B), in particular for haemophilia B, the primary analysis of treated bleeds in the overall population is considered most relevant to this submission, and informs the base case economic analysis (see Section B.3.2). However, for completeness, scenario analyses have been conducted in which the subgroup analyses by haemophilia type are used to inform the efficacy of marstacimab and factor prophylaxis in the model.

## **B.2.9** _**Post-hoc analyses to inform cost-effectiveness model**_ 

Efficacy results from the BASIS trial, presented in Section B.2.6, censored bleeding records on or after a dose escalation to 300 mg during the ATP, as prespecified in the BASIS trial protocol. 

Additional post hoc analyses were conducted to inform the data used in the economic model; the structure of the model and rationale for these post hoc analyses is described further in Section B.3.1.2. For factor prophylaxis and marstacimab, ABRtreat and AJBRtreat reported in the BASIS ATP and OP, respectively, for patients who received routine prophylaxis during the OP, informed the rate of bleed events in the “Bleeds” health state. These were further analysed post hoc in two ways to provide the relevant inputs for the model: 

- Firstly, the ABRtreat and AJBRtreat for the model included data from all patients who received marstacimab during the ATP, including data after dose escalation for those who escalated their marstacimab dose. In comparison, the BASIS trial primary outcome ABRtreat and AJBRtreat data censored results on or after a dose escalation to 300 mg for the 11 patients who had their marstacimab dose escalated. 

- Additionally, ABRtreat and AJBRtreat for the model were measured amongst those who experienced at least one bleeding event (i.e. excluding those with zero treated bleeding events who enter the “No bleeds” health state at model entry).

## **B.2.11** _**Indirect and mixed treatment comparisons**_ 

_**Results from an unanchored indirect treatment comparison (ITC) of marstacimab and emicizumab suggest that the efficacy of marstacimab is comparable to that of emicizumab with respect to the control of bleeding events among adults or adolescents with severe haemophilia A, without inhibitors, and who received prior prophylaxis**_ 

- In the absence of head-to-head evidence between marstacimab and emicizumab, an unanchored simulated treatment comparison (STC) was conducted 

- The STC accounted for differences in important prognostic variables and treatment effect modifiers between BASIS and HAVEN 3 (Cohort D), the two studies informing efficacy for marstacimab and emicizumab respectively: prior ABRtotal, presence of target joints, age, BMI, ethnicity and race were controlled for in the outcome regression models 

- Point estimate results from the STC favoured emicizumab, which was associated with lower proportions of patients experiencing total and treated bleeds, and lower rates of treated and total bleeds 

- However, none of the results reached statistical significance, and the analysis was associated with limitations which should be acknowledged. Whilst attempts were made to account for confounding, the possibility of residual confounding remains. Additionally, differences treatment of bleeds between BASIS and HAVEN 3 may have led to an underestimation of marstacimab’s treatment effect 

Whilst the BASIS trial provides a comparison between marstacimab and factor prophylaxis products, no direct comparative evidence between marstacimab and emicizumab exists. Given this absence of direct head-to-head evidence, an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) was conducted to inform the relative efficacy estimates for marstacimab versus emicizumab in patients with haemophilia A; following a feasibility assessment, an STC was identified as the most appropriate approach. The following section provides an overview of the feasibility assessment and the subsequent STC methodology and results, with additional details presented in Appendix D. 

## **B.2.11.1 Identification of comparator data and feasibility assessment** 

As detailed in Section B.2.1 and Appendix D, a clinical SLR was conducted to identify relevant clinical evidence for adults and adolescents with severe haemophilia A or B, in line with the 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 79 -->

expected indication for marstacimab. A total of 79 unique trials reported in 333 records were included in the SLR, including two trials assessing marstacimab. 

Of the 77 comparator trials identified in the SLR, 47 studies were excluded from consideration in an ITC based on a feasibility assessment with respect to data availability, outcome measurement, geography, and trial phase. Of the remaining 30 trials, 28 were excluded because they did not report on a relevant comparator of interest. Since factor replacement therapy was evaluated in the BASIS trial, studies assessing these therapies (n=22) were not considered for inclusion into the ITC analyses. In addition, six trials were excluded because they assessed gene therapies (n=4) or rebalancing agents (n=2) which were not relevant candidate therapies for the target population of this submission. A flow chart demonstrating the initial feasibility assessment of the studies identified in the SLR for use in an ITC is presented in Appendix D, with the list of excluded studies, including reasons for exclusion, presented in Appendix D.1.3. 

The remaining two trials, HAVEN 3 and HAVEN 4, both evaluating emicizumab were identified and carried forward to the feasibility assessment (Table 33). 

## **Feasibility assessment** 

## _**Trial populations**_ 

The similarity of the HAVEN 3 and HAVEN 4 study populations to that of the BASIS trial was first assessed. HAVEN 3 and HAVEN 4 trials both exclusively enrolled individuals with haemophilia A whereas the BASIS trial included individuals with haemophilia A and B. In order to minimise any potential heterogeneity and maximise overlap of the two populations, the feasibility assessment and subsequent ITC focused on the subgroup of patients with haemophilia A in the BASIS trial. 

HAVEN-3 consisted of multiple treatment cohorts: Cohorts A and B evaluated emicizumab at two different doses in patients who received prior on-demand therapy; Cohort C evaluated no prophylaxis use in patients who received prior on-demand therapy; and Cohort D evaluated emicizumab in patients who received prior prophylaxis. Cohort D was therefore considered the only relevant cohort from the HAVEN 3 trial to the decision problem of this evaluation, and the only cohort of relevance for the feasibility assessment. 

Relative to the haemophilia A subgroup of the BASIS trial, Cohort D of the HAVEN 3 trial was found to have a comparable study population in terms of its restriction to individuals who had severe disease and who did not have inhibitors. In contrast, the HAVEN 4 trial included individuals both with or without inhibitors. Although stratified outcome data were available for the HAVEN 4 trial, baseline data were not reported for the without inhibitors subgroup. The HAVEN 4 trial was therefore excluded from the ITC analyses since the overall study population was not comparable to that of the BASIS trial and since baseline characteristics were not reported for the without inhibitor subgroup.

## _**Assessment of outcomes**_ 

Five efficacy outcomes were assessed for the ITC feasibility assessment, which were reported for both BASIS and HAVEN 3 and relevant for use in the economic model. These included ABRtotal, ABRtreat, AJBRtreat. percentage with zero total bleeding events and percentage with zero treated bleeding events. Although the definitions of these endpoints were comparable, there were notable differences in the proportion of treated versus total bleeds. Specifically, the proportion of bleeding events that were treated was considerably lower in the HAVEN 3 trial (23.9% of all bleeding events were treated) than in the BASIS trial (83.3% [haemophilia A subgroup]). Similarly, the ratio of ABRtreat versus ABRtotal was much lower in the HAVEN 3 prior prophylaxis emicizumab arm (0.48) compared with the corresponding BASIS subgroup (0.84). Clinical experts consulted for this appraisal noted that bleeds are very subjective, and the reporting of bleeds in trials can also be subjective; the experts were unable to rationalise the difference in ratio of treated bleeds to total bleeds in HAVEN 3 compared with BASIS.[68] Since such differences cannot be controlled for in an unanchored ITC, treated bleeding rates may not be directly comparable between the BASIS and HAVEN 3 trials. 

To address this issue, both total and treated bleeding events were considered as outcomes of interest in the ITC analyses. In the economic modelling, whilst the comparative ABRtreat rate ratio (RR) is used in the cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) versus emicizumab, a scenario is conducted using the comparative ABRtotal RR to explore this uncertainty (see Section B.3.10.3 for further detail). 

## _**Assessment of effect modifiers and prognostic factors**_ 

The distribution of effect modifiers and prognostic factors was compared between the HAVEN 3 and BASIS trials. Based on published literature,[116-120] input from three clinical experts, and results from regression analyses conducted using individual-level data from the BASIS trial, the following variables were identified as important effect modifiers and/or prognostic factors: 

- Prior total ABR (rate) 

- Target joints (yes/no) 

- Age (years) 

- BMI (kg/m[2] ) 

- Race/ethnicity 

Among individuals with severe haemophilia A, without inhibitors, and who received prior prophylaxis, there were clinically meaningful imbalances in the distribution of age, prior total ABR, target joints, and race/ethnicity between the HAVEN 3 and BASIS trials. Due to the presence of such imbalances, an unadjusted (naïve) ITC was considered inappropriate. 

Further information on the identification of relevant effect modifiers and prognostic variables is presented in Appendix D.1.5.1. 

## _**Summary of feasibility assessment**_ 

In summary, an ITC of marstacimab (BASIS) relative to emicizumab (HAVEN 3) with respect to total bleeding events among individuals with haemophilia A was deemed feasible. Large

between-trial differences in the distribution of effect modifiers and prognostic factors were observed which necessitates the use of population-adjustment methods to reduce bias. 

## **B.2.11.2 Methods of the indirect treatment comparison** 

## **Choice of methodology** 

A population-adjusted unanchored ITC was conducted to compare efficacy outcomes for marstacimab relative to emicizumab. Since the Phase 3 BASIS study was a single-arm crossover trial that lacked a randomised control group, methods for anchored ITCs such as a network meta-analysis or network meta-regression were not feasible. An anchored ITC based on intrapatient comparisons of the BASIS and HAVEN 3 trials was not considered due to likely differences in disease management during the non-interventional and interventional treatment periods, the reduced sample size of HAVEN 3 Cohort D compared with BASIS haemophilia A subgroup (N=48 versus N=63) and the lack of reporting of key baseline characteristics for the HAVEN 3 Cohort D intrapatient comparison. An unadjusted (naïve) unanchored ITC was also not feasible due to large imbalances in the distribution of effect modifiers and prognostic factors as noted in the feasibility assessment. 

Population adjustment was therefore necessary and, following consideration of different methods, was performed using a STC: 

- A multi-level network meta-regression (ML-NMR) was not considered for these analyses because its implementation within unanchored settings is currently under development and because it is unlikely to provide any meaningful improvements over an STC in this particular two-study setting where there is only one treatment comparison of interest.[121, 122] Moreover, the same can be said about network meta-interpolation (NMI), where its necessary data requirements also fell short in terms of its lack of development for use within unanchored settings.[30] 

- An STC was selected over a matching adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) based on recommendations from the 2020 National Institute for Health and Care Excellence Decision Support Unit (NICE-DSU) review of methods for evidence synthesis.[122] This review notes that unanchored ITCs require all prognostic factors and effect modifiers to be adjusted for, which is unlikely to be achieved in practice but the STC methodology can reduce bias in these unanchored comparisons. Additionally, it recommends that in anchored comparisons, MAICs should not be used under any circumstances and that STCs can be used for twostudy scenarios, as there is with the BASIS and HAVEN 3 trials.[122] Further, a recent publication which presents a novel methodology for the implementation of an unanchored STC states that an STC approach could be more efficient than a MAIC approach because regression-based approaches give more precise estimates.[123] Finally, conducting a MAIC was considered inappropriate due to the limited sample size and considerable lack of overlap in the distribution of baseline characteristics, with recent simulation research indicating that a MAIC performs poorly in these settings.[121] 

## **Methodology** 

## _**Study populations**_ 

The HAVEN 3 trial included four separate treatment arms for emicizumab. Three of these arms were assessed among individuals who received prior on-demand therapy, which does not reflect 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 84 -->

the current standard of care for haemophilia in the UK. As such, analyses were restricted to individuals who received prior prophylaxis in both trials (Group D of the HAVEN 3 trial). As described above, to reduce heterogeneity, the BASIS trial was also restricted to the subgroup of those with haemophilia A. 

## _**Statistical analyses**_ 

The STC was implemented in accordance with guidance from the NICE-DSU-Technical Support Document 18 (NICE DSU TSD18) using individual-level data (IPD) from the BASIS trial and aggregate-level data from the HAVEN 3 trial.[124] Given that aggregate level data for ABRtreat and ABRtotal from the HAVEN 3 trial were reported in the overall population of patients, ABRtreat and ABRtotal results from the BASIS trial in all haemophilia A patients were used (i.e., as opposed to the population of patients who experienced bleeds). 

With respect to the effect modifiers and prognostic factors identified in the feasibility assessment, prior total ABR (rate), target joints (yes/no), age (years), body mass index (BMI; kg/m[2] ), percent white, and percent Hispanic/Latino were all controlled for in the outcome regression models. Considering the number of patients included in the analyses, the list of variables can be considered a reasonable number of characteristics to adjust for. Categorical variables were modelled as indicator variables and linearity was assumed with respect to the continuous covariates. 

ABRtotal was modelled using negative binomial regression with log-time included as an offset and zero total bleeding events (Yes/No) was modelled using logistic regression. The conditional outcomes for marstacimab on the linear predictor scale (i.e., the log-rate for ABRtotal and the log odds for zero total bleeding events) were estimated at the mean values of the covariates from the HAVEN 3 trial. This estimation was accomplished using the intercept and corresponding variance estimates from the outcome regression models after centering the covariates within the BASIS trial to the mean observed values from the HAVEN 3 trial. A non-identity link function was used within the analyses, therefore the marginal and conditional outcomes of each trial may differ.[125, ] 126 

Relative treatment effects were estimated on the linear predictor scale and were expressed as RR and odds ratios (OR) for rate and binary outcomes, respectively. Both unadjusted (naïve) and adjusted effects were presented alongside the corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI) and p-values. All analyses were conducted using R.

## **B.2.11.4 Uncertainties in the indirect and mixed treatment comparisons** 

## **Strengths and weaknesses of the analyses** 

In alignment with NICE DSU TSD 18, the effect modifiers and prognostic variables to be included for adjustment were carefully considered;[124] the variables chosen to be accounted for in the analyses were identified based on an evidence-based process. The comprehensive assessment of the between study heterogeneity and potential sources of bias through the feasibility assessment represents a key strength of these analyses. 

Unanchored ITCs rely on the assumption that all prognostic variables and effect modifiers are known, observed and fully accounted for. In reality, bias due to residual confounding and unaccounted unobserved residual bias cannot be excluded from the analyses. Whilst differences such as how BASIS included patients with more severe disease at baseline than those in the HAVEN 3 trial were controlled for in the analyses there remains a risk of bias due to residual imbalances. In contrast, some geographic and temporal differences could not be fully accounted for: for example, the data cut-off of the HAVEN 3 trial was September 2017, whereas enrolment for the BASIS trial began in March 2020. Additionally, some baseline characteristics were not reported in the primary publication of the HAVEN 3 trial. 

The implementation of the STC analyses resulted in a comparison of marginal and conditional outcomes which may have introduced bias. Specifically, the outcomes from the HAVEN 3 trial corresponded to marginal outcomes whereas the STC-adjusted outcomes of the BASIS trial corresponded to conditional outcomes.[125] Since a non-identity link function was used within the analyses, the marginal and conditional outcomes of each trial may differ.[125, 126] Due to the current implementation of the STC, there is therefore a risk of bias due to potential differences between the marginal and conditional outcomes. 

In order to reduce heterogeneity in the analyses, the BASIS trial population was restricted to those with haemophilia A, without inhibitors and having previously receiving FVIII prophylaxis only, to align with the HAVEN 3 trial Cohort D. The BASIS trial however was not designed to detect subgroup differences based on haemophilia type, and the reduced sample size resulted in wide confidence intervals. 

Finally, as noted in Section B.2.11.1, there were notable differences in terms of the ratio between ABRtotal and ABRtreat between the BASIS and HAVEN 3 trials, with substantially fewer bleeds being treated in the HAVEN 3 trial. This indicates that there are important trial differences in the 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 88 -->

clinical management of bleeding events, and as such, the comparative results from the ABRtreat STC may not be reflective of the true comparative efficacy of marstacimab and emicizumab; the comparison of ABRtotal may therefore provide a more accurate reflection of the comparative efficacy. To address this uncertainty, scenarios are conducted in the CEA to explore the impact of the different ORs (see Section B.3.10.3 for further detail). 

## **Summary of results of the ITCs** 

Overall, the results of the ITC presented above show emicizumab being associated with numerical improvements in ABRs (total and treated) and numerically lower proportions of patients experiencing bleeds (total and treated). However, no results reached statistical significance, meaning that the true difference in treatment effect between both treatments is associated with important uncertainty. Furthermore, whilst important differences in prognostic variables and effect modifiers were adjusted for, important differences in methodology and treatment practices between trials may exist, which cannot be accounted for within the STC and available data. In particular, treatment of bleeds may have differed between BASIS and HAVEN 3, likely leading to greater differences in treated bleed rates and proportion of patients experiencing treated bleeds, as compared with total bleeds. 

## **B.2.12** _**Adverse reactions**_ 

_**The BASIS trial safety analysis results showed that marstacimab is well tolerated with no notable safety findings. Marstacimab exhibited an acceptable safety profile when compared with factor prophylaxis.**_ 

- Ninety-one participants with prior prophylactic factor treatment entered the study, of whom 84 completed the 6 month OP. Eighty-three participants then entered the ATP of whom 78 completed the 12 month analysis period. One patient discontinued from the ATP due to an adverse event, meningioma, however this was not considered treatment related 

- Treatment emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 22.0% of patients during the 6 month OP and 74.7% of patients during the 12 month marstacimab ATP. TEAEs in the OP were mild or moderate with only one patient reporting a TEAE of Grade 3 severity 

- Seven participants reported serious adverse events during the marstacimab ATP, with one (Grade 1 peripheral calf swelling) considered by the investigator to be treatment related 

- No thrombosis events or deaths were reported during the BASIS trial 

- Forty-six patients reported adverse events of special interest (AESIs) during the 12 month marstacimab ATP. COVID-19 infection was the most common AESI, occurring in 18 (21.7%) patients in the ATP 

- The overall safety profile of marstacimab is considered manageable and tolerable in this patient population, with no new safety signals identified 

## **B.2.12.1 Clinical safety results** 

The safety data presented in this section are based on data reported in the BASIS trial. In the BASIS trial, adverse events (AEs) during the 6 month OP were collected during two clinic visits and three phone calls, whereas AEs during the 12 month ATP were collected during nine clinic visits and five phone calls. 

With consideration to the differences in study phase duration, frequency of study visits, opportunities to report AEs and external factors, marstacimab exhibits an acceptable safety profile versus standard of care.

## **B.2.14** _**Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence**_ 

## **Clinical efficacy for marstacimab** 

The clinical efficacy and safety evidence for marstacimab as a treatment for severe haemophilia is derived from the BASIS trial. In BASIS, patients received treatment with routine factor prophylaxis during the 6 month OP, followed by treatment with marstacimab in the 12 month ATP. Results from the BASIS trial showed marstacimab to be effective at controlling patient bleeding. Marstacimab demonstrated non-inferiority and superiority over routine prophylaxis as measured by ABRtreat, the primary endpoint of the BASIS trial. The mean model-based estimated ABRtreat for marstacimab prophylaxis during the ATP was 5.08 (95% CI: 3.40, 6.77) compared with 7.85 (95% CI: 5.09, 10.61) for routine prophylaxis during the OP, equating to a 35.2% (95% CI: 5.6, 55.6) decrease. 

Marstacimab also demonstrated non-inferiority to factor prophylaxis in all bleed-related secondary efficacy outcomes, reducing the incidence of AJBRtreat, ABRtarget joint, ABRspontaneous and ABRtotal from the OP to the ATP. Importantly, reductions in joint bleeds following treatment with marstacimab were reflected in improved HJHS reported by patients completing the ATP, with an estimated median difference between marstacimab and routine factor prophylaxis of –2.2 (95% CI: –4.8, 0.3). The efficacy of marstacimab was consistent across subgroups and all point estimates of differences were consistently under 2.5, the non-inferiority margin for the primary analysis. These results provide strong evidence for marstacimab’s ability to maintain or improve patients’ joint health, an important treatment goal in haemophilia (see Section B.1.3.1.4). 

The improvements in measured efficacy outcomes associated with marstacimab were accompanied with numerically improved HRQoL measures across a variety of patient surveys, both general and specific to haemophilia. 

## **Comparative efficacy for marstacimab** 

The BASIS trial provides direct, intrapatient comparative efficacy evidence for marstacimab versus factor prophylaxis in patients with severe haemophilia without inhibitors. As described above, results from the OP and ATP of the BASIS trial show marstacimab to be associated with statistically significant reductions in treated bleed rates, the primary outcome in the BASIS trial This was accompanied by numerical improvements in total bleeds, joint bleeds, and HRQoL outcomes. 

In the absence of direct comparative efficacy evidence for marstacimab versus emicizumab in patients with severe haemophilia A, an unanchored STC was conducted to estimate relative efficacy of each treatment. The STC adjusted for differences in a number of important prognostic variables and treatment effect modifiers between BASIS and HAVEN 3 (Cohort D), the two trials which informed the comparison. Results from an unanchored ITC of marstacimab and emicizumab suggest that the efficacy of marstacimab is comparable to that of emicizumab with respect to the control of bleeding events among adults or adolescents with severe haemophilia 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 95 -->

A, without inhibitors, and who received prior prophylaxis. Residual confounding post-adjustment cannot be ruled out, and the analyses were subject to limitations which could not be overcome. As such, the STC provides a plausible but uncertain estimate of relative treatment efficacy between marstacimab and emicizumab. The STC informs the comparison between marstacimab and emicizumab in the economic model (see Sections B.3.2.2 and B.3.2.3), however scenario analyses have been conducted exploring different assumptions around the relative efficacy of each treatment. 

## **Safety evidence for marstacimab** 

The BASIS safety analysis results showed that marstacimab is well tolerated with no notable safety findings. Marstacimab exhibited an acceptable safety profile when compared with factor prophylaxis. The most frequently observed treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) (≥ 5%) during the 12 month marstacimab ATP were pruritus, upper respiratory tract infection, joint range of motion decreased, headache, contusion, and events related to COVID-19. There were no thrombosis events or deaths in patients without inhibitors, with only one SAE deemed to be treatment related. 

## **B.2.14.1 Conclusions** 

BASIS is a methodologically robust and well-reported trial, and the results reported demonstrate that marstacimab provides significant improvements in ABRtreat, and clinically meaningful improvements in ABRtotal and AJBRtreat for adults and adolescents with severe haemophilia compared with currently available factor prophylaxis treatments. These benefits have been demonstrated to continue in the OLE of the BASIS trial. Furthermore, marstacimab has a tolerable and manageable safety profile and does not present any additional safety signals compared with currently available treatment options. 

Data for marstacimab from the BASIS trial provide strong evidence to suggest it would be a valuable addition to the treatment pathway for individuals with severe haemophilia without inhibitors, offering a conveniently administered prophylaxis therapy to patients with a high existing treatment burden.

## **B.3 Cost effectiveness** 

_**Model structure and approach**_ 

- A cost-effectiveness model was developed to assess the cost-effectiveness of marstacimab for the treatment of severe haemophilia 

- • The model adopted a Markov approach with three health states (“Bleeds” [consisting of treated bleeds, both joint and non-joint], “No bleeds” and an absorbing “Dead” state), over a lifetime time horizon 

- • Separate analyses are presented for patients with severe haemophilia A and those with severe haemophilia B, given the different comparator treatments used in each subpopulation. The base case analysis assumes a common treatment effect across haemophilia A and B for marstacimab and factor prophylaxis, in line with the evidence base from the BASIS trial. 

- • Three comparators were modelled: emicizumab and a basket of FVIII prophylaxis therapies in haemophilia A; and a basket of FIX prophylaxis therapies in haemophilia B. The two baskets of FVIII and FIX therapies were weighted according to real-world market share data in the UK in haemophilia A and B, respectively. 

- • Efficacy for factor prophylaxis treatments and marstacimab was informed by data collected following the OP and ATP of the Phase 3 BASIS trial (Section B.2.3), respectively. The efficacy of emicizumab was informed by a simulated treatment comparison (STC), using BASIS and relevant clinical trials 

- • Health state utility values (HSUVs) were the same in the “Bleeds” and “No Bleeds” health states, derived from EQ-5D data collected at baseline in the ATP of the BASIS trial. Differentiation in utility between treatments was derived from disutility reported in external sources applied to bleed events experienced by patients in the “Bleeds” health state and treatment administrationrelated utility decrements for each IV and SC injection. 

- • Costs included in the model comprised drug acquisition costs and treatment management costs of acute bleed events 

- _**Cost-effectiveness analysis results**_ • Marstacimab was found to be more effective and less costly than both FVIII and FIX prophylaxis comparator baskets (i.e. dominant) across analyses conducted; in the base case, marstacimab (with PAS) was associated with positive deterministic NHB versus FVIII and FIX prophylaxis of ***** and ******, respectively, at a WTP of £30,000 per QALY gained 

- • Versus emicizumab, marstacimab resulted in fewer QALYs but was less costly, resulting in a positive deterministic NHB of ****** at a WTP of £30,000 saved per QALY forgone 

- • In probabilistic sensitivity analyses, marstacimab had a 100% probability of being cost-effective against all comparators, and the deterministic sensitivity analyses demonstrated that the model was largely robust to individual parameter uncertainty 

- • Conducted scenario analyses additionally demonstrated that marstacimab remained costeffective versus all comparators 

- _**Overall, marstacimab for the treatment of severe haemophilia, can be considered a costeffective use of NHS resources, whilst also expanding the choice of therapies available to both patients with haemophilia and their clinicians, offering a convenient, easy-toadminister prophylaxis therapy.**_ 

## **B.3.1** _**Published cost-effectiveness studies**_ 

An SLR was conducted in August 2020 and updated in May 2024 in order to identify economic evidence in the field of haemophilia. Literature searches were conducted for cost-effectiveness studies (Appendix G), utility studies (Appendix H) and HCRU studies (Appendix I), with each record identified assessed for eligibility for inclusion on the SLR. 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 97 -->

Across all three evidence streams in the original SLR, a total of 5,519 records were retrieved from the electronic databases, of which 2,611 were duplicates, resulting in 2,908 novel records that were screened at the title/abstract review stage. Subsequently, 663 full publications were screened against the eligibility criteria for all 3 SLRs at full-text review. Following this, 387 publications were excluded. 276 publications were included in total, comprising of 151 haemophilia A studies, 58 haemophilia B studies and 67 studies reporting on non-separable haemophilia. 

A total of 192 publications did not report relevant economic outcomes, resulting in 84 publications being included in the review. To prioritise evidence most relevant to this submission, included records were prioritised for extraction if they were key studies informing the structure of the economic model in this submission, or informed utilities or costs in the economic model. This resulted in prioritisation of data extraction of four articles from the original SLR. Following pooling of records across all three evidence streams, a total of 2,831 records were retrieved from the electronic databases, of which 1,495 were duplicates (including duplicates against the original SLR searches), resulting in 1,336 novel records that were screened at the title/abstract review stage. Subsequently, 284 full publications were screened against the eligibility criteria for all three evidence streams at full-text review. 

In total, 134 articles reporting included in the SLR. A full list of these studies is presented in Appendix G. No prior economic evaluations were identified for marstacimab in the population of relevance to this submission. Therefore, a _de novo_ health economic analysis was conducted for the purpose of this appraisal. 

In line with the NICE reference case, the analysis of costs was conducted from the perspective of the NHS and Personal Social Services (PSS) in the UK and included direct medical costs over a lifetime horizon.[12] 

## **B.3.1.1 Patient population** 

In line with the decision problem addressed in this submission (Section B.1.1), and the anticipated licensed indication for marstacimab, the modelled population included patients aged 12 and above, with documented severe haemophilia (defined as <1% circulating factor level) without factor inhibitors. 

The model considers two populations, differentiated by haemophilia type, A and B. Marstacimab is the intervention of interest in both populations, whilst different comparators are considered in each population: emicizumab and FVIII prophylaxis in haemophilia A, and FIX prophylaxis in haemophilia B (see Section B.3.1.3). Given clinical feedback indicating that no differences in marstacimab treatment effect would be expected between haemophilia A and B, a common marstacimab treatment effect is assumed across both populations in the base case analysis, in line with the evidence base from the BASIS trial. Similarly, clinical advisors consulted for this appraisal agreed that it is appropriate to assume all factor replacement products are equal in efficacy.[68] Therefore the same treatment effect is assumed for all FVIII and FIX prophylaxes in haemophilia A and B respectively, derived from the BASIS trial (see Section B.3.2). A number of scenario analyses around the efficacy assumptions for marstacimab and the comparators, including separate efficacy inputs for haemophilia A and B and across SHLs and EHLs, were also explored (see Section B.3.2.4).

## **B.3.1.2 Model structure** 

A cohort disease state transition model was built in Microsoft Excel[®] and followed a Markov structure. 

## **Justification of model structure** 

The use of a state transition model structure (Markov or semi-Markov) is consistent with previous cost-effectiveness models in haemophilia, which have followed either a cohort approach[128, 129] or microsimulation[130, 131] (where individual patients are simulated through the health states). Justifications provided for the use of a more complex microsimulation approach included incorporating patient heterogeneity and patient history into the disease course.[130, 131] A cohort Markov state transition model was deemed sufficient to capture relevant outcomes over time and thus was used in this appraisal, in line with the NICE haemophilia appraisals of etranacogene dezaparvovec (ID3812), fidanacogene elaparvovec (ID4032) and efanesoctocog alfa (ID6170).[9, ] 10, 84 

There is no set consensus on the structure of cost-effectiveness models to assess interventions in haemophilia across previously published literature.[128, 129, 131-133] However, the occurrence of bleeds remains a consistent factor in the models identified, as well as forming the primary endpoint of the BASIS trial and comparator trials, leading to its selection as the focus of this model. The economic model for marstacimab was composed of three health states: two defined by the presence or absence of bleeds (“Bleeds” and “No bleeds”), and an absorbing “Dead” state, as described below. This model structure is similar to a model submitted to Canada’s Drug and Health Technology Agency (CADTH) for emicizumab, which utilised a simple approach in which the only health states were “Alive” and “Dead”, accounting for the occurrence of bleeds within the “Alive” state.[134] 

The model structure is aligned with that used in the ongoing appraisals for fidanacogene elaparvovec as a treatment for haemophilia B (ID4032) and efanescotocog alfa as a treatment for haemophilia A (ID6170).[9, 84] Both the fidanacogene elaparvovec and efanesoctocog alfa models also consisted of “Bleeds” and “No bleeds” health states, with patients able to transition between the bleeds and no bleeds health states. 

The economic model submitted in the prior NICE appraisal of etranacogene dezaparvovec (ID3812) included health states according to the occurrence of bleeds, with transition to the separate bleed health states being determined by annual (joint) bleed rates: “No bleed”, “Bleed (joint)”, “Bleed (not joint)” and “Death”.[10] This means that joint and non-joint bleeds are assumed to be mutually exclusive, with a steady-state distribution modelled across the “Bleed (joint)” and “Bleed (not joint)” health states.[10] ** ********* ** *** ************ *********** ******** ****** ****** ******** *** ****** **** ******* ****** ****** **** ********* **** * ****** ******** ****** ****** ***** ******** *** ******* ** ********** ** ******* ****** ** ***** *** ********* ****** *** ***** *** ********* ***** ***** *** ********** ** *** ********** ******* ******** *** *****[**] The _de novo_ model mirrors that of fidanacogene elaparvovec (ID4032) and efanescotocog alfa (ID6170), using the single “Bleeds” health state (see Section B.3.2.3). 

Prior models in haemophilia have used ABRtotal to inform the various “Bleeds” and “No Bleeds” health states in their structures.[9, 10, 84] The marstacimab model however utilises ABRtreat in the efficacy analysis. The choice of modelling treated rather than total bleeds in this evaluation instead, was made to align with the primary outcome in the BASIS trial, and to reflect the fact that 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 99 -->

bleed events in the model incur treatment costs (see Section B.3.4.2). Furthermore, treated bleeds are likely to have a greater impact on patients’ lives than those not requiring treatment, and were therefore considered a more meaningful outcome, better able to reflect treatment impact on patients’ QoL. 

Joint health and its progression have also been incorporated in previous cost-effectiveness models in haemophilia, by tracking target joint status,[132] Pettersson score,[129] or joint surgery and joint damage as health states.[130] In this model, any impact associated with joint pain is assumed to be implicitly included in the utility values. This is similar to the approach taken in the models submitted as part of the NICE evaluations for etranacogene dezaparvovec (ID3812),[10] fidanacogene elaparvovec (ID4032)[84] and efanescotocog alfa (ID6170)[9] where the benefit of preventing joint damage and associated joint replacement surgeries was excluded due to data limitations. As marstacimab has been shown to reduce AJBR compared with prophylactic factor replacement in the BASIS trial (Section B.2.6) and maintain these improvements when continuing marstacimab up to an additional 16 months (Section B.2.7.2), it is therefore expected that patients may receive additional long-term benefit by the reduction of joint damage not captured in the economic model. Improvements in joint health in the short term may translate to long-term reductions in joint pain, improved mobility, and better quality of life. Additionally, if patients experienced fewer joint surgeries, this could be expected to provide cost-savings for the health system. Therefore, the decision to not include the occurrence of, or costs associated with, joint damage in the model could be considered a conservative assessment of the costeffectiveness of marstacimab. 

## **Model health states and patient flow** 

At model entry, patients receiving factor prophylaxis or marstacimab are distributed among the “No bleeds” and “Bleeds” health states, based on the BASIS OP and ATP trial results, respectively, for the proportion of patients with zero _treated_ bleeding events. For emicizumab, health state occupation was derived by applying an odds ratio to the health state distribution of marstacimab patients (see B.3.2.2). The odds ratio was derived from the STC using IPD from BASIS and cohort-level data from HAVEN 3 (see Section B.2.11). In the factor prophylaxis and emicizumab arms, distribution across the “No bleeds” and “Bleeds” health states is unchanged across the model time horizon, and patients are assumed to remain on treatment whilst alive. In the marstacimab arm of the model, health state distribution is assumed to remain constant over time whilst on treatment; subsequent redistribution across these health states occurs to reflect discontinuation, as described in Section B.2.12.1. 

Within the “Bleeds” health state, both joint and non-joint treated bleeds are considered. ABRtreat and AJBRtreat were estimated from post-hoc analyses of the BASIS trial for marstacimab and factor prophylaxis, and from the ITC for emicizumab (see Section B.3.2). An overview of the model health states is provided below and in Figure 11: 

- **No bleeds:** Patients with no bleeding events. 

- **Bleeds:** Patients are assumed to experience an average number of bleeds annually within this state. The average number of bleeds per annual cycle is assumed to remain constant, with no natural increase in bleed likelihood. Within this state, ABRtreat and AJBRtreat were modelled separately to inform corresponding costs and utility decrements per bleed event, as described in Section B.3.2.3. The model applies costs and disutilities associated with these acute bleed events.

## **Features of the cost-effectiveness analysis** 

Costs and health-related utilities were allocated to each health state and multiplied by state occupancy to calculate the weighted costs and QALYs per cycle. The analysis was conducted from the perspective of the NHS in England, including direct medical costs and PSS costs over a lifetime horizon of the patient cohort from the initiation of treatment, in line with the ongoing etranacogene dezaparvovec (ID3812) and fidanacogene elaparvovec (ID4032) evaluations, and the NICE reference case.[10, 12] A one-year cycle length was selected to align with the period of time over which the primary endpoint of the Phase 3 BASIS trial was assessed and to align with the unit of measurement defining health states, ABRtreat, which is also the principal outcome of interest in clinical trials in haemophilia. Whilst the one-year cycle length is not aligned with the administration schedule of products used for prophylaxis, patients receiving prophylaxis are not modelled as being able to alter their administration schedule and are assumed to receive continuous treatment throughout the model time horizon. Within this model framework, a oneweek model cycle is not necessary to model prophylaxis administration; this would yield the same costs as with a one-year model cycle, whilst adding additional modelling complexity. Costs and utilities associated with short-term events, i.e., a single acute treated bleed event, are therefore accumulated over a year based on the number of events per year, rather than modelled explicitly as one-off events. A half-cycle correction was applied to account for the fact that clinical events can occur at any point during the cycle, not necessarily at the start or end of each cycle. An annual discount rate of 3.5% was applied to both costs and benefits, in line with the NICE reference case.[12] The key features of the economic analysis are summarised in Table 47.

## **B.3.1.3 Intervention technology and comparators** 

## **Marstacimab** 

The intervention considered in the cost effectiveness analysis was marstacimab. The model included the recommended marstacimab dose, administered as a weekly 150 mg SC injection following an initial one-off loading dose of 300 mg, in line with the dosing regimen included in the Phase 3 BASIS trial and the draft SmPC.[5, 104] 

In line with the BASIS trial protocol and draft SmPC, the model base case also included a proportion of patients receiving 300 mg weekly to account for patients who had their dose of marstacimab escalated. Dose escalation was determined by clinician discretion, with criteria including patients experiencing two or more spontaneous bleeds (joint bleeds or significant soft tissue/muscle or other site bleeds) treated with infusion(s) of FVIII or FIX over a 6 month period. Eleven patients (13%) in the BASIS trial ATP had their marstacimab dose escalated from 150 mg to 300 mg weekly. 

Efficacy data in the model for marstacimab were derived from post-hoc analyses of the BASIS Phase 3 trial, inclusive of data from eleven patients who received dose escalation, as presented in Section B.2.9. A scenario analysis was also conducted in which no marstacimab dose escalation was modelled; in this scenario, efficacy data in the model were informed by post hoc analyses of the BASIS trial, in which bleeding records on or after a dose escalation to 300 mg during the ATP were censored. Efficacy data informing this scenario are presented in Appendix N.1. 

## **Comparators** 

## **Factor prophylaxis** 

As detailed in Section B.1.3.2.2, prophylactic factor therapy represents an important treatment option in haemophilia in the UK. The basket comparators consisting of FVIII and FIX treatments reflect this established clinical management for people with severe haemophilia A and B, respectively, in the UK. This approach was taken to align with the requested analysis from the committee in the ongoing evaluation of etranacogene dezaparvovec (ID3812),[10] in which a comparison versus a comparator basket was requested. The committee considered that using a basket of prophylaxis treatments weighted by NHS market share was the most appropriate comparator for the economic modelling and best reflects the most commonly used treatments in clinical practice.[11] This approach was further validated by clinicians consulted as part of this appraisal, who agreed that assuming equal efficacy across factor treatments was an appropriate approach.[68] The treatments included are in line with UK clinical recommendations developed by the BSH, expert clinical opinion, and real-world treatment sales data derived from the IQVIA MIDAS database. As described in Section B.1.3.2.2, currently available recombinant factor therapies include SHL products and EHL products.[13, 14] In haemophilia A, SHL products require administration 3 to 4 times a week, while EHL products are typically administered twice weekly.[69-] 75 In haemophilia B, SHL products can require administration twice per week, whilst EHL products are typically administered at frequencies from once a week to once every two weeks for those whose bleeding is well controlled.[76-79] 

Each factor basket comparator includes SHL and EHL products relevant to UK clinical practice, as presented in Table 48. The FVIII basket includes four SHL products and three EHL products.

As described in Section B.1.3.2.3, management of haemophilia in the UK may also involve ondemand administration of factor replacement products, either on its own or in addition to factor prophylaxis, with the aim of stopping bleeding once it has occurred, as may be required following trauma or surgery.[81] On-demand treatment on its own is therefore not recommended for use in severe haemophilia, as per WFH and BSH guidelines.[13, 14] The low usage of on-demand factor treatment in UK clinical practice was confirmed by clinicians.[68] In addition, patients enrolled in the BASIS trial had received at least six months of treatment with prophylaxis (the lead-in period) before marstacimab administration. Therefore, on-demand factor therapy was not included as a standalone comparator in this submission, in line with the etranacogene dezaparvovec and fidanacogene elaparvovec NICE appraisals (ID3812, ID4032).[10][84] On-demand factor therapy alongside marstacimab and comparator therapies has been included in the model in the form of acute bleed event management costs, as described in Section B.3.4.2. 

## **Emicizumab** 

As detailed in Section B.1.3.2.4, emicizumab, administered as a SC prophylactic therapy, also represents a key comparator in the population of patients with haemophilia A. Based on the previously mentioned IQVIA sales data, emicizumab makes up ** ** *** of prophylactic therapies administered to patients with haemophilia A in the UK.[80] Emicizumab is given as a 3 mg/kg dose once weekly for the first four weeks (loading dose), followed by a maintenance dose from Week 5, of either 1.5 mg/kg once weekly, 3 mg/kg every two weeks, or 6 mg/kg every four weeks, with all doses administered as a SC injection. 

## **B.3.2** _**Clinical parameters and variables**_ 

## **B.3.2.1 Baseline characteristics** 

The baseline characteristics for the modelled population in terms of age and weight were derived from UKHCDO analysis and can be found in Table 51. Patients enrolled in the BASIS trial were younger and had a lower mean body weight compared with UKHCDO data. Therefore, to ensure the baseline characteristics in the model are most aligned with the UK clinical population, the baseline characteristics of patients studied in the UKHCDO analysis were used.[40] Clinical experts consulted as part of this submission agreed that the average body weight derived from the UKHCDO of **** kg was more representative of their patients’ weight than that in the BASIS study.[68] The mean age in the UKHCDO and BASIS trial were very similar (**** and 33.0 years, respectively), however a scenario analysis was conducted in which the age in the BASIS trial was used instead. All patients were modelled as male, in line with the population enrolled in the BASIS trial. However, as noted in Sections B.1.1 and B.1.4, this evaluation is not expected to exclude the small number of female patients living with haemophilia.

## **B.3.2.2 Health state distributions** 

## **Starting model health state distributions** 

## _**Marstacimab and factor prophylaxis**_ 

At model entry, patients are distributed among the “No bleeds” and “Bleeds” health states. In the intervention arm, the starting proportion of patients in each health state is informed by the proportion of patients who reported no treated bleed events following treatment with marstacimab during the ATP in the BASIS trial. As noted in Section B.3.1.2, this analysis includes data from all patients who received marstacimab in the ATP, including data for those who received a dose escalation. Whilst differing from the primary analysis of treated bleeds in the BASIS trial, which censored data for patients after they received dose escalation, this analysis was chosen to inform bleed rates in the model to reflect the efficacy of dose escalation observed in the trial, and detailed in the draft SmPC for marstacimab.[5] This aligns with the approach taken to marstacimab costs, which reflect the dose escalation seen in the trial (Section B.3.4.1). ************ ***** ***** 

**** ******** ** *** ***** ****** **** *** ******** ********** ******* ********** *** *** *** ** ****** ***** **** 

**** *** ******** ** ******* ***** **** * ******* ***** ****** ** *** ***** ***** .[8] 

The proportion of patients experiencing no treated bleed events in those receiving marstacimab and factor prophylaxis is shown in Table 52. 

It should also be noted that a discrepancy exists between the timepoints of assessments informing the proportion of patients experiencing zero bleeds at model entry for factor treatments and marstacimab. For factor prophylaxis, this was measured following six months of treatment in the BASIS OP, as opposed to 12 months in the BASIS ATP for marstacimab. Therefore, patients in the BASIS OP may have subsequently experienced a bleed(s) had the OP lasted 12 months, prior to initiating treatment with marstacimab. Consequently, the proportion of patients experiencing zero bleeds with factor prophylaxis in the model may be an underestimate. Whilst this represents an inherent limitation of the available data, the use of a shorter period of assessment for factor prophylaxis to inform the model health state distribution should be considered a conservative approach.

This method of deriving comparator treatment effect for emicizumab ensures that the relative effects of the treatments, adjusted for differences in confounding variables, are maintained and applied to the population informing the model. However, certain limitations of this method should be recognised. 

The unanchored STC method used to derive relative treatment effect assumes that all effect modifiers and prognostic variables have been accounted for. Whilst the analysis adjusted for important differences between the BASIS and HAVEN 3 populations, residual confounding cannot be ruled out. Furthermore, the ITC analyses of the proportion of treated bleeds did not reach statistical significance following adjustment, meaning a high degree of uncertainty exists surrounding the true treatment effect of marstacimab relative to emicizumab. 

The resulting odds of experiencing no treated bleed events were used to derive the proportion of patients experiencing no treated bleed events of emicizumab, which are shown alongside the intervention in Table 52.

In order to align with the chosen model structure based on treated bleeds, the relative efficacy of treated bleeds from the STC was used to inform the relative proportion of emicizumab patients in the “Bleeds” and “No Bleeds” health states at model entry. The ITC predicted a lower odds ratio of treated bleeds compared with total bleeds (see Section B.2.11.3), indicating fewer bleeds were treated in HAVEN 3 compared with BASIS. Clinical experts consulted for this appraisal noted that bleeds are very subjective, and the reporting of bleeds in trials can also be subjective; the experts were unable to rationalise the difference in ratio of treated bleeds to total bleeds in HAVEN 3 compared with BASIS.[68] An alternative source of comparative efficacy was therefore explored in a scenario analysis, where the odds ratio for the proportion of patients experiencing no total bleeds was instead used to inform the starting distributions for patients receiving emicizumab in the model (see Section B.3.10.3). Considering the non-significance of the ITC results, an additional scenario was also conducted in which no difference in efficacy between marstacimab and emicizumab was assumed. 

## **Health state transitions** 

As noted in the description of the model structure in Section B.3.1.2 above, the model allows for patients in the intervention arm to transition between health states, in order to account for discontinuation of treatment. In the intervention arm, 6.02% of marstacimab patients are modelled as discontinuing from treatment and returning to factor prophylaxis as a one-off event in the first model cycle. This was derived from marstacimab discontinuation rates during the year- 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 110 -->

long ATP of the BASIS trial.[104] In the comparisons versus haemophilia A comparators (FVIII prophylaxis and emicizumab), patients who discontinue are then assumed to experience the bleed rate and costs associated with FVIII prophylaxis, supported by clinical feedback that haemophilia A patients would most likely return to factor prophylaxis upon discontinuation.[68] In the comparison versus the haemophilia B comparator (FIX prophylaxis), discontinuing patients experience the bleed rate and costs associated with FIX prophylaxis. Clinical feedback indicated that any discontinuation from marstacimab is likely to occur early on, therefore the base case approach does not consider subsequent discontinuation from marstacimab following the first model cycle.[68] Scenario analyses exploring this assumption were conducted and are described in Section B.3.2.5. 

To model discontinuation, the proportion of patients discontinuing marstacimab is redistributed between the "Bleeds" and "No Bleeds" health states to match the health state distribution in the factor prophylaxis comparator arms (FVIII and FIX prophylaxis in the haemophilia A and B comparisons, respectively). The proportion of discontinuing patients experiencing treated bleeds experience ABRtreat associated with the factor prophylaxis basket they discontinue on to. Clinical expert opinion received as part of this submission indicated that very few patients receiving emicizumab would be expected to discontinue treatment in clinical practice,[68] therefore no discontinuation is modelled from emicizumab in the model, with all patients receiving treatment throughout the model time horizon. 

The distribution amongst health states in the model of patients receiving factor prophylaxis is assumed to remain constant over the model time horizon. This is in line with the assumption that patients receiving factor prophylaxis experience constant bleed rates throughout the model time horizon, the rationale for which is detailed further in Section B.3.2.3 below. 

## **B.3.2.3 Annualised bleeding rates and annualised joint bleeding rates** 

## **Marstacimab and factor prophylaxis** 

As described in Section B.3.1.2, patients are assumed to experience an average number of treated bleeds annually within the “Bleeds” health state. Within this state, joint and non-joint bleed rates were modelled separately to inform corresponding costs and utility decrements per joint and non-joint bleed events. 

Within each health state, treated bleed rates were modelled as treatment-specific. For factor prophylaxis and marstacimab, post hoc analyses of ABRtreat and AJBRtreat in the BASIS ATP and OP respectively informed the rate of bleed events in the “Bleeds” health state. As presented in Section B.2.9, the post hoc analyses included all patients who received marstacimab during the ATP, i.e. including those who received dose escalation of marstacimab. Additionally, ABRtreat was measured amongst those who experienced at least one bleeding event (i.e. excluding those with zero treated bleeding events who enter the “No bleeds” health state at model entry, see Section B.3.1.2). 

The rate of non-joint events was calculated by subtracting the post hoc analysed AJBRtreat from ABRtreat. Annual joint and non-joint bleed rates were then multiplied by the respective costs and disutilities for each treated bleed event type to inform per-cycle costs and QALYs as reported in later sections of this submission. ABRtreat and AJBRtreat input bleeding rates for marstacimab and the factor comparator baskets are presented in Table 53.
