As with the odds ratio of treated bleeds, the ratio of ABRtreat between marstacimab and emicizumab may be overestimated, due to differences in treatment of bleeds in the BASIS and HAVEN 3 trials informing the ITC analysis (see Section B.2.11.4). In the scenario analysis described in Section B.3.2.2, in which the odds ratio of the proportion of patients with no total (rather than treated bleeds) is used, the same approach is used to derive ABRs associated with emicizumab, using the rate ratio of total rather than treated bleeds (scenario number 12 in Table 76). 

The average number of bleeds per cycle is assumed to remain constant in each treatment arm, with no natural increase in bleed likelihood. The rationale for this approach is as follows. The bleed rates of patients have historically improved, likely due to an increased uptake of prophylaxis and improvement in management generally and individualised treatment optimisation strategies, which have helped patients better manage their disease.[47] ,[143, 144] Recent studies reporting longitudinal data of patients with haemophilia A suggest that bleed rates do not further improve with the current SOC prophylaxis.[145, 146] Furthermore, a constant bleed distribution approach is consistent with previous cost-effectiveness models in haemophilia, which did not consider a change in the ABR over time for patients receiving prophylaxis.[129-131] 

## **B.3.2.4 Scenario efficacy analyses** 

As described in Sections B.2.9, B.3.2.2 and B.3.2.3, additional post hoc analyses from the BASIS trial are used to inform the efficacy of marstacimab and factor prophylaxis in the base case costeffectiveness analyses. ABRtreat and AJBRtreat reported in the BASIS ATP and OP, respectively, for patients who received routine prophylaxis during the OP, informed the rate of bleed events in the “Bleeds” health state. These were further analysed post hoc in two ways to provide the relevant inputs for the model: 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 112 -->

- Firstly, the ABRtreat and AJBRtreat for the model included all patients who received marstacimab during the ATP, including the 11 patients who escalated their marstacimab dose. 

- Additionally, ABRtreat and AJBRtreat for the model were measured amongst those who experienced at least one bleeding event (i.e. excluding those with zero treated bleeding events who enter the “No bleeds” health state at model entry). 

In line with the primary outcomes from the BASIS trial, these data include patients with both haemophilia A and B, providing one pooled efficacy regardless of haemophilia type. This approach is aligned with clinical feedback indicating that no differences in marstacimab treatment effect would be expected between haemophilia A and B, and that it is appropriate to assume all factor replacement products are equal in efficacy.[68] 

A number of scenarios were conducted to explore the uncertainty in key assumptions related to the efficacy estimates in the model. Each of these are described below, with the data informing these scenarios presented in Appendix N. 

## _**Scenario analysis excluding dose escalation**_ 

To align with the primary outcome of the BASIS trial, a scenario was conducted using post hoc efficacy data excluding those who escalated their marstacimab dose. The costs of marstacimab treatment are also updated in this scenario, with all patients receiving the 150 mg dose. 

## _**Scenario analyses by type of haemophilia**_ 

It is acknowledged that differences in point estimates of marstacimab’s treatment effect relative to factor prophylaxis were seen in subgroup analyses of the BASIS trial across haemophilia A and B (see Section B.2.8 above). The results of these subgroup analyses should be interpreted with caution for the following two reasons: 1) these are informed by very small patient numbers (particularly in the haemophilia B subgroup [n=18]) and were not powered to detect statistically significant differences between marstacimab and factor prophylaxis; 2) clinical feedback received as part of this submission indicated that there was no biological reason identified which could explain the different point estimates seen in each haemophilia type subgroup, and that these could most likely be attributed to the small sample sizes at play leading to random variation in observed efficacy.[68] 

The overall efficacy estimates derived from the trial are considered to be most appropriate to model treatment efficacy for marstacimab, and FVIII and FIX prophylaxis. Clinical experts also agreed that using the overall clinical trial data to inform efficacy for factor prophylaxis products was appropriate for this submission.[68] Nonetheless, scenario analyses have been conducted in which these treatments’ efficacy in the model is derived from the equivalent post-hoc subgroup analysis of the BASIS trial used in the base case, for the subgroups of haemophilia A and haemophilia B separately. These data are analogous to the that of overall population, and include the **** and ***** of patients who received an escalated dose of marstacimab in the haemophilia A and B subgroups, respectively, which is also captured within the treatment costs in the model. As above, these data are based on increasingly small sample sizes, and the BASIS trial was not powered to detect differences between the two types of haemophilia. Additional scenario analyses are also presented in which dose-escalated patients are excluded from the post hoc subgroup analyses. 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 113 -->

## _**Scenario analyses by EHL and SHL products**_ 

No inherent differences in treatment effectiveness may be expected between EHL and SHL factor products given their identical mechanisms of action. However, the less demanding administration schedule of EHL products has been associated with improved adherence and clinical outcomes, including ABR, when switching from SHL products.[147, 148] To explore any uncertainty around potential differences in EHL and SHL efficacy, scenario analyses were conducted in which separate efficacy estimates were applied for EHL and SHL products in both the FVIII and FIX baskets for haemophilia A and B, respectively. Due to the small sample sizes, it was not possible to explore the subgroups of patients receiving EHL and SHL products within the subgroups of haemophilia type, and an overall efficacy of EHL and SHL products across haemophilia is used in this scenario. 

## **B.3.2.5 Treatment discontinuation** 

As reported in Section B.2.12.1, 6.02% (n=5) of patients who received marstacimab during the BASIS trial ATP discontinued the weekly treatment.[104] To reflect the BASIS trial results, a one-off discontinuation rate of 6.02% is applied in the first model cycle for patients receiving marstacimab. No discontinuation is modelled for patients receiving emicizumab or factor prophylaxis. 

Patients discontinuing marstacimab in the BASIS trial returned to the factor prophylaxis treatment they were receiving in the prior OP. This reflects expected clinical practice, as indicated by clinical feedback received. As such, all patients discontinuing marstacimab in the model base case are assumed to receive FVIII in the case of patients with haemophilia A, and FIX in the case of patients with haemophilia B, and are assumed to then remain on these treatments indefinitely. Upon discontinuation, patients are redistributed between the “Bleeds” and “No Bleeds” health state based on the starting health state distributions for factor prophylaxis (see Table 52 above). 

As noted in Section B.3.2.2 above, clinicians consulted as part of this submission indicated that any discontinuation from marstacimab is likely to occur early on following treatment initiation. As such, no discontinuation from marstacimab was modelled past the first model cycle. However, in the absence of long-term data on discontinuation from marstacimab, uncertainty exists around the best approach to modelling long-term discontinuation from marstacimab. Two scenario analyses relating to the long-term rate of marstacimab discontinuation were therefore conducted, one optimistic and one conservative. In the optimistic scenario, no discontinuation is modelled at all (either in the first model cycle or subsequently), and in the conservative scenario the 6.02% rate is applied annually, rather than as a one-off event (see Section B.3.11). 

## **B.3.2.6 Adverse events** 

In the base case analysis, no AEs were modelled. This is because, as reported in Section B.2.12.1, SAEs (Grade 3+) were reported in 8.4% of patients in the BASIS trial, with each SAE occurring in a single patient (1.2% of the trial population). The 5% threshold for severe AEs is commonly used for inclusion in economic models, representing AEs likely to incur meaningful decrements in utility and costs to the healthcare system.[149] As such, AEs reported in BASIS are unlikely to materially impact estimates of cost-effectiveness, and were therefore not included in the base case, either for the intervention or comparator.

## **B.3.2.7 Mortality** 

In the base case, transition probabilities from all health states to the ‘Death’ health state are informed by age- and sex-matched general population mortality statistics from the Office for National Statistics 2018–2020.[150] No additional haemophilia-specific mortality was modelled, in line with the etranacogene dezaparvovec NICE appraisal (ID3812).[10] Due to a lack of evidence, no direct treatment effect on mortality is considered in the base case analysis. 

However, some evidence suggests that people with haemophilia have a higher mortality risk than the general population.[52, 53] A recent meta-analysis showed that people with severe haemophilia have a standardised mortality ratio (SMR) of 4.1 (95% CI: 2.5–6.7) compared with the general population. However, three of the five studies included in the meta-analysis were published between the 1980s and 1990s, and one study was published in 2006; therefore, this SMR is likely an overestimation. In the fifth included study, which used data from 2001–2018 (N=1,031), an SMR of 2.4 (95% CI: 1.8, 3.0) was reported for Dutch people with severe haemophilia compared with the general Dutch population, which is more likely reflective of current clinical practice. The primary causes of death were intracranial bleeding and malignancies.[52] 

Additionally, as noted above in Section B.1.3.1.4, the UKHCDO 2023 report suggest that patients with moderate and severe haemophilia have a lower life expectancy than those with mild haemophilia.[4, 150] Therefore, a scenario analysis was conducted where the death risk for patients in the “Bleed” health state of the model was calculated by applying a disease-specific SMR of 2.4 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 115 -->

relative to the general population. This was justified because intracranial bleeding is the leading cause of death among people with haemophilia, and a patient with zero bleeds can be assumed to have the same risk of intracranial bleeding as the general population. 

## **B.3.3** _**Measurement and valuation of health effects**_ 

## **B.3.3.1 Health-related quality-of-life data from clinical trials** 

## **Health-state utility values** 

HRQoL outcomes were measured using EQ-5D-5L, Haem-A-QoL and HAL in the BASIS trial (Section B.2.6). For use in the model, data on the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system collected in BASIS were mapped to the 3L value set in accordance with the NICE reference-case. The mapping function used to generate utility values was based on the mapping function developed by the NICE Decision Support Unit using the ‘EEPRU’ dataset, as specified in the NICE process and methods guide (PMG36).[12] 

The treatment-independent health state utility values (HSUVs) used in the economic analysis are shown in Table 55. HRQoL data from the BASIS trial showed numerical but non-significant improvement in EQ-5D-5L and ED-VAS scores in patients receiving 12 months of marstacimab during the ATP, compared to 6 months of factor prophylaxis in the OP. Additionally, there were numerical but non-significant improvements in Haem-A-QoL and Haemo-QoL values for adults and adolescents, respectively. Given that differences between PROs were not significant between marstacimab and factor prophylaxis groups, it was assumed that treatment-independent HSUVs would be used for both marstacimab and factor prophylaxis. In the absence of comparative utility evidence versus emicizumab, the same HSUV taken from the BASIS trial was applied in this comparison. 

The EQ-5D-5L data reported in the BASIS trial reflected the HRQoL of patients experiencing both bleeds and no bleeds, as a single utility value. Both health states in the model are therefore associated with the same utility value, as shown in Table 55 above. Differential QoL between treatments is instead captured in the model via short-term utility decrements associated with acute treated bleeds, which occur at different rates in each treatment arm (see Table 53 above).

As shown in Table 55 above, no differences in HSUVs were explicitly modelled in the economic analysis. Differences in quality of life between the “Bleeds” and “No bleeds” health states were instead derived via utility decrements applied to acute joint and non-joint bleed events, which only occur in the “Bleeds” state. This approach of separating acute treated bleed events from

health state HRQoL allows for the occurrence of multiple, relatively short bleed events to be more accurately captured within the year-long cycle length. 

EQ-5D patient scores were collected at pre-specified timepoints within the BASIS trial which, depending on the timing of EQ-5D measurements compared with timings of a bleed, may not have been reflective of change in QoL related to acute bleed events. It was therefore considered unfeasible to use EQ-5D data from the BASIS trial to derive utility values associated with bleeds in the model. As such, utility values for joint and non-joint events were sourced from the literature instead. The joint bleed utility decrement was based on a study by Mazza _et al._ (2016), whilst those for non-joint bleeds were sourced from Neufeld _et al._ (2012). Both utility decrements were assumed to last 4.5 days, in line with the previous CEA published by ICER,[129] and NICE’s evaluations of etranacogene dezaparvovec and fidanacogene elaparvovec.[10, 84] The disutility, duration and resulting annual decrement applied to joint and non-joint bleed events in the model are shown in Table 56 below.

## **Age-related utility decrements** 

The model considered additional age-related decrements as the modelled population became older over the time horizon. The decrements were derived from Health Survey for England (HSE) 2014, as recommended by the NICE DSU.[152] Adjustments were calculated for each age range to reflect the impact associated with age on utility. For each given age, the same adjustment was applied to all utility inputs regardless of health states. 

It should be noted that the age-related utility decrements derived from HSE 2014 begin at age 16. Given the anticipated marketing authorisation for marstacimab includes adolescents (aged 12 to 18), a scenario analysis was conducted where the starting age was set to age 12. An assumption was made that the utility decrement for those aged 16 was the same as the utility decrement for those aged 12 to 16. 

## **Administration-related utility decrements** 

An important difference between marstacimab and factor prophylaxis relates to the administration of both therapies. Marstacimab is given as a flat-dose subcutaneous injection by pre-filled pen, and therefore represents a more convenient and less burdensome method of administration compared to factor prophylaxis treatments, which are administered via IV infusion. Furthermore, clinical feedback indicated that the ease of marstacimab SC administration via a flat-dosed, pre-filled pen represented an important benefit, which should be reflected in the economic modelling.[101] Given this difference in administration, and the potential impact on patients as a result, the base case analysis considered treatment administration-related utility decrements. The decrements were derived from Johnson et al, 2021, a vignette-based time

trade-off utilities elicitation conducted in Canadian adults with haemophilia A.[153] The peradministration disutilities applied were 0.0003 for each intravenous infusion, applied to factor prophylaxis, and 0.0002 for each subcutaneous injection, applied to marstacimab and emicizumab. A scenario analysis was conducted in which administration-related utility decrements are not included in the CEA.

## **B.3.4** _**Cost and healthcare resource use identification,**_ 

## _**measurement and valuation**_ 

As described in Section B.3.1, a SLR was conducted in August 2020 and updated in May 2024 in order to identify clinical and economic evidence in the field of haemophilia. Simultaneous literature searches were conducted for utility studies (Appendix H) and healthcare resource use studies (Appendix I). In total, 13 articles reporting on 10 unique healthcare resource use studies were included in the SLR. 

The following cost categories were included in the model base case: 

- Drug acquisition costs 

- Management costs of acute bleed events (including acquisition costs for on-demand factor replacement therapy) 

The economic analysis was conducted from an NHS and PSS perspective and therefore included only costs that would be incurred by the NHS and PSS. Cost inputs were based on British National Formulary (BNF) 2024, Monthly Index of Medical Specialities (MIMS) and National Schedule of NHS costs (2021/2022).[138-140]

## **B.3.4.2 Health-state unit costs and resource use** 

## **Management of acute bleed events** 

Disease management costs were assumed to be entirely related to the management of acute bleed events. The health care interaction costs associated with managing acute bleeds in the model is shown in Table 65. The treatment acquisition costs for the use of on-demand factor prophylaxis therapy was calculated as a weighted average of the distribution of prophylactic factor replacement therapies, as reported in Table 66 and Table 67. 

UK clinical expert feedback indicated that acute bleeds are treated with one additional dose of factor prophylaxis. Feedback also indicated that joint and non-joint bleeds are typically treated in a similar manner, with the same doses of factor treatment.[68] As such, the base case assumes that joint and non-joint bleeds are associated with the same management costs, with patients receiving one additional dose of factor prophylaxis per acute bleed. 

However, some publications provide different estimates of factor prophylaxis doses to be used to treat joint and non-joint bleeds, and previous submissions to NICE have assumed that joint bleeds are associated with higher management costs.[10] Additionally, as part of consultations with clinical experts for this appraisal, one advisor stated that they might recommend for a patient to take a second dose for a joint bleed.[68] As such, a scenario analysis was conducted in which joint

## **B.3.4.4 Miscellaneous unit costs and resource use** 

No additional costs were considered in the base case of the economic model. Haemophilia patients are likely to incur costs for ongoing standard disease management which may include orthopaedist visits, physiotherapist appointments, and standard laboratory tests. However, these costs are assumed to be incurred by all haemophilia patients, regardless of treatment. As a result, these costs are not expected to substantially impact the estimate of marstacimab’s costeffectiveness, and were therefore not included in the model. Additionally, previous research has revealed that factor treatment acquisition costs comprise almost all (99%) of total annual haemophilia-related direct medical costs in haemophilia patients.[45, 58] Therefore, it was considered appropriate to not include other miscellaneous costs for the factor prophylaxis treatment arm, though this can be considered a conservative approach. 

A scenario analysis was carried out, in which direct (such as transportation) and indirect (such as lost productivity) non-medical costs for patients were included in the economic analysis. Indirect costs were assumed to be £3,290.09 for all haemophilia A and B patients with and without bleeds. This cost was sourced from Burke et al. 2021,[58] which reported the mean annual indirect cost for patients with haemophilia B in the UK. Since costs were reported in Euros, a conversion of 1 Euro = 0.88 GBP was assumed. The cost was also inflated to 2022 GBP, with the resulting costs shown in Table 69 below.

## **B.3.5** _**Severity**_ 

The expected quality-adjusted life expectancy (QALE) for the general population was calculated in line with the methods provided by McNamara _et al_ . (2023).[163] The total life expectancy for the modelled population was calculated using population mortality data from the Office for National Statistics for 2018–2020.[150] The total life expectancy was quality-adjusted using UK population norm values for EQ-5D as reported by Hernández Alava _et al_ . (2022) through the NICE DSU.[152] 

The total discounted QALYs for the current population of patients with severe haemophilia receiving existing treatments were calculated from the economic model (Table 71). The absolute QALY shortfall and proportional QALY shortfall compared to the population receiving treatment with existing treatments (baseline characteristics reported in Section B.3.2.1) were below the threshold, therefore, no severity weights were used in the present analysis. ## **B.3.6** _**Uncertainty**_ 

Given that severe haemophilia A and B are rare diseases, the number of patients able to be recruited for a clinical trial is low. The BASIS trial investigating marstacimab recruited 91 patients who received factor prophylaxis during the OP, with 83 progressing to the ATP. This small population size meant that the trial was not powered to detect differences in subgroups. Only 18 patients with haemophilia B and receiving prior factor prophylaxis participated in the ATP of the trial. Haemophilia A and B are largely indistinguishable with regards to clinical outcomes, and clinical expert feedback has indicated that no differences in marstacimab treatment effect would 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 128 -->

be expected between haemophilia A and B.[2, 68] As such, the model base case used a single efficacy value for marstacimab across both haemophilia A and B, in line with the efficacy data from the BASIS trial. To explore uncertainty around this assumption, marstacimab was also compared to factor prophylaxis for haemophilia A and B in scenario analyses which utilised specific subgroup post hoc efficacy data, however the efficacy data informing this were not powered for significance. 

Another source of uncertainty was the lack of data available to inform the long-term impact on joint health for patients with haemophilia. Joint health is an important factor for patients with haemophilia and can have a significant impact on their quality of life, as explained in Section B.1.3.1.5. However, data evaluating the long-term impact of marstacimab on joint damage is lacking. Therefore, improvements in joint health and reductions in joint pain following treatment with marstacimab, compared with factor prophylaxis, seen in the BASIS trial ATP and OLE may therefore not be fully captured in the model. As a result, the model likely underestimates the potential health and cost benefits that marstacimab may offer through reduction of long-term joint damage as a result of the observed improvements in joint bleed rates and joint health.

No managed access proposal is planned for marstacimab.

## **B.3.9** _**Base-case results**_ 

## **B.3.9.1 Base-case incremental cost-effectiveness analysis results** 

Table 74 presents the _deterministic_ base case results of the economic evaluation of marstacimab versus FVIII prophylaxis, emicizumab and FIX prophylaxis. These show marstacimab to be a ***** cost-effective alternative to all three comparator therapies, with net health benefit (NHBs) of , ****** and ****** versus FVIII prophylaxis, emicizumab, and FIX prophylaxis, respectively, at a willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of £30,000. In the comparison versus FVIII and FIX prophylaxis (in patients with haemophilia A and B, respectively), marstacimab was dominant, being associated with both lower costs and greater health benefits (i.e., higher total QALYs). In the comparison versus emicizumab, marstacimab resulted in fewer overall QALYs, however resulted in cost savings large enough to be considered cost-effective at a WTP threshold of £30,000 saved per QALY forgone. 

Table 75 presents the _probabilistic_ base case results of the economic evaluation of marstacimab versus FVIII prophylaxis, emicizumab and FIX prophylaxis. These show concordant results to the deterministic results, with all NHB results within 1% of the deterministic model results, indicating that cost-effectiveness results are largely insensitive to joint parameter uncertainty. 

The clinical outcomes and disaggregated base case cost-effectiveness results (by cost category, including health states) and QALYs (by health state) are presented in Appendix J. Fully incremental and pairwise comparisons to individual treatments included in the comparator baskets have been presented in Appendix O.

## **B.3.10** _**Exploring uncertainty**_ 

Parameter uncertainty in the model was assessed via both probabilistic and deterministic sensitivity analyses the results of which are presented in Sections B.3.10.1 and B.3.10.2, respectively. In addition, key assumptions in the model were explored in several probabilistic scenario analyses, the results of which are presented in Section B.3.10.3. Overall, it is considered that all relevant uncertainties included in the analyses have been adequately accounted for and the base case results were found to be robust to uncertainty in the key model inputs and assumptions. 

## **B.3.10.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

A PSA was conducted in order to assess the simultaneous effect of uncertainty in the different model parameters and to demonstrate whether the model results are robust to those variations. A Monte-Carlo simulation with 1,000 iterations was performed where model inputs were randomly sampled from the specified probability distributions. The values of the inputs were determined by random variation with statistical distributions as outlined in Table 72. 

An ICER convergence plot and probabilistic cost-effectiveness place versus FVIII prophylaxis and emicizimuab (haemophilia A) are shown in Figure 12 and Figure 13. An ICER convergence plot and probabilistic cost-effectiveness place versus FIX prophylaxis (haemophilia B) are shown in Figure 14 and Figure 15.

## **B.3.10.2 Deterministic sensitivity analysis** 

In order to assess the robustness of the base case cost-effectiveness results, DSA were conducted, in which individual inputs (Table 72, Section B.3.8.1) were varied whilst keeping all other model inputs constant. The impact of varying individual inputs on the NHB associated with marstacimab compared to FVIII prophylaxis, emicizumab, and FIX prophylaxis is shown in the form of tornado diagrams in Figure 16, Figure 17, and Figure 18, respectively. 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 140 -->

In all comparisons, the input with the greatest impact on cost-effectiveness estimates was the starting weight of patients in the model, with a higher weight resulting in greater NHB associated with marstacimab. This can be rationalised by the fact that marstacimab is administered as a flat dose, whilst all comparator treatment doses are based on patient weight, with a higher weight requiring higher doses, and therefore incurring greater costs in the model. 

The other model input with an appreciable impact on cost-effectiveness estimates is patient starting age, which is to be expected given the relatively young starting age, the lifetime model horizon, and the lifetime costs incurred by patients in all treatment arms. 

With the exception of patients’ starting weight and age, no variation of individual inputs had any substantial impact on cost-effectiveness estimates, showing the model to be largely robust to individual parameter uncertainty. It should be further noted that, whilst weight and age have large impacts on numerical model results, the conclusions of marstacimab’s cost-effectiveness against each comparator remain unchanged, with input variation still resulting in large NHB across all comparisons.

## **B.3.10.3 Scenario analysis** 

Several probabilistic scenario analyses were conducted to assess the impact of the uncertainty associated with key inputs and assumptions in the economic model, as detailed in Table 73. Results of these scenario analyses in the haemophilia A and B analyses are presented in Table 76 and Table 77, respectively. Some variation may exist in the interpretation of these results relative to the base case results due to the probabilistic nature of the analyses. 

The majority of scenarios had a limited impact on cost-effectiveness results, and marstacimab remained consistently dominant versus both FVIII and FIX prophylaxes across all tested scenarios, and cost-effective against emicizumab. The scenario in which the discontinuation rate of 6.02% is applied annually to marstacimab patients had the largest impact on results, resulting in the lowest NHB against each comparator, however this result remained above the accepted cost-effectiveness thresholds set by NICE.

## **B.3.11** _**Subgroup analysis**_ 

The base case considers separate analyses for haemophilia A and B, and their relevant comparator products, however efficacy data used are the same for both populations, in line with the BASIS trial. Scenario analyses present results using post-hoc data from the BASIS trial which considers specific and distinct efficacy of FVIII, FIX and marstacimab in haemophilia A and B populations. 

## **B.3.12** _**Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation**_ 

The economic model presented in this submission captures the key benefit of marstacimab compared with current therapy options, the observed reductions in bleeding rates from the BASIS trial compared with individuals receiving factor prophylaxis. Whilst this represents an important aspect of treatment with marstacimab, there are additional benefits that are not able to be captured in the model. 

## **Impact of long-term joint damage on HRQoL and costs** 

As outlined in Section B.1.3.1.4, long-term damage to joints represents a substantial burden associated with haemophilia bleeds. Due to limited availability of data from comparator trials and a lack of long-term studies evaluating the impact of marstacimab on joint damage, the _de novo_ model structure in this submission does not explicitly capture long-term joint damage or future surgery as part of the health state definitions. The improvements in joint health and reductions in joint pain following treatment with marstacimab, compared with factor prophylaxis, seen in the BASIS trial ATP and OLE may therefore not be fully captured in the model. For example, improvements in joint health in the short term may translate to long-term reductions in the development of joint arthropathy, improved mobility, reduced chronic pain, and reduced chronic disability. Additionally, if patients experience fewer joint surgeries in the long term, this could be expected to provide cost-savings to the NHS. In summary, the model likely underestimates the potential health and cost benefits that marstacimab may offer through reduction of long-term joint damage as a result of the observed improvements in joint bleed rates and joint health. 

## **Psychological benefits of reduced treatment burden and increased simplicity of administration** 

Beyond the physical and psychological aspects of the condition, haemophilia is associated with a substantial treatment burden as highlighted in Section B.1.3.1.5. Factor prophylaxis treatment for both haemophilia A and B requires frequent IV infusions which are strenuous and time consuming. This can interfere with an individual’s daily life, employment and travel. While emicizumab is administered as a SC injection, issues remain due to its complex weight based dosing schedule and the fact patients have to draw up their own vials. Additionally, there is no SC treatment option available for patients with haemophilia B. Treatment with marstacimab as a fixed-dose, pre-filled SC pen has the potential to free patients from the burden of regular factor infusions, allowing patients to live life more freely, and reducing the amount that haemophilia is on their mind. In the model, the baseline HRQoL utility was assumed to be the same for patients receiving marstacimab or factor prophylaxis. This could be seen as a conservative assumption as it does not capture the benefits highlighted above.

## **B.3.13** _**Validation**_ 

## **B.3.13.1 Validation of cost-effectiveness analysis** 

## **Clinical expert opinion** 

Expert clinical opinion was sought during the development of this evaluation to ensure that the inputs and assumptions used in the analysis were relevant to UK clinical practice. In order to obtain this expert opinion, Pfizer obtained partnership agreements with 5 clinical experts (4 NHS haemophilia specialists and one haemophilia scientist) experienced in the treatment of haemophilia in the UK. The objective of the partnerships were to obtain the experts’ opinion on key assumptions and/or inputs which included: 

- The use of a basket comparator of FVIII and FIX products 

- The pooling of BASIS trial efficacy 

- The disutility applied for administration of treatment 

- The rate of discontinuation from marstacimab and the products patients discontinue onto 

- The absence of marstacimab treatment waning over time 

Outputs from these discussions are detailed throughout the submission alongside the descriptions of the relevant assumptions and approaches. 

## **Technical validation** 

In alignment with best practice, a number of technical and internal consistency checks were completed by an independent health economist prior to submission to ensure that the model functioned as intended and generated accurate results which were consistent with input data and robust to extreme analyses. This model quality control check was conducted in line with the published TECH-VER checklist.[164] 

The validation process also aimed to ensure that a high degree of transparency was maintained throughout the model and adaptations were carried out where necessary to ensure the validity of the model. 

## **B.3.14** _**Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence**_ 

## **Summary of cost-effectiveness evidence** 

In order to assess the cost-effectiveness of marstacimab in severe haemophilia in patients in the UK, a _de novo_ cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted from the perspective of the NHS and PSS in the UK. The model considered a population in line with the anticipated market authorisation for marstacimab: people aged 12 or over with severe haemophilia A (without inhibitors) or severe haemophilia B (without inhibitors). This reflects the population in BASIS, the pivotal Phase 3 trial for marstacimab, which also informed the modelled efficacy of marstacimab. The comparators in haemophilia A consisted of a basket of FVIII prophylaxis treatment and emicizumab, and the comparator in haemophilia B consisted of a basket comparator of FIX prophylaxis treatment. Clinical expert feedback considered these comparators to be reflective of current treatment options for haemophilia B in the UK. The relative efficacy of comparator factor 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 151 -->

prophylaxis (FVIII and FIX) was derived from a direct intrapatient comparison of the percentage of patients experiencing treated bleeds and the rate of treated bleeds in the OP and ATP phases of the BASIS trial. In the absence of direct comparative efficacy data for emicizumab versus marstacimab, the treatment efficacy of emicizumab relative to marstacimab was derived from STC analysis using data from the BASIS and HAVEN trials. 

Marstacimab was found to be more effective and less costly than both FVIII and FIX prophylaxis comparator baskets (i.e. dominant) across all analyses conducted. In the base case, marstacimab (with PAS) was associated with positive deterministic NHB versus FVIII and FIX prophylaxis of ***** and ****** QALYs, respectively, at a WTP of £30,000 per QALY gained. Marstacimab resulted in fewer QALYs but was less costly than emicizumab, resulting in a positive deterministic NHB of ****** at a WTP of £30,000 saved per QALY forgone. The probabilistic base case analysis showed very similar results, with marstacimab resulting in positive NHBs versus FVIII prophylaxis, emicizumab, and FIX prophylaxis of *****, ******, and ****** QALYs at a WTP of £30,000 per QALY, respectively, indicating the base case results to be robust to uncertainty in parameter estimates. Marstacimab had a 100% probability of being costeffective against all comparators, across all 1,000 probabilistic simulations. 

The DSA results identified two influential parameters (patient age and weight), however the model was largely robust to individual parameter uncertainty and marstacimab remained costeffective across all extreme variables. Scenario analyses were conducted to explore the impact of certain assumptions within the model, all of which showed similarly cost-effective results for marstacimab in the comparison against each comparator, with minimum NHBs of *****, ****** and ***** against QALYs at a WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY against FVIII prophylaxis, emicizumab, and FIX prophylaxis, respectively. These minimum NHBs were all in the scenario in which an annual discontinuation rate of 6.02% is applied to marstacimab, which, as per expert clinician feedback, can be considered highly conservative.[68] 

Overall, all analyses demonstrated marstacimab to be a cost-effective treatment option at the WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY. 

## **Strengths** 

The clinical evidence base for marstacimab and comparators in this submission has been derived from a robust SLR of clinical trials investigating treatments for severe haemophilia. Results from the marstacimab trial demonstrate that marstacimab is associated with a reduced risk of bleeds and treated bleeds compared with routine factor prophylaxis. The promising early results observed in the BASIS trial ATP are supported by its OLE study, showing sustained reductions in bleed rates compared with treatment with routine factor prophylaxis in the trial OP. The results of the BASIS trial in the overall population of patients with severe haemophilia (both A and B) informed the efficacy of marstacimab, and both FVIII and FIX prophylaxis. Scenario analyses were conducted in which subgroup analyses from the BASIS trial by haemophilia type (A or B) were instead used to inform efficacy of these three treatments. 

Unlike the comparison with factor prophylaxis treatments, no direct comparative evidence existed between marstacimab and emicizumab. In the absence of any such direct evidence, an unanchored STC was conducted to compare marstacimab to emicizumab in patients with severe haemophilia A, informed by data from the BASIS and HAVEN 3 trials. Emicizumab was found to be associated with a slight reduction in treated joint and non-joint bleed rates compared with marstacimab, however none of the results reached statistical significance (Section B.2.11). 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 152 -->

A cost-utility analysis was selected to assess the cost-effectiveness of marstacimab in severe haemophilia A and severe haemophilia B. The model was built to align with the NICE reference case, adopting an NHS and PSS perspective, a lifetime time horizon to fully capture all costs and QALY gains associated with modelled treatments, and discount rates for costs and benefits of 3.5%. As discussed in Section B.3.13, the model underwent rigorous internal validation, and clinical expert feedback was sought to validate many of the assumptions and inputs used in the model. 

## **Limitations** 

A key limitation of the clinical evidence base was the lack of appropriate head-to-head trial evidence for marstacimab versus emicizumab. An unanchored STC was conducted in order to obtain relative efficacy estimates to inform the economic analysis, which are subject to inherent uncertainty. Whilst clinically important covariates were adjusted to better match populations across included studies, it is unlikely that all confounding was accounted for, an assumption and limitation inherent to all unanchored ITCs. Furthermore, results did not reach statistical significance, therefore the true difference in treatment effect is uncertain. Despite these limitations, the STC analysis represents a rigorous method of accounting for confounding, using the best available comparator trial data. 

As noted in Section B.3.12, whilst the model attempted to capture the health and HRQoL outcomes of most relevance to patients with moderately severe to severe haemophilia B, a lack of appropriate data meant that not all important aspects of the disease could be explicitly captured. 

Finally, whilst BASIS provides robust evidence for the efficacy of marstacimab for a year, and the BASIS OLE for a further six months, the model extends over a lifetime horizon. This therefore necessitated long-term extrapolation of treatment effect, and assumptions around the long-term rate of discontinuation from marstacimab. Uncertainty therefore exists in the long-term treatment efficacy of marstacimab, as well as the three comparators, whose efficacy is informed by the BASIS trial (directly or indirectly). Long-term efficacy, in particular the long-term rate of marstacimab discontinuation, represents the principal source of uncertainty which has a large impact on the cost-effectiveness estimates of marstacimab. Scenario analyses were conducted using different sources of efficacy, and different assumptions around long-term marstacimab discontinuation. These show marstacimab to be cost-effective under all analyses conducted, against all comparators. 

## **Conclusion** 

Patients with severe haemophilia face a serious unmet need for a treatment with a simple method of administration, which is able to maintain low bleed rates and improve patient QoL. Marstacimab represents a convenient, efficacious and well tolerated treatment, with an acceptable safety profile and novel mechanism of action, offering less burdensome administration requirements for patients. Results from the BASIS trial show improvements in ABRtreat compared with factor prophylaxis, supported by numerical improvements in EQ-5D-5L scores. 

In the cost-effectiveness analysis, marstacimab was shown to be associated with a greater number of QALYs and fewer costs than the FVIII and FIX basket comparators, and associated with substantial cost savings against emicizumab. This led to cost-effective economic model 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 153 -->

results against all three comparators, across all analyses conducted. Marstacimab therefore represents a cost-effective treatment option at a WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY, and its reimbursement for the treatment of severe haemophilia can be considered a cost-effective use of NHS resources, whilst also expanding the choice of therapies available to both patients with haemophilia and their clinicians.

## **What is the SIP?** 

The Summary of Information for Patients (SIP) is written by the company who is seeking approval from NICE for their treatment to be sold to the NHS for use in England.  It is a plain English summary of their submission written for patients participating in the evaluation.  It is not independently checked, although members of the public involvement team at NICE will have read it to doublecheck for marketing and promotional content before it is sent to you. 

The **Summary of Information for Patients** template has been adapted for use at NICE from the – Health Technology Assessment International Patient & Citizens Involvement Group (HTAi PCIG). Information about the development is available in an open-access IJTAHC journal article

## **SECTION 2: Current landscape** 

## **2a) The condition – clinical presentation and impact** 

Please provide a few sentences to describe the condition that is being assessed by NICE and the number of people who are currently living with this condition in England. 

Please outline in general terms how the condition affects the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers. Please highlight any mortality/morbidity data relating to the condition if available. If the company is making a case for the impact of the treatment on carers this should be clearly stated and explained. 

Haemophilia is a lifelong, rare genetic condition that affects the blood's ability to clot.[2,3] Typically, if a person bleeds, substances in the blood known as clotting factors mix with blood cells called platelets to make the blood sticky and form a clot, ensuring the bleeding stops.[2,3] People with haemophilia have less clotting factors in their blood meaning they bleed for longer than usual.[2] 

There are two main types of the condition, haemophilia A and haemophilia B, and both are caused by defects in the genes responsible for producing proteins that help the blood clot. These proteins are known as clotting factors and the type of haemophilia is defined by which clotting factor is affected. 

Individuals with Haemophilia A have a defect in the gene responsible for producing factor VIII (eight), referred to as FVIII.[4] In contrast, individuals with haemophilia B have a defect in the gene responsible for producing factor IX (nine), known as FIX.[4] Haemophilia B is rarer than haemophilia 



<!-- page 166 -->

A, and both conditions mostly impact males.[ 6,9] In 2022/23 in the UK,  2,128 people were treated for severe haemophilia A and 329 people were treated for severe haemophilia B.[5] 

FVIII and FIX are important proteins within the blood clotting process; and an absence or reduced amount of either causes a delay in clot formation once bleeding has occurred.[6,7] Consequently, people with haemophilia A or B can experience prolonged bleeding events. Depending on how severe the disease is, these bleeding events can occur either spontaneously or following trauma (e.g., after an injury or surgery).[8,9] Bleeding episodes most commonly occur in joints, but can also occur in other locations including muscles, soft tissue, the gastrointestinal (digestive) system, and the brain or spinal cord.[8] Repeated bleeding into joints can cause considerable pain, reduced range of motion and poor mobility, all of which reduce quality of life. These challenges can limit the ability of those with haemophilia to do daily activities or to live spontaneously. 

The severity of haemophilia A or B depends on the level of FVIII or FIX in the blood compared to normal levels and are classified as mild (>5% to <40% of normal), moderate (1–5% of normal) or severe (<1% of normal). This submission focusses on severe haemophilia A or B (FVIII or FIX activity levels of <1% of normal).[8,10,11] 

Haemophilia has a large impact on patients and carers due to the symptoms and treatments, with reduced quality of life arising from pain, functional impairment, anxiety and depression due to unpredictability of bleeding events and frustration with treatment burden, a reduction in work productivity, and an increase in healthcare spending.[ 10,12-15] 

## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

Haemophilia can be diagnosed before birth if there is a family history of haemophilia.[2,16] There are several tests for genetic conditions, such as chorionic villus sampling (CVS) in early pregnancy.[16] An alternative is free-foetal DNA testing – this does not diagnose haemophilia but it can identify the sex of the baby in the womb, which is particularly helpful in what are known as X-linked disorders, like haemophilia, that mainly affect males.[16] 

After birth, a diagnosis of haemophilia will often be made after unexplained bleeding in an otherwise healthy infant.[17] Haemophilia can then be diagnosed using a sample of blood for testing in a laboratory.[16] A test to measure how long a sample takes to clot may suggest a clotting disorder, which would then be investigated further for specific clotting factors.[16] Doctors will try to identify the gene mutation as well, as this can be helpful in planning for future children.[16 ] 



<!-- page 167 -->

## **2c) Current treatment options:** 

The purpose of this section is to set the scene on how the condition is currently managed: 

- What is the treatment pathway for this condition and where in this pathway the medicine is likely to be used? Please use diagrams to accompany text where possible. Please give emphasis to the specific setting and condition being considered by NICE in this review. For example, by referencing current treatment guidelines.  It may be relevant to show the treatments people may have before and after the treatment under consideration in this SIP. 

- Please also consider: 

   - if there are multiple treatment options, and data suggest that some are more commonly used than others in the setting and condition being considered in this SIP, please report these data. 

   - are there any drug–drug interactions and/or contraindications that commonly cause challenges for patient populations? If so, please explain what these are. 

Haemophilia A and B are life-long conditions and there is currently no treatment that provides a cure. Given that recurrent bleeding episodes can lead to irreversible joint damage, the main treatment goal is to reduce or prevent bleeding while allowing patients to lead active lives and achieve a quality of life comparable to individuals not affected by the condition.[18] 

Most medicines for haemophilia A and B focus on replacing the missing clotting protein (FVIII or FIX). The standard of care, as recommended by the World Federation of Hemophilia (WFH), is regular injections of FVIII or FIX into the vein (intravenous injections) to raise the level of FVIII or FIX in the blood and therefore prevent bleeding.[8] This is known as a prophylactic (or preventative) treatment and is how the majority of individuals with severe haemophilia are managed. Following a bleeding episode, FVIII or FIX injections can also be administered “on-demand” with the aim of stopping bleeding once it has occurred.[19] 

FVIII or FIX replacement medicines are available in two forms: standard half-life (SHL) products, which require administration multiple times per week, and extended half-life (EHL) products, which are typically administered at frequencies from once a week to once every two weeks for those whose bleeding is well controlled.[20-30] Due to their reduced frequency of administration and therefore reduced treatment burden, EHL products tend to be favoured over SHL products. 

For people with haemophilia A there is also an alternative treatment option called emicizumab (brand name Hemlibra[®] ) which is the most commonly used treatment for severe haemophilia A in the UK[5] . Emicizumab is a monoclonal antibody (MAb) and is administered every 1-4 weeks.[31] Unlike medicines that focus on replacing the missing factor, emicizumab is administered subcutaneously (injection into fatty tissue, just under the skin) rather than intravenously. However, self-administration of emicizumab requires the individual to first determine their correct dose (based on their body weight) and then draw this up into the syringe, prior to administration.[31] 

Medicines used for current clinical management of severe haemophilia A and B in the UK is presented in Figure 1 (described further in Document B, Section B1.3.2).

FVIII and FIX prophylaxis treatments have a high treatment burden, as the need for frequent selfadministered intravenous infusions disrupts day-to-day activities that others without the condition may take for granted.[15,33] Additionally, despite regular FVIII and FIX prophylaxis, people with severe haemophilia A or B can still experience bleeds. As mentioned previously, frequent bleeds into single or multiple joints has a negative impact on quality of life and can lead to joint damage.[34] 

## **2d) Patient-based evidence (PBE) about living with the condition** 

**Context:** 

- **Patient-based evidence (PBE)** is when patients input into scientific research, specifically to provide experiences of their symptoms, needs, perceptions, quality of life issues or experiences of the medicine they are currently taking. PBE might also include carer burden and outputs from patient preference studies, when conducted in order to show what matters most to patients and carers and where their greatest needs are. Such research can inform the selection of patient-relevant endpoints in clinical trials. 

In this section, please provide a summary of any PBE that has been collected or published to demonstrate what is understood about **patient needs and disease experiences** . Please include the methods used for collecting this evidence. Any such evidence included in the SIP should be formally referenced wherever possible and references included. 

Severe haemophilia A and B both have a substantial physical, psychological, and economic impact on patients with the condition. Additionally, a substantial treatment burden exists due to the regular IV injections associated with FVIII and FIX prophylaxis. 



<!-- page 169 -->

## **Bleeding, joint damage and pain** 

The recurrent bleeding episodes patients experience with severe haemophilia A and B can lead to progressive joint damage (arthropathy) and pain, resulting in physical impairment and negatively impacting quality of life.[12,35-38] Recent discussions with patients with severe haemophilia B attending a workshop (n=5), and interviews (n=4) conducted by a specialist organisation called Haemnet on behalf of Pfizer revealed that bleeding rates are a key driver of reduced quality of life in this population.[39] 

_“Having so many bleeds, it was so disruptive to my work, just to life in general.”_ 

The development of joint damage as a result of repeated bleeding episodes represents one of the most debilitating consequences of haemophilia A and B. Evidence for this comes from the CHESS (Cost of Haemophilia across Europe – a Socioeconomic Survey) study in which individuals with haemophilia and physicians from five European countries (including the UK) completed questionnaires between 2014 and 2015.[37] Analysis of these questionnaires revealed there is a strong association between the number of damaged joints and worsening quality of life.[13] Participants with severe haemophilia interviewed in the Haemnet study also raised the issue of joint health and the frustrations this causes on multiple occasions.[39 ] 

_“Speaking as somebody who has long-term joint damage and, you know, really painful long-term joint damage, it really affects my mobility and so I can’t be as spontaneous as I would like to be.”_ 

Pain is another factor that can have a high impact on individuals with haemophilia A or B. Evidence for this comes from the CHESS II study which collected data between 2019 and 2020 and aimed to build on the original CHESS study.[40] Data from CHESS II reported that 76% of participants with severe haemophilia B had mild or moderate chronic pain, and 5% endured chronic pain, which consequently resulted in low quality of life scores.[40] Similar experiences were found in the United States in the pain, functional impairment and quality of life (P-FiQ) study, an observational study on 381 adults with haemophilia A or B.[12] In this study, pain due to haemophilia caused substantial interference across many aspects of the patients’ lives, including the ability to enjoy life, work normally, sleep and walk, all of which are areas that individuals without the disease may take for granted. Finally, UK participants in the recent workshop and interviews by Haemnet raised the issue of pain and associated frustrations, including having to manage it constantly. The indifferent attitude of people with haemophilia may often mask the true impact of the disease, as revealed by one UK participant in the recent interviews conducted by Haemnet:[39] 

_“You get pain whatever, don’t you, really, so you just deal with it.”_ 

## **Impact on daily living** 

The physical impairments that can develop as a result of bleeding are closely linked with challenges in performing routine activities of daily living, including physical activity and household tasks.[12,13] Education, employment, and physical leisure activities can also be affected in individuals with haemophilia. During the Haemnet patient discussions, one participant noted:[39] 



<!-- page 170 -->

_“My earliest memory of a consultant was [them saying] ‘you will not play football, you will not play cricket, you will not play rugby, you will not play basketball, you will not do PE at school’ and I was bored, and I got fed up.”_ 

## **Psychological impacts** 

Beyond the physical aspects of the condition, anxiety and depression are commonly reported in people with haemophilia A or B, highlighting how aspects of living with the condition can result in an additional psychological (mental) burden.[13-15,41] Psychological well-being was also explored within a study involving members of The Haemophilia Society.[14] The inability to participate in activities that individuals valued, along with a lack of independence, were reported as reasons for depression. Feelings of anger and frustration were also raised as described by one individual: 

_“I think there are a lot of us who are angry and haemophilia is definitely frustrating, it can bring on an awful lot of anxiety”; “I sometimes feel ... why me and I do get angry because it’s not my fault that I’ve got this thing which now I have to live with every day because I know it’s not going to ever go away.”_ 

## **Impact on employment** 

Severe haemophilia A and B are also associated with significant social and financial burden resulting from reduced work productivity and a negative impact on education. People with haemophilia A or B are up to four times more likely to be unemployed among people of working age and to experience restrictions in performing their job due to pain and frequent absences.[42,43] Participants discussed the impact of haemophilia on employment:[39] 

_“It [bleeding] was basically every month and I was having to have, like, a week off work and then come in in a wheelchair the next week, and it was just like … it was crap.”_ 

## **Treatment burden associated current therapies** 

FVIII and FIX prophylaxis requires time-consuming and frequent intravenous injections over the lifetime of an individual to try and prevent bleeding. As individuals are primarily responsible for their administration of FIX prophylaxis, such frequent infusions can substantially interfere with opportunities to take part in day-to-day activities. The effect of treatment burden interfering with daily life was identified in the Hemo-TEM study, where participants reported that travel and social activities were often impacted and that they had to stop activities to treat bleeds.[15] In the 

Haemnet workshop and interviews with people with haemophilia B, current treatment burden and its impact on the ability to travel was also mentioned;[39] 

_“I’d love to go exploring, I’d love to do stuff like that, that’s one of the reasons why I wanted to join the Forces. I’d love to go hiking, I’d love to try all these different things, but not if I’ve got to take factor with me because it’s limiting.”_

## **SECTION 3: The treatment** 

## **3a) How does the new treatment work?** 

What are the important features of this treatment? 

Please outline as clearly as possible important details that you consider relevant to patients relating to the mechanism of action and how the medicine interacts with the body 

Where possible, please describe how you feel the medicine is innovative or novel, and how this might be important to patients and their communities. 

If there are relevant documents which have been produced to support your regulatory submission such as a summary of product characteristics or patient information leaflet, please provide a link to these. 

Marstacimab belongs to a group of medicines called monoclonal antibodies.  Monoclonal antibodies are a type of protein that recognize and bind to a target in the body. Discovered by Pfizer scientists, marstacimab works differently to FVIII and FIX replacement treatments[44] . Instead of replacing missing or insufficient clotting factors, marstacimab works by targeting a protein called tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) that is naturally produced in the body. TFPI prevents blood clot formation, known as an anticoagulation protein. Marstacimab works to block TFPI, enhancing the body’s ability to form clots, therefore reducing excessive and spontaneous bleeds. 

## **Marstacimab can be taken once weekly by the patient giving themself an injection under the** 

**skin (subcutaneous) using a pre-filled pen** . This offers patients a practical alternative to current treatments. With its subcutaneous administration, marstacimab aims to free patients from the requirement for regular intravenous injections, thereby reducing treatment burden and its associated impact on daily living. Additionally, as marstacimab is given as pre-filled pen, it eliminates the need for complicated weight-based dosing calculations and the requirement for patients to prepare and draw up their own dose. 

## **3b) Combinations with other medicines** 

Is the medicine intended to be used in combination with any other medicines? 

• Yes / No If yes, please explain why and how the medicines work together. Please outline the mechanism of action of those other medicines so it is clear to patients why they are used together. If yes, please also provide information on the availability of the other medicine(s) as well as the main side effects. **If this submission is for a combination treatment, please ensure the sections on efficacy (3e), quality of life (3f) and safety/side effects (3g) focus on data that relate to the combination, rather than the individual treatments.** 

No, marstacimab is not intended to be used in combination with other medicines for the routine prophylaxis of bleeding episodes. 



<!-- page 172 -->

## **3c) Administration and dosing** 

How and where is the treatment given or taken? Please include the dose, how often the treatment should be given/taken, and how long the treatment should be given/taken for. 

How will this administration method or dosing potentially affect patients and caregivers? How does this differ to existing treatments? 

Treatment with marstacimab will be started under the supervision of a healthcare professional experienced in the treatment of haemophilia. It can then be self-administered by patients or caregivers after a doctor, nurse or pharmacist has shown the patient how to administer it using the pre-filled pen. 

The recommended dose for patients 12 years of age and older, weighing at least 35 kg, is an initial dose of 300 mg as a loading dose, given by subcutaneous injection by an experienced healthcare professional in the treatment of haemophilia. Thereafter, this will be followed by 150 mg by subcutaneous injection once weekly which can be self-administered by the patient. 

Dosing may be increased to 300 mg weekly in patients weighing ≥ 50 kg if bleeding is still considered uncontrolled by the healthcare professional. Marstacimab can be administered at any time of day. The recommended injection sites are the abdomen and thigh with recommendation for injection site rotation.

## **3e) Efficacy** 

Efficacy is the measure of how well a treatment works in treating a specific condition. 

In this section, please summarise all data that demonstrate how effective the treatment is compared with current treatments at treating the condition outlined in section 2a. Are any of the outcomes more important to patients than others and why? Are there any limitations to the data which may affect how to interpret the results? Please do not include academic or commercial in confidence information but where necessary reference the section of the company submission where this can be found. 

## **Efficacy results from the BASIS trial** 

The efficacy and safety of marstacimab compared with prior routine prophylaxis was demonstrated in the BASIS Phase 3 trial, described in Document B, Section B.2.6. 

## **Primary endpoint – Annualised bleeding rate for treated bleeds (ABRtreat):** 

This was the primary endpoint of the trial and represents the average number of treated bleeds per year experienced by patients. There was a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction (35.2%) in ABRtreat after 12 months of marstacimab prophylaxis in the ATP compared with 6 months of factor prophylaxis in the OP. 

## **Secondary endpoints:** 

Marstacimab also demonstrated numerically similar results to factor prophylaxis in other bleedrelated outcomes, with non-significant reductions in ABRjoint, ABRtarget joint, ABRspontaneous and ABRtotal observed between the OP and the ATP. Finally, the BASIS trial measured patients’ Haemophilia Joint Health Score (HJHS) which provides a measure of joint health for the knees, ankles, and elbows. Results at 6 months of the ATP revealed a numerical but non-significant improvement in joint health following marstacimab prophylaxis, compared to the 6 month OP value. 

## **Indirect treatment comparison (ITC)** 

Whilst the BASIS trial provides a comparison between marstacimab and factor prophylaxis products, there is no trial comparing marstacimab and emicizumab for patients with haemophilia A. Therefore, a statistical method was used to indirectly compare the marstacimab and emicizumab clinical trials to determine how their efficacy compare. The statistical method is known as an indirect treatment comparison (ITC), and the particular type of ITC used was a simulated treatment comparison (STC). 

Two clinical trials were used to provide clinical data on marstacimab (BASIS trial) and emicizumab (HAVEN3 trial). When the STC was used to indirectly compare the two drugs, overall, the results showed that the efficacy of marstacimab was similar to that of emicizumab for the prevention of bleeding events, with no statistically significant differences between results. 

## **Summary** 

The lack of direct head-to-head comparator trials and the limitations associated with conducting an indirect treatment comparison against emicizumab means there is some uncertainty associated with the efficacy results. However, the results from the BASIS trial demonstrate that marstacimab could provide a clinical benefit to patients, compared with current factor products used for prophylaxis, and the indirect treatment comparison revealed no statistically significant differences when marstacimab was compared to emicizumab.

## **3f) Quality of life impact of the medicine and patient preference information** 

What is the clinical evidence for a potential impact of this medicine on the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers? What quality of life instrument was used? If the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D) was used does it sufficiently capture quality of life for this condition? Are there other disease specific quality of life measures that should also be considered as supplementary information? 

Please outline in plain language any quality of life related data such as **patient reported outcomes (PROs).** Please include any **patient preference information (PPI)** relating to the drug profile, for instance research to understand willingness to accept the risk of side effects given the added benefit of treatment. Please include all references as required. 

## **Phase 3 BASIS trial** _**[45]**_ 

In the BASIS trial, several health-related quality of life (HRQoL) questionnaires were used to understand the impact of haemophilia disease and treatment options on a patients’ quality of life. Descriptions of these questionnaires are presented below. Full results are presented in Document B, Section B 2.6.3. 

## **EuroQol 5-dimension 5-level (EQ-5D-5L)** 

The EQ-5D-5L questionnaire measures 5 areas of health on a 5-point scale: Mobility, Self-care, Usual activities, Pain/discomfort, and Anxiety/depression. EQ-5D results can be used to generate utility values, where 1.0 represents perfect health and 0.0 represents death, which can then be applied in an economic analysis. Results showed that the change in quality of life from baseline for participants following marstacimab prophylaxis in the ATP was greater than the change from baseline for participants following routine prophylaxis in the OP, but this difference was statistically non-significant. 

## **Haemophilia Quality of Life Questionnaire for Adults (Haem-A-QoL)** 

This is a disease specific measure of HRQoL intended for adults with haemophilia. It assesses 10 areas of health: Physical Health, Feelings, View of Self, Sport/Leisure, Work/school, Dealing with Haemophilia, Treatment, Future, Family Planning, and Partnership and Sexuality. Results showed marstacimab prophylaxis maintained the benefit of prior routine prophylaxis, as measured by the change from baseline to 6 months for the Haem-A-QoL physical health domain and total score. 

## **Patients Global Impression of Change Haemophilia (PGIC-H)** 

Patients Global Impression of Change Haemophilia (PGIC-H) is a Haemophilia focused 7-point scale representing a patient’s rating of overall improvement in their life. Patients rate their change as “very much improved,” “much improved,” “minimally improved,” “no change,” “minimally worse,” “much worse,” or “very much worse”. Marstacimab prophylaxis during the BASIS study improved patient global impression of change in health state as assessed by the PGIC-H compared with prior routine prophylaxis. 

## **Haemophilia Activities List (HAL)** 

This is a measure of the impact of haemophilia on a patient’s ability to function. It assesses 7 domains: lying/sitting/kneeling/standing, lower (leg) functioning, upper (arm) functioning, transportation, self-care, household tasks, and sports/Leisure. Results showed treatment with 



<!-- page 176 -->

marstacimab was comparable to routine prophylaxis in improving a haemophilia patients’ ability to function. 

## **Haemophilia Life Impacts Questionnaire (HLIQ)** 

This is a 9-item assessment of the life impacts associated with living with and receiving treatment for haemophilia. With treatment with marstacimab, improvements in most HLIQ domains related to life impacts associated with living with and receiving treatment for haemophilia were observed. For example, from baseline to Year 1, the number of patients reporting that haemophilia was not on their mind at all increased from 16% to 26.7%. Detailed results of the haemophilia life impact questionnaire (HLIQ) are presented in Appendix M.2.4. 

## **Summary** 

Overall, marstacimab is comparable to routine prophylactic factor treatments with respect to disease specific and general patient reported HRQoL outcomes. 

## **3g) Safety of the medicine and side effects** 

When NICE appraises a treatment, it will pay close attention to the balance of the benefits of the treatment in relation to its potential risks and any side effects. Therefore, please outline the main side effects (as opposed to a complete list) of this treatment and include details of a benefit/risk assessment where possible. This will support patient reviewers to consider the potential overall benefits and side effects that the medicine can offer. 

Based on available data, please outline the most common side effects, how frequently they happen compared with standard treatment, how they could potentially be managed and how many people had treatment adjustments or stopped treatment. Where it will add value or context for patient readers, please include references to the Summary of Product Characteristics from regulatory agencies etc. 

Marstacimab was generally well tolerated in the clinical trial with no notable safety findings when compared with factor prophylaxis, as demonstrated in the BASIS trial. No deaths were reported and there have been no thrombotic (when a blood clots forms in an artery or vein) or embolic (a block in an artery caused by a blood clot or other substances) adverse events (AEs) recorded by patients treated with marstacimab during the BASIS trial. Marstacimab exhibits an acceptable safety profile versus factor prophylaxis. 

The majority of treatment emergent adverse event (an adverse event that starts or worsens after starting the medicine) were mild to moderate in severity. The most frequently observed treatment emergent adverse event (TEAEs) occurring in 5% or more patients during the 12months of marstacimab treatment were: COVID-19-related, itching, upper respiratory tract infection (infection affecting the nose, throat and airways), joint range of motion decreased, headache, and bruising. Furthermore, the overall occurrence and severity of TEAEs was generally similar across age subgroups (12 to <18 and ≥18 years).

## **3h) Summary of key benefits of treatment for patients** 

Issues to consider in your response: 

- Please outline what you feel are the key benefits of the treatment for patients, caregivers and their communities when compared with current treatments. 

- Please include benefits related to the mode of action, effectiveness, safety and mode of administration 

Overall, data for marstacimab show strong evidence to suggest it would be a valuable addition to the treatment pathway for patients with severe haemophilia A or B, without inhibitors. It offers an effective and conveniently administered prophylaxis therapy to patients, especially for haemophilia B patients for whom there is currently no subcutaneous treatment option available. 

## **Reduced treatment burden for patients:** 

As a once-weekly, subcutaneous injection, marstacimab has the potential to reduce the burden of current treatment with FVIII and FIX prophylaxis products which require frequent intravenous injections. This is particularly true in haemophilia B where there are currently no subcutaneous treatment options available to NHS patients. A subcutaneous option is also likely to be desirable for patients who currently struggle with venous access, required for intravenous products. 

## **Prevention of bleeding events:** 

Clinical evidence results from the BASIS trial showed marstacimab to be effective at controlling patient bleeding. Patients reported significant reductions in treated bleeds during the ATP compared with routine factor prophylaxis treatment in the OP. Marstacimab also showed improvements compared to routine factor prophylaxis in other bleed related end points, such as joint bleeds, spontaneous bleeds and total bleeds (treated and untreated), though these improvements were not significant. In summary, marstacimab has the potential to reduce the risk of bleeding episodes that are associated with pain, long-term joint damage, and anxiety and depression. 

In an indirect treatment comparison against emicizumab, the results showed that the efficacy of marstacimab was similar to that of emicizumab for the prevention of bleeding events, with no statistically significant differences between results. 

## **Acceptable safety profile:** 

The BASIS safety analysis results showed that marstacimab is well tolerated with no notable safety findings compared with factor prophylaxis.
