Though marstacimab is generally well tolerated, in the BASIS clinical trial a small number of patients experienced a serious AE (SAE). However, only one of those SAEs (Grade 1 peripheral calf swelling) were considered to be related to the treatment marstacimab. Overall, marstacimab is well tolerated with no notable safety findings. 

## **3j) Value and economic considerations** 

## **Introduction for patients:** 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g., whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g., travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

## **How the model reflects severe haemophilia A and B** 

A health economic model has been developed to assess the value of the drug marstacimab to the NHS. The model is split into three health states which is designed to reflect the condition of patients. The three health states are: 

- Bleeds (consisting of both joint and non-joint bleeds) 

- No bleeds 

- Dead 

The model estimated the total costs of treating a patient with marstacimab across their lifetime. As mentioned, the main treatment options for patients with severe haemophilia A or B are emicizumab, FVIII and FIX prophylaxis. As such, the model aimed to compare the cost of managing a patient with marstacimab against the cost of managing a patient with each of the three current treatment options (comparators). 

## **Modelling how marstacimab extends life** 

There is no scientific evidence that marstacimab extends life compared to current treatments and therefore no effect on mortality is considered in the model. 



<!-- page 179 -->

## **Modelling how marstacimab improves quality of life** 

Marstacimab is able to improve quality of life via two routes. The first route is by reducing the number of bleeding events experienced by a patient. In the model, each individual bleeding event results in a short-term reduction in quality of life. To inform bleeding rates in the model, efficacy data for factor prophylaxis treatments and marstacimab was informed by data collected from the Phase 3 BASIS trial. The efficacy of emicizumab was informed by the results of the ITC mentioned previously. The second route intends to capture the impact of treatment administration on quality of life. Clinical experts consulted as part of this appraisal agreed that both the route of administration (SC vs IV) and the frequency of administration would have an impact on a patient’s quality of life. Therefore, in the model, each injection results in a short-term reduction in quality of life. Consequently, an intervention that reduces bleeding, has a subcutaneous administration, and is administered less frequency, will result in a better quality of life for patients. 

## **Modelling the costs for different treatments** 

Research has shown that drug costs account for the majority (99%) of direct medical costs for patients with haemophilia[40] . In the model, drug costs for prophylaxis are included for each treatment. Additionally, drug costs associated with “on-demand” treatment of bleeding are included for each individual bleeding event. Beyond drug costs, the model also includes costs of managing bleeding events such as the cost of hospital stays, orthopaedist visits, haematologist visits and visits to A&E. The cost of managing adverse events was also included in the model in a scenario analysis. 

## **Uncertainty** 

The model made several assumptions including the use of the overall BASIS trial data to inform efficacy for both FVIII and FIX products and the use of an ITC to inform the efficacy of emicizumab. These assumptions are further described in Section B3.9.2. In order to explore the uncertainty in the assumptions made, alternative model scenarios were also calculated to see if the results changed significantly. 

## **Cost-effectiveness results** 

Marstacimab was found to be more effective and less costly than both FVIII and FIX prophylaxis. Compared to emicizumab, marstacimab resulted in fewer quality adjusted life years (QALYs) but was less costly, resulting in cost-savings for the NHS. Alternative model scenarios demonstrated that marstacimab consistently remained cost-effective against all comparators, even when different assumptions were used. Overall, marstacimab can be considered a cost-effective use of NHS resources, whilst also expanding the choice of therapies available to both patients with haemophilia and their clinicians, offering a convenient, easy to use prophylaxis therapy. 

## **Limitations of the cost-effectiveness analysis:** 

A key limitation was the lack of data available to inform the long-term impact on joint health for patients with haemophilia. Joint health is an important factor for patients with haemophilia and can have a significant impact on their quality of life, as explained in Section B.1.3.1.5 of 



<!-- page 180 -->

Document B. However, data on the long-term impact of marstacimab on joint damage is lacking. Therefore, any long-term improvements in joint health and reductions in joint pain following treatment with marstacimab, compared with factor prophylaxis, may not be fully captured in the model. As a result, the model could underestimate the potential health and cost benefits that marstacimab may offer through reduction of long-term joint damage as a result of the observed improvements in joint bleed rates. Other limitations include the lack of direct trial evidence comparing marstacimab to emicizumab and the lack of long-term data for marstacimab beyond the open-label extension (OLE) data from BASIS. 

## **3k) Innovation** 

NICE considers how innovative a new treatment is when making its recommendations. If the company considers the new treatment to be innovative please explain how it represents a ‘step change’ in treatment and/ or effectiveness compared with current treatments. Are there any QALY benefits that have not been captured in the economic model that also need to be considered (see section 3f) 

Factor prophylaxis treatment is associated with substantial administration burden; the need for frequent self-administered intravenous infusions greatly interferes with an individual’s ability to take part in day-to-day activities that others without the condition may take for granted.[8,15,33] Additionally, although emicizumab offers a subcutaneous option for individuals with haemophilia A, self-administration of emicizumab still requires the individual to first determine their correct dose (based on their body weight) and then draw this up into the syringe, prior to administration.[31] 

Therefore, a substantial unmet need exists for an efficacious therapy with a novel mechanism of action and a convenient and simple method of administration, especially for individuals with haemophilia B where there are currently no subcutaneous treatment options available to NHS patients. Marstacimab is an innovative therapy that offers a practical pre-filled subcutaneous, self-administered, prophylactic option for individuals with severe haemophilia A or B. Treatment with marstacimab has the potential to free patients from the burden of regular factor infusions, allowing patients to live life more freely.

## **4b) Glossary of terms** 

**Annualised bleeding rate (ABR):** The number of bleeding events a person experiences each year. **ABRtreat:** annualised bleeding rate of treated bleeds. 

**ABRjoint:** annual bleed rate of treated joint bleeds. **ABRtarget joint:** annualised bleeding rate of treated target joint bleeds. **ABRspontaneous:** annualised bleeding rate of spontaneous bleeds. **ABRtotal:** annualised bleeding rate of total (treated and untreated) bleeds. 

**Factor VIII:** A protein that helps the blood to clot. Individuals with haemophilia A have a defect in the gene responsible for producing factor VIII. 

**Factor IX (FIX)** : A protein that helps the blood to clot. Individuals with haemophilia B have a defect in the gene responsible for producing factor IX, known as FIX. 

**Indirect treatment comparison (ITC):** In the absence of direct evidence (e.g., a single trial comparing different treatments), indirect treatment comparisons can estimate the relative treatment effects of two or more treatments. 

**Quality adjusted life year (QALY):** The number of additional years patients spend alive; however this measure also takes into account the quality of these additional years. 

**On-demand treatment:** Following a bleeding episode, administration of Factor VIII/IX can also be given “on-demand” with the aim of stopping bleeding once it has occurred. 

**Prophylaxis treatment:** Regular injections of Factor VIII/IX into the vein to raise the factor levels in the blood with the aim of preventing bleeding. 

**Standard half-life (SHL) products:** Drugs which require administration multiple times per week. **Extended half-life (EHL) products:** Drugs which are typically administered once weekly. **Health-related quality of life (HRQoL):** A broad concept commonly used to examine the impact of health status on quality of life. Simply, it narrows quality of life to aspects relevant to health. **Infusion:** Medication is administered via a needle into a vein.

## **Clarification response summary from the company** 

There are a number of questions requesting additional data analysis for haemophilia A and B subtypes. However, due to the targeting of marstacimab as a treatment for both haemophilia A and B, the BASIS study was not powered to detect differences within subgroups. Given the lack of powering and small sample sizes associated with the subgroup analyses by haemophilia type (A or B, particularly for haemophilia B), the company has provided the information requested for completeness in response to questions (e.g. A25, A26, A27, A28, A37, A40, B5). However, we recommend that these data are interpreted with caution. 

Additionally, there were a number of requests for data for other subgroups including with and without censoring for dose escalation (e.g. A26, A27, A28, A39, A40), factor prophylaxis therapy type (e.g. A23, B2, B3, B4) and weight and age (e.g. B6). The company has provided the information requested for completeness in response to these questions however, given the small sample sizes, the company recommend that these data are interpreted with caution. 

The original company submission presented data from a March 2023 data cut of the open label extension (OLE) study. A more recent analysis comprising of a 4-month safety update was conducted in October 2023 and presented at the European Haematology Association conference in June 2024. The October 2023 data cut was a limited data cut primarily assessing safety for regulatory commitments and no study report is available. However, main trial endpoints were also analysed and this October 2023 data-cut has been used to respond to the majority of the OLE requests in these clarification questions. However, not all trial endpoints were assessed as part of this interim analysis (e.g., patient reported outcomes) and therefore, for some clarification question responses, data from the original March 2023 data cut has been presented. 

For clarity, a summary of the different data sources used to respond to each clarification question related to the marstacimab clinical trials is provided in Table 1 below. The company have also clarified in the individual questions responses which OLE data set has been used. An updated company submission document (Document B) including the topline results from the October 2023 data cut will also be provided.

**A13. Annualised Bleeding Rate (ABR) is measured as either total bleeds, treated bleeds, joint bleeds, or non-joint bleeds. Please provide additional details on the definition of a bleed and how it was measured, providing evidence from the literature on standardised methods to measure bleeding. What guidance was given to participants about recording and seeking treatment for their bleeds? Please confirm how simultaneous (or near simultaneous) bleeds on multiple joints were classified? Is there the potential for overcounting when these rates are applied in the economic model?** 

As a result of the treatment shift from on-demand to prophylactic management of haemophilia, bleeds, rather than factor activity levels, have become the primary outcome to evaluate new therapies.[5] However, it is recognised that not all bleeds are the same and the need to subdivide this parameter has evolved. For instance, as the goal of prophylactic treatment is primarily driven by the preservation of joint health, joint-specific ABR is commonly included as a secondary outcome. Moreover, the concept of breakthrough bleeding has originally been proposed to reflect the overall haemostatic efficacy of a treatment that has historically been characterised by peaks and troughs of factor activity, resulting in the further delineation of treated and total bleeding events across all contemporary clinical programs.[6-8] 

The strengths of ABR as a primary efficacy endpoint are two-fold: first, it is a meaningful, singular clinical event that patients associate with their haemophilia management. Second, ABR is also strongly associated with joint function and serves as a surrogate for long-term joint health. While other assessment modalities for joint function exist (like the Haemophilia Joint Health Score [HJHS]), they require a much longer observation period.[9-11] 

ABR is not without limitations. The subjective nature of patient-reported bleeding, especially joint bleeding, limits its reliability, as joint pain and swelling may indicate arthritis and inflammation rather than bleeding.[12] Clinically, patients are instructed to treat any suspected bleeding, as under ‐ treatment or delayed treatment may accelerate joint deterioration, and thus may result in over ‐ reporting of bleeding to prevent long ‐ term complications. Therefore, haemophilia providers ‐ acknowledge the possibility of over treatment, especially in patients with established joint disease.[13] 

The identification of a bleeding episode is clarified in the Protocol Appendix 10.10.[2] Any sign or symptom of a bleed, regardless of whether or not medication/treatment is administered, was reported as a “bleed” or “bleeding episode”. Bleeds related to a procedure/surgery such as haematomas/bruising resulting from any surgeries or invasive procedures (e.g., tooth extractions, venipuncture, or subcutaneous drug administrations) or invasive diagnostic procedures (e.g., lumbar puncture, endoscopy with biopsy) were not counted as bleeds. All data during the 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 195 -->

preventative treatment for medical/dental procedures, sport activity, or physical therapy (plus 72 hours) were not included in the derivation of the ABR. 

A treated bleed from the same location occurring >72 hours after stopping treatment from the original bleed for which treatment was initiated, or a treated bleed occurring at a different site regardless of the time of the bleed, was considered a new treated bleed. In addition, the determination of whether a bleed is treated needed to satisfy two conditions: 1) the participant reported the bleed as “treated” in the Bleed Diary, and 2) an infusion AFTER the bleed was reported in the Infusion Diary.[2] 

Multiple concurrent bleeds (spontaneous or traumatic) on the same date and time but in different locations were recorded as 1 bleed for that participant. However, the bleed was counted towards all attributable locations in summaries of bleeds of specific site. If concurrent bleeds occurred on the same day but different times and different locations, they were counted as independent bleeds. On the other hand, if concurrent bleeds occurred on the same day but different times at the SAME location, they were counted as 1 bleed. Overall, the company believe the potential for overcounting simultaneous bleeds in the economic model is negligible. 

Teaching materials were not provided as part of BASIS prior to study initiation, however, instruction on how to recognise bleeds is standard care for patients with haemophilia and their caregivers.[14] At enrolment in BASIS, participants were provided Bleeding/Treatment Diary training (including the timing and nature of the information to be entered). At each study visit following Enrolment, the participant’s diary was reviewed to ensure compliance with prescribed haemophilia treatments (including those used to treat breakthrough bleeding) and assessment of bleeds (including bleeding site and if bleeds were “spontaneous” or “traumatic”) as outlined in Protocol Amendment 7 Section 1.3.[2] Additionally, within the eTouch device under the Bleed Log, the definitions of Spontaneous, Traumatic and Medical/Dental Procedure were available to participants. Considering a participant’s prior knowledge of bleed recognition, assessment, and discussion of bleed type at every visit and the definitions provided by the eTouch device, the company is confident that participants were competent to distinguish between the different bleeding types. 

## **A14. The results available for BASIS OLE are from an interim analysis from March 2023, when do you anticipate publication of these (or subsequent data cuts) of BASIS?** 

Additional follow-up data (4-month safety update; cut-off October 2023) was recently presented at the European Haematology Association (EHA, June 13-16 2024).[4] The October 2023 data cut was a limited data cut primarily assessing safety for regulatory commitments and no study report is available. However, main trial endpoints were also analysed and this October 2023 data-cut has been used to respond to the majority of the OLE requests in these clarification questions. However, not all trial endpoints were assessed as part of this interim analysis (e.g., patient reported outcomes) and therefore, for some clarification question responses, data from the original March 2023 data cut has been presented. For clarity, a summary of the different data cuts used to respond to each clarification question related to the marstacimab clinical trials is provided in Table 1 at the start of this response document. 

At the time of this analysis, 107 of 116 (92.2%) of non-inhibitor participants from the pivotal study had enrolled in the OLE study (32 from the prior on-demand group and 75 from the prior prophylaxis group). Participants on marstacimab prophylaxis demonstrated sustained reductions 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 196 -->

in treated ABR (OD: 3.70 [95% CI: 2.19, 6.26]; RP: 2.79 [95% CI: 1.95, 3.98]). The next interim analysis is planned for the OLE cohort when 12 months of follow-up data is available for all noninhibitor participants (estimated date of data availability October 2024). 

The primary completion date (Last Subject Last Visit) for the OLE is currently anticipated as Q3 2030 but this is potentially subject to change. The final Clinical Study Report will be available within ~4 months of the primary completion date, i.e., it is anticipated Q4 2030, assuming no change to the primary completion date.

## **A20. Table 4 of the BASIS Trial Clinical Study Report, p.50 states several incorrect/incomplete patient-reported outcomes (PROs). Please detail how these were accounted for in the analysis.** 

For the physical health domain and the total score of Haem-A-QoL, as well as EQ-5D-5L index score and EQ-VAS score, the superiority and non-inferiority testing was conducted as outlined in Sections 5.1.2 and 5.1.3 of the BASIS statistical analysis plan (SAP), based on the Wilcoxon signed rank test.[16] In summary, missing observations for these endpoints were handled via multiple imputation approach under the ‘missing at random’ assumption for the main analyses. Sensitivity tipping point analyses were also conducted via successively applying pessimistic assumptions for missingness due to withdrawals due to AE or lack of efficacy. More detail is provided below. 

For the Wilcoxon signed rank test used to analyse physical health domain and the total score of Haem-A-QoL, as well as EQ-5D-5L index score and EQ-VAS scores, a multiple imputation approach with 10 imputations was applied via monotone or fully conditional specification (FCS) regression approach utilising the ‘missing at random’ assumption. The same approach was used for the following endpoints: HJHS total score, Haemo-QoL total score, HAL/pedHAL total score, and PGIC. For the domain or component scores (9 in Haem-A-QoL, 12 in Haemo-QoL, 10 in HAL, and 7 in pedHAL), a single imputation procedure using the month 6 OP value was used for the Wilcoxon signed rank test. Further information regarding missing data is detailed in Section 5.3.5.3 Methods to Manage Missing Data of the BASIS statistical analysis plan.[16] Appendix 5 of the SAP includes example SAS and R codes for multiple imputation, analysis of each imputed data set, and the final combined testing and inferences. 

The BASIS CSR states PRO questionnaires not completed resulted in missing PRO data, however, the impact of the missing data was minimal on the overall analysis of the PRO data.[1]

Participants in the non-inhibitor factor prophylaxis and on-demand haemophilia A and haemophilia B study populations were evaluated in BASIS if they met criteria for dose escalation and whether or not they dose escalated. In the routine prophylaxis group ****% (*****) of haemophilia A participants compared to ****% (****) of haemophilia B participants met dose escalation criteria, however, only * (****%) of the factor prophylaxis haemophilia A participants that met dose escalation criteria were dose escalated while * ***** of the factor prophylaxis haemophilia B participants that met criteria were dose escalated. 

According to the protocol (Protocol Amendment 7 Section 6.6) “modification of study intervention dose is not required, but under certain circumstances, is allowed”.[2] The same guidance was used for both the primary study as well as the OLE. Following 6 months of active treatment with marstacimab and at any time after completion of Visit 14, the dose may be escalated from 150 mg SC QW to 300 mg SC QW if the following criterion is met: 

- The participant must weigh at least 50 kg in order to escalate to the 300 mg SC QW dose 

- The participant must have two or more spontaneous bleeds (consisting of joint bleeds or significant soft tissue/muscle or other site bleeds) treated with infusions of FVIII or FIX over a 6-month period in the absence of a confirmed FVIII or FIX inhibitor, respectively. 

The choice to escalate a participant’s dose was at the discretion of the investigator and the decision not to increase did not need to be discussed with the sponsor.

## **A24. Please confirm how pausing of marstacimab for COVID-19 impacted patients in BASIS and how this was factored into data-collection and analyses (i.e. duration of discontinuation, alternative therapies received, how key trial data were collected and analysed).** 

The study began on 09 March 2020 and was ongoing at the time of last patient last visit for the non-inhibitor cohort, which included the period during which the COVID-19 pandemic was occurring globally. The study was safely conducted, despite the impact of the pandemic, and the objectives of the primary analysis for the non-inhibitor cohort were achieved. The overall COVID19 impact on the study was minimal. 

No sites were closed due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Protocol deviations related to COVID- 19 were reported during the study (as described in Section 4.2 of the BASIS CSR).[1] 


Clarification questions 



<!-- page 201 -->

No participants discontinued study intervention due to COVID-19 related events. No SAEs or deaths due to COVID-19 occurred during the study. 

Treatment with marstacimab was suspended for any participant with presumed or confirmed symptomatic COVID-19 infection (see amendment to Protocol Section 7.1).[2] These patients were discussed with the Pfizer Medical Monitor to determine next steps prior to resumption of treatment with the study intervention. Management was individualised and varied; however, the majority of patients required no change in treatment and recommenced marstacimab once the COVID-19 infection had resolved. 3 patients required factor replacement during the time they had COVID-19 infection.

If possible, please also perform the analyses using data from months 1-7 of the ATP period, and with/without censoring for dose escalation.** 

Although participants receiving routine prophylaxis during the OP were only followed for 6 months, routine prophylaxis is considered standard of care and it is likely these participants were receiving prophylactic treatment for a period of time before enrolment in the OP. In contrast, participants receiving marstacimab in the ATP were new to marstacimab and therefore follow-up is required to observe clinical outcomes once steady-state concentrations are reached. Additionally, except for the endpoint ‘proportion with no bleed’, the other endpoints are annualised bleeding rates and therefore are already adjusted for the follow-up time period. Therefore, the company believe that utilising the entirety of the 12 month ATP follow-up for analysis is most appropriate.

## **Additionally, results from EconLit and NHS EED are recorded in the PRISMA diagram (Appendix D.1.3 Fig. 1) but not elsewhere for the clinical SLR.** 

Initially, the scope for both clinical and economics SLRs were covered in a single search strategy and screening process. In 2023 the SLRs were split out, each with separate search strategies, methods and reporting. The results in the search strategy tables provides the results related to the clinical SLR only. In contrast, the PRISMA diagram included results from the original SLR, including both the clinical and economic SLR, which explains this discrepancy. 

As noted in Appendix section G.1.1. NHS Economic Evaluation Database (EED) was searched as part of the original SLR. However, this database was discontinued in 2015, and therefore were not searched as part of the SLR update. EconLIT was also not searched as part of the SLR update. 

Results for the search of EconLit in 2020 are presented in Table 29 of the Appendices of the Company Submission and results of the search on NHS EED in 2020 are presented in Table 30 of the Appendices of the Company Submission.

## **B1. Within the PSA it appears that the treated ABR is sampled but the treated AJBR is not. Is this the case and if so why? Is there a condition that imposes ABR ≥ AJBR?** 

The company can confirm that within the PSA of the originally submitted economic model, the treated AJBR was sampled but the treated ABR was not (n.b. this is slightly different from what has been stated in the question above). However, the company agrees that both treated ABR and treated AJBR should ideally be sampled within the PSA (and DSA, for completeness) and that there should also be a condition imposing ABR ≥ AJBR in this case. 

This has now been included within the updated model version provided with this response (with corresponding changes in the Parameters, DSA Inputs and PSA Inputs sheets indicated via green highlighting). 

Whilst the inclusion of treated ABR leads to an overall slightly larger spread of the probabilistic results (Figure 1 and Figure 2), which is to be expected based on introducing additional uncertainty to the PSA by adding new parameters to it, the probabilistic average results are essentially unchanged from the originally submitted analyses (Table 11).

## **B7. Please confirm whether the various ABRs used in the economic model have come from fitting a GEE model or not (e.g. Table 30). Please provide ABR estimates from whichever approach is currently omitted.** 

All ABRs used within the economic analysis have been directly derived from BASIS trial observations and did not include any additional fitting (see Document B, Table 30 of the Company Submission for the values used in the model base case). These were deemed the most appropriate choice for the purpose of the model given they lead to consistent results between subgroups, which may not be the case for independently fitted subgroup ABR sets and represent the actual rates of bleeds seen in the BASIS trial. 

As demonstrated in Table 15 for the model base case-relevant parameters, GEE model-fitted ABRtreat and AJBRtreat estimates do not significantly differ from the trial-observed equivalent values, it would therefore not be expected that their possible inclusion would change the results and conclusion of the economic analysis.

## **Identification, selection and synthesis of clinical evidence** 

**==> picture [21 x 12] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Identification and selection of relevant studies** 

A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted on the 4[th] August 2020 (original SLR) and subsequently updated on the 21[st] August 2023 and 17[th] May 2024. The objective of the SLR was to identify all relevant clinical efficacy and safety evidence for marstacimab and relevant comparator therapies for the treatment of severe haemophilia A and moderately severe to severe haemophilia B without a history of factor VIII or IX inhibitors. The SLR was wider in scope than the proposed indication in this submission, as it additionally included patients with moderately severe haemophilia B. This reflects the enrolment protocol for the BASIS trial, however, the trial ultimately did not enrol any patients with moderately severe haemophilia B. 

The SLR was performed in accordance with the methodological principles of conduct for SLRs as detailed in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions[1] and guidelines outlined by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).[2, 3] 

## **D.1.1. Search strategy** 

## **Electronic database searches** 

Across the original SLR and the 2023 and 2024 SLR updates, the following electronic databases were searched via the OvidSP® platform: 

- MEDLINE® and Epub Ahead of Print, In-Process, In-Data-Review & Other Non-Indexed Citations and Daily 

- EMBASE 

- Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) 

- Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR) 

- Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects (DARE) 

The original SLR was limited to records published after 2000 to capture the most relevant and recent evidence reflecting current treatments that have become available during the last decade. DARE was discontinued in 2015; therefore, only the archived databases (until 2015) were searched. 

Search terms used for the electronic database searches are presented below (Table 1–Table 14). The search terms for each database included a combination of free-text search terms and controlled vocabulary terms. Searches were restricted to studies conducted in humans and published in English. 

The 2024 update used the same strategy as 2023, however the following amendments were made to the search strategy between the 2020 SLR and the first update in 2023.

- The searches were modified from the 4[th] August 2020 search strategy to combine the terms for haemophilia A and haemophilia B together and to remove terms for economic and observational studies 

- The Embase search strategy was expanded to include any conference indexed in the database 

- Terms related to publication type that were not relevant to the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were removed (i.e., terms to limit to clinical trials or exclude review articles are not needed as only records of clinical trials are included in this database) 

- The DARE database was not searched in 2023 or 2024 as the database has been discontinued in 2015

## **Clinical Trial Registries** 

Keyword searches were conducted across the following clinical trial registries: 

- ClinicalTrials.gov 

- WHO ICTRP 

- EMA EPARs 

Clinical trial registry records were linked to trial publications when possible. Clinical trial registry records that could not be linked to a publication were only included when trial results were available. Ongoing trials with no available results were excluded. 

## **Conferences and Congresses** 

Embase includes abstracts from many major conferences, dating back to 2009. As there is sometimes a delay in when conference abstracts are indexed in Embase, manual searches were conducted for the most current meeting year after each electronic database search for the following conferences. 

- Congress of the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) 

- Annual Congress of the European Association for Haemophilia and Allied Disorders (EAHAD) 

- World Congress of the World Federation of Hemophilia (WFH) 

- Annual Meeting of the American Society of Hematology (ASH) 

- Annual Congress of European Hematology Association (EHA) 

## **Bibliography searches** 

The bibliographies of relevant published reviews evaluating treatments for haemophilia were reviewed as another method to identify relevant studies. 

## **D.1.2. Study selection** 

Studies were selected for inclusion in two stages: first, the titles and abstracts of the search results were reviewed for relevance according to the eligibility criteria for the SLR; second, the full texts of potentially relevant articles were screened in order to obtain the final list of included studies. 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for the treatment of severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 244 -->

The eligibility criteria for the clinical SLR are listed in Table 15. Trials meeting the PICOTS criteria after full-text review were linked (results for the same trial reported in more than one publication, the relevant reports were grouped per trial) and included for data extraction. The screening process for all records and full-text reports was recorded in an Excel file. The file included the full list of reports and the final decision regarding each inclusion or exclusion. In the case of exclusion, the reason based on the PICOTS criteria was also recorded. The criteria are presented according to the Population, Intervention, Comparators, Outcomes, Timing, and Study design (PICOTS) format.[4] 

## **Title/abstract review** 

The titles and abstracts of all unique records identified from the searches were screened independently by two reviewers with disagreements adjudicated by a third reviewer. Trials meeting the PICOTS criteria after full-text review were linked (results for the same trial reported in more than one publication, the relevant reports were grouped per trial) and included for data extraction. The screening process for all records and full-text reports was recorded in an Excel file. The file included the full list of reports and the final decision regarding each inclusion or exclusion. In the case of exclusion, the reason based on the PICOTS criteria was also recorded. 

Furthermore, DistillerSR’s artificial intelligence technology was used to re-screen all excluded records and assign each a probability of likelihood for inclusion based on the final inclusion and exclusion decisions of each record. Any reference with a probability ranking over 85% was rescreened by a third reviewer. 

## **Full-text review** 

Each full-text of relevant records identified from the title and abstract screening was then reviewed against the eligibility criteria by two independent reviewers, with disagreements adjudicated by a third reviewer (Table 15). Trials meeting the PICOTS criteria after full-text review were linked (results for the same trial reported in more than one publication, the relevant reports were grouped per trial) and included for data extraction. The screening process for all records and full-text reports was recorded in an Excel file. The file included the full list of reports and the final decision regarding each inclusion or exclusion. In the case of exclusion, the reason based on the PICOTS criteria was also recorded.

## **Quality assessment** 

As recommended by NICE, the quality assessment of all included studies was conducted using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool 2 (RoB 2) for RCTs. In addition, non-randomised trials including single-arm trials were assessed using a modified version of the Downs and Black Checklist.

## **D.1.4. Summary of trials used for indirect or mixed treatment comparisons** 

Included studies were prioritised for the ITC feasibility assessment. The initial feasibility assessment comprised of the following criteria: 

- Were baseline characteristics reported for the target population? (Yes or no); baseline data are important for assessing the comparability of trial populations 

- Did the trial report at least one primary or secondary outcome from the BASIS trial? (Yes or no); similar outcome measures are required for conducting ITC analysis 

- Did the trial include any individuals from North America, Europe, or the United Kingdom? (Yes or no); settings that may affect health care or patient management should be minimised to reduce differences between trial populations 

- Were outcome data available between 6-months and 24-months after treatment initiation? (Yes or no); follow-up time between trials should be comparable 

- Were later trial phase data available (e.g., Phase 3 or 4) for treatments evaluated in trials described as Phase 1 or 2? (Yes or no); the ITC should focus on the most relevant data for a given comparator treatment (e.g., recommended dose, regimen, clinical outcomes) 

- Other criteria for exclusion: 

   - Historical product that is not widely used in clinical practice 

   - Experimental treatments for which the manufacturer has terminated development 

Among the 79 trials included in the SLR, two investigated marstacimab (BASIS trial and a Phase 2 trial), of which the BASIS trial was selected as the referenced for comparison, and 77 investigated comparator treatments. The prioritisation process to identify trials for inclusion in the ITC feasibility assessment yielded 30 trials to proceed for evaluation within the feasibility assessment. The reasons for deprioritising the excluded 48 comparator studies are presented in Table 17.

Of the remaining 30 studies, evaluating 22 different interventions, 28 were subsequently excluded because they did not report on a relevant comparator of interest to the decision problem: 

- Since factor replacement therapy was evaluated in the BASIS trial, studies assessing these therapies (n=22) were not considered for inclusion into the ITC analyses. 

- In addition, six trials were excluded because they assessed gene therapies (n=4) or rebalancing agents (n=2) which were not relevant candidate therapies for the target population of this submission. 

The reasons for excluding these remaining 28 studies are presented in Table 17. The remaining two trials, HAVEN-3 and HAVEN-4, both evaluating emicizumab, were identified and carried forward to the feasibility assessment reported in Section B.2.11.1 of Document B.

## **D.1.5.1. Identification of effect modifiers and prognostic variables** 

Relevant effect modifiers and/or prognostic variables to include into the unanchored ITCs were identified based on a review of the literature, input from clinical experts, and results of regression 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for the treatment of severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 271 -->

analyses. First, an initial set of potentially relevant variables was identified based on prior publications which included the following covariates: age, race/ethnicity, body weight or BMI, prior bleeding events (e.g., number of prior bleeds or prior total ABR), target joints, and prior factor product class product (i.e., extended half-life vs. standard half-life).[5-9] This initial list of variables was reviewed by clinical experts who confirmed their clinical relevance. 

Second, the selected covariates were examined in a series of regression analyses to assess the degree to which they were prognostic using individual-level data from the BASIS trial. Body weight, prior factor product class product, and number of bleeds prior to enrolment were excluded from the analyses due to collinearity with BMI, dose-schedule of prior therapy, and prior total ABR, respectively. Rate ratios were estimated for total ABR using negative binomial regression with log-time as an offset term and odds ratios for zero total bleed events (Yes/No) was modelled using logistic regression. Both univariable and multivariable regression analyses were performed. Given the limited sample size of the BASIS trial, a liberal p-value of 0.1 was used to define statistical significance within the multivariable analyses. A complete case analysis was performed whereby one individual was excluded from the analyses due to missing information on race/ethnicity. 

Based on results of the regression analyses, age, race/ethnicity, target joints, and prior total ABR were identified as statistically significant prognostic factors (Table 18). Notably, prior total ABR was the only covariate that remained statistically significant within the multivariable analyses for both outcomes.

## **D.1.8. Risk of bias of studies included in indirect or mixed treatment** 

## **comparisons** 

A quality assessment of the HAVEN 3 trial was performed using a modified version of the Downs and Black Checklist.[10] In this checklist, up to one point can be awarded for 26 questions and up to 2 for one question giving a maximum of 28 points per trial. Overall, the HAVEN 3 trial had a score of 13 which falls within the “poor” category (Table 19).

## **F.1.2. Clinical laboratory values** 

Overall, clinical laboratory results, as measured by change from baseline, for blood chemistry, haematology and other parameters showed no clinically important findings in the BASIS trial. Parameters indicative of bleeding, such as haemoglobin levels, remained stable or improved during marstacimab treatment in the ATP, compared with the OP. 

None of the laboratory test anomalies were considered to be clinically significant or reported as AEs by the investigator. 

## **Anti-drug antibodies** 

Across both on-demand and prior prophylaxis cohorts, 116 patients were evaluable for anti-drug (marstacimab) antibodies (ADA). Twenty-three patients (19.8%) were ADA positive, with ADAs transient in 14 patients (61%) and persistent in 9 patients (39%). By the end of the study, ADAs were resolved in 22 of the 23 patients (95.7%). Overall, ADA analysis indicated that marstacimab immunogenicity in the study population was of low incidence and mostly transient in nature. 

## **Haemoglobin parameters** 

Haemoglobin levels in the OP were generally comparable with the marstacimab ATP. Mean change from baseline to last visit on treatment was –0.3 g/L (SD: 10.83) in the OP versus 0.1 g/L (SD: 9.73) in the ATP. Haemoglobin remained within the normal range during the ATP. 

## **Fibrinogen** 

Fibrinogen values reported during the 6 month OP were compared to values reported during the 12 month ATP. Most fibrinogen values reported were normal in the OP, with small decreases detected during the ATP which is consistent with the known pharmacology of marstacimab. The mean change from baseline to last visit on treatment for fibrinogen during the OP was –0.3 g/L 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for the treatment of severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 281 -->

(SD: 0.97), compared with –0.2 g/L (SD: 0.64) during the marstacimab ATP. There were no AEs related to decreases in fibrinogen.

## **Additional safety data from the OLE** 

## **Original submission – March 2023 OLE data cut** 

Safety data from the OLE indicated that long term administration of marstacimab beyond 12 months in the BASIS trial ATP and up to an average of 16 months was well tolerated in patients with haemophilia. During the OLE, 22 of the 58 patients who had been receiving factor prophylaxis in the BASIS trial OP experienced an adverse event (37.9%). There were two (3.4%) serious adverse events, however neither were considered treatment related. 

Treatment-related AEs were reported in 3 participants (5.2%) and included one injection site bruising, one injection site induration and one injection site swelling. 

There were no deaths or discontinuations from the OLE due to AEs. Three individuals (5.2%) temporarily discontinued marstacimab prophylaxis; two (3.4%) due to COVID-19 and one (1.7%) due to haemarthrosis, neither of which were deemed to be treatment related. Two participants (3.4%) experienced SAEs however none were considered treatment related by the investigator. Eleven participants (19.0%) experienced an AESI, however only three (5.2%), all injection site reactions, were considered treatment related. 

## **Updated submission – October 2023 OLE data cut** 

Safety data from the OLE indicated that long term administration of marstacimab beyond 12 months in the BASIS trial ATP and up to 23 months was well tolerated in patients with haemophilia. 

Those patients who received routine prophylaxis in the OP and went on to enter the OLE (n=75), 20% (n=15) reported AESIs; four patients (5.3%) had COVID-19, four patients (5.3%) had haemorrhage, four patients (5.3%) had hypersensitivity, two patients (2.7%) had hypertension, six patients (8.0%) had injection site reactions. Five patients (6.7%) experienced a SAE, although none were considered treatment related and no patients discontinued due to SAEs.[12, 13] 

There were no deaths or thromboembolic events reported in the OLE.

## **Published cost-effectiveness studies** 

## **G.1. Identification of studies** 

A SLR was conducted on 4[th] August 2020 (original SLR) in order to identify clinical efficacy and safety outcomes, as well as novel economic evidence in the form of economic evaluations, utility/health-related quality of life (utility/HRQoL) studies and healthcare cost and resource use (HCRU) studies in people with moderately severe-to-severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B. The SLR was updated on 30[th] May 2024 with a focus on the economic evidence only. The SLR was wider in scope than the proposed indication in this submission, as it additionally included patients with moderately severe disease, to ensure that no relevant information was missed; however, data for subgroups with severe disease were extracted separately where available. 

The databases and hand searches were conducted simultaneously for the SLR of economic evaluations (Appendix G), utility/HRQoL studies (Appendix H) and HCRU studies (Appendix I). Each record identified in these searches was assessed for eligibility across all three data streams simultaneously (economic evaluations, utility/HRQoL and HCRU). Each study identified could therefore be included in one or more streams of the SLR. Appendix G.1.1 presents the search strategy across all three streams of the SLR; study selection and extracted data are presented for each stream individually in Appendix G, Appendix H and Appendix I. 

The SLR was performed in accordance with a pre-specified protocol. This involved searching electronic databases, manual hand-searching of key conference proceedings from the last two years, manual hand-searching of key HTA body websites and health economics databases, and manual hand-searching of the bibliographies of any relevant systematic reviews, (network) metaanalyses ([N]MAs), economic evaluations or HTAs identified during the review. Full details of the SLR and update are provided below. 

## **G.1.1. Search strategy** 

The SLR were performed in accordance with the methodological principles of conduct for SLRs as detailed in the University of York Centre for Reviews and Dissemination’s “Guidance for Undertaking Reviews in Health Care”.[14] 

For all applicable searches (i.e. of databases with complex search functionality) the search terms to capture economic studies are based on the validated Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN) filter set,[15] with the addition of extra terms from other sources.

## _**Original SLR**_ 

The following databases were searched from inception on 4[th] August 2020: 

- MEDLINE, including MEDLINE In-Process, MEDLINE Daily and MEDLINE Epub Ahead of Print

## **G.1.2. Study selection** 

Studies were selected for inclusion in two stages: first, the abstracts of the search results were reviewed for relevance using the eligibility criteria; second, the full texts of potentially relevant articles were screened in order to obtain the final list of included studies. 

The review of abstracts and full texts was performed using predefined eligibility criteria, based on the decision problem for this submission and developed using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes and Study design (PICOS) framework. The eligibility of each study captured in the database and hand searching was reviewed for inclusion across all three evidence streams (economic evaluations, utility/HRQoL, and HCRU). The eligibility presented here is specific to the cost-effectiveness evidence stream (Appendix G); eligibility for the other streams is reported in the relevant appendices (utility/HRQoL: Appendix H and HCRU: Appendix I). 

## _**Title/abstract review**_ 

Each title and abstract were assessed for inclusion by two independent reviewers using the eligibility criteria (Table 73). Where the applicability of the inclusion criteria was unclear, the record was included at this stage to ensure that all potentially relevant studies were captured. The results of the two reviewers were compared and any disagreements were resolved by discussion until a consensus was met. If necessary, a third independent reviewer made the final decision. 

## _**Full text review**_ 

Each full-text record was then assessed for inclusion by two independent reviewers using the eligibility criteria (Table 73). In cases where the record did not give enough information to be sure that it met the inclusion criteria, the record was excluded to ensure that only relevant records were ultimately included in the SLR. The results of the two reviewers were compared and any disagreements were resolved by discussion until a consensus was met. If necessary, a third independent reviewer made the final decision. 

## _**Duplicate and companion publications**_ 

Any full duplicates found during the screening phase were excluded. All publications ultimately included in all iterations of the SLR were reviewed, in order to group those reporting on the same study. The primary publication for a study was regarded as the most recent journal article that reported outcomes of interest for the study. Secondary publications were considered as any publications related to the primary study, such as conference abstracts, which reported outcomes of interest. Records reporting on the Cost of Haemophilia in Europe: a Socioeconomic Survey (CHESS; I, II and PAEDS) study were extracted separately and counted as unique studies, except for those published by the same group of authors, which were reference linked. 

At subsequent stages of the review (data extraction, quality assessment and write-up), each study was considered as a single unit and only primary publications were extracted. 

## _**Evidence prioritisation for data extraction**_ 

Due to a large volume of evidence identified as relevant after the full-text review stage, a number of steps were taken to ensure that the most recent and relevant economic evaluations to the decision problem for this submission were prioritised for extraction. Economic evaluations were prioritised for extraction if they: 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for the treatment of severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 322 -->

- Fulfilled all the following criteria: 

   - Cost-utility analyses (CUAs) or CEAs 

   - And, conducted in a US, EU4 and/or UK setting 

   - And, were identified during the SLR update 

- Or, were key studies chosen to inform the structure of the economic model for this submission, based on prior NICE evaluations in haemophilia 

## _**Data extraction**_ 

Key information from relevant primary publications was extracted into a pre-specified data extraction grid in Microsoft Word. Where more than one publication was identified reporting data on a unique study, each publication was referenced in the table to recognise that more than one publication may have contributed to the entry. 

Data extraction was performed in line with guidelines from the University of York CRD,[14] by a single individual for each included study. When the initial extraction was completed, a second individual then independently verified the extracted information and checked that no relevant information had been missed. Any discrepancies or missing information identified by the second individual was discussed by both individuals until a consensus was reached on the information that should be presented in the extraction grid. If necessary, a third individual arbitrated the final decision. 

## _**Quality assessment**_ 

The quality of economic evaluation studies was assessed using the Drummond checklist,[16] as required by NICE. No quality assessment was performed for utility/HRQoL or HCRU studies. The quality assessments were completed by one individual and verified by another individual.

## **G.1.3. Description of identified studies** 

The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow diagram for the economic SLR is presented in Figure 4, covering all three evidence streams, the original SLR and the SLR update. 

## _**Original searches (all evidence streams)**_ 

Across all three evidence streams, a total of 5,519 records were retrieved from the electronic databases, of which 2,611 were duplicates, resulting in 2,908 novel records that were screened at the title/abstract review stage. Subsequently, 663 full publications were screened against the eligibility criteria for all three evidence streams at full-text review. Following this, 387 publications were excluded. 276 publications were included in total, comprising of 151 haemophilia A studies, 58 haemophilia B studies and 67 studies reporting on non-separable haemophilia. 

A total of 123 publications did not report relevant economic outcomes, resulting in 153 publications being included in the review. To prioritise evidence most relevant to this submission, included records were prioritised for extraction if they were key studies informing the structure of the economic model in this submission, or informed utilities or costs in the economic model. This resulted in prioritisation of data extraction of 4 records from the original SLR. 

## _**Update searches (all evidence streams)**_ 

Following pooling of records across all three evidence streams, a total of 2,831 records were retrieved from the electronic databases, of which 1,495 were duplicates (including duplicates against the original SLR searches), resulting in 1,336 novel records that were screened at the title/abstract review stage. Subsequently, 284 full publications were screened against the eligibility criteria for all three evidence streams at full-text review. Following this, 190 publications were excluded; these are listed in Table 74 along with the brief rationale for exclusion. This resulted in 94 records being included from the electronic database searches. 

Supplementary searches retrieved an additional 40 records (2 from HTA websites, 1 from reference lists and 37 from conference searches), resulting in a total of 134 records being included in the SLR update, across all three evidence streams. Records were then prioritised for extraction as described in Appendices G.1.2 (economic evaluations), H.1.2 (utility/HRQoL) and I.1.2 (HCRU). This resulted in 26 records being extracted for the submission across all evidence streams in the SLR update. 

Lists of the studies deprioritised for data extraction in each evidence stream are presented in Table 75 (economic evaluations), Table 81 (utility/HRQoL) and Table 86 (HCRU). 

## _**Total economic evaluations evidence**_ 

In total, 12 records reporting on 12 unique studies were prioritised for extraction in the economic evaluations evidence stream of the SLR. A full list of these studies is presented in Table 76. Full details of the prioritised economic evaluations are provided in Table 77 and Table 78.

## **Identification of studies** 

The databases and hand searches were conducted simultaneously for the utility/HRQoL stream alongside the cost-effectiveness stream (Appendix G), and HCRU stream (Appendix I). Each record identified in these searches was assessed for eligibility across all three data streams (cost-effectiveness, utility/HRQoL, and HCRU). Each study identified could therefore be included in one or more of the evidence streams. 

## **H.1.1. Search strategy** 

The information for evidence sources searched for the utilities stream are presented in Appendix G. 

## _**Electronic databases**_ 

A list of the search terms used in the electronic databases are provided in Appendix G.1.1 for the original SLR and SLR update. 

## _**Grey literature sources**_ 

## **Conference proceedings** 

An overview of the conference website searches undertaken in the SLR update is provided in Table 69 (Appendix G.1.1). 

## **HTA websites and additional sources** 

Search terms used in the HTA and economic website searches, are provided in Table 70 and Table 71, respectively, for the SLR update (Appendix G.1.1). 

## **H.1.2. Study selection** 

The methods used for study selection are detailed in Appendix G.1.2. The review of abstracts and full texts was performed using predefined eligibility criteria (Table 80), based on the decision problem for this submission and developed using the PICOS framework. 

## _**Evidence prioritisation for data extraction**_ 

Due to a large volume of evidence identified as relevant after the full-text review stage, a number of steps were taken to ensure that the most recent and relevant studies to the decision problem for this submission were prioritised for extraction. For the utility/HRQoL stream, studies were prioritised if they: 

- Fulfilled the following criteria: 

   - Reported utilities derived using UK preference weights, in line with NICE preferences 

   - `o` And, were identified during the SLR update 

- Or, were key studies chosen to inform utilities in the economic model for this submission, based on prior NICE evaluations in haemophilia

## **Identification of studies** 

The databases and hand searches were conducted simultaneously for the HCRU stream alongside the cost-effectiveness stream (Appendix G), and utility/HRQoL stream (Appendix I). Each record identified in these searches was assessed for eligibility across all three data streams (cost-effectiveness, utility/HRQoL, and HCRU). Each study identified could therefore be included in one or more of the evidence streams. 

## **I.1.1. Search Strategy** 

The information for evidence sources searched for the HCRU SLR are presented in Appendix G. 

## _**Electronic databases**_ 

A list of the search terms used in the electronic databases are provided in Appendix G.1.1 for the original SLR and SLR update. 

## _**Grey literature sources**_ 

## _**Conference proceedings**_ 

An overview of the conference website searches undertaken in the SLR update is provided in Table 69 (Appendix G.1.1). 

## _**HTA websites and additional sources**_ 

Search terms used in the HTA and economic website searches, are provided in Table 70 and Table 71, respectively, for the SLR update (Appendix G.1.1). 

## **I.1.2. Study selection** 

The methods used for study selection are detailed in Appendix G.1.2. The review of abstracts and full texts was performed using predefined eligibility criteria, based on the decision problem for this submission and developed using the PICOS framework. 

## _**Evidence prioritisation for data extraction**_ 

Due to a large volume of evidence identified as relevant after the full-text review stage, a number of steps were taken to ensure that the most recent and relevant studies to the decision problem for this submission were prioritised for extraction. For the HCRU evidence stream, studies were prioritised if they: 

- Fulfilled the following criteria: 

   - Included patients in the UK 

   - And, were identified during the SLR update 

Company evidence submission template for marstacimab for the treatment of severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

© Pfizer (2024). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 410 -->

   - And, did not report solely indirect costs and/or incidental HCRU (defined for this SLR as HCRU data that were not pre-specified as a study outcome, treatment doses, factor consumption and treatment usage) 

- Or, were key studies chosen to inform HCRU in the economic model for this submission based on prior NICE evaluations in haemophilia 

## _**Eligibility criteria**_ 

The eligibility of each study captured in the database and grey literature searching was reviewed for inclusion across all three streams (cost effectiveness studies, HRQoL/utilities, and HCRU). The eligibility presented here is specific to that assessed for inclusion into the HCRU evidence stream (see Table 85), eligibility for the other streams are reported in other appendices (costeffectiveness studies; Appendix G.1.2 and HRQoL/utility studies; Appendix H.1.2).

## **Additional information from the marstacimab** 

# **Phase 3 clinical trial programme: BASIS and its OLE** 

**==> picture [22 x 12] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Additional methodological details** 

## **M.1.1. Eligibility criteria** 

The majority of eligibility criteria for BASIS are presented in Document B, Section B.2.3.1.1. Additional specific lab-based exclusion criteria are presented in Table 98 below. The eligibility criteria for the OLE were identical to that for the BASIS trial. 

**Table 98: Additional details of the BASIS trial eligibility criteria** 

**Additional exclusion criteria:** • Abnormal renal or hepatic function as defined by the following laboratory results at screening: `o` Alanine transaminase (ALT) >2 × upper limit of normal (ULN) `o` Bilirubin >1.5 × ULN (isolated bilirubin >1.5 × ULN is acceptable if bilirubin is fractionated and direct bilirubin <35%) `o` Current unstable liver or biliary disease per investigator assessment defined by the presence of ascites, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hypoalbuminaemia, oesophageal or gastric varices, persistent jaundice, or cirrhosis. NOTE: Stable chronic liver disease (including Gilbert’s syndrome, asymptomatic gallstones, and chronic stable hepatitis B or C -eg, presence of hepatitis B surface antigen [HBsAg] **Eligibility criteria** or positive hepatitis C antibody test result at screening or within 3 months prior to starting study intervention) is acceptable if the participant otherwise meets entry criteria `o` Serum albumin less than the lower limit of normal (LLN). `o` Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <30 mL/min/1.73 m[2] • Abnormal haematology values as defined by the following laboratory tests at screening: `o` Platelet count <100,000/uL `o` Hemoglobin level <10 g/dL • QTcF >450 msec for male participants or QTcF >480 msec in participants with bundle branch block. 

**Abbreviations:** ALT: alanine transaminase; eGFR: estimated glomerular filtration rate; g/dL: grams per decilitre; HBsAg; hepatitis B surface antigen; LNL: lower limit of normal; msec: millisecond; QTcF: QT interval; uL: microlitres; ULN: upper limit of normal. **Source:** Pfizer marstacimab Phase 3 BASIS trial protocol, 2022.[20] 

## **M.1.2. OLE Baseline characteristics** 

A total of 88 patients entered the treatment phase. Subsequently, two discontinued due to participant withdrawal and one entered the follow-up phase. ## **M.2.2. Factor consumption (exploratory endpoint)** 

In the BASIS trial, factor replacement consumption, as measured by IU/kg per month/year and total annualised IU, reduced from 248,871 IU (mean total annualised) during the OP to 16,246 IU during the ATP when patients were receiving marstacimab (Table 102). In addition, the total days requiring factor replacement treatment were also reduced during the ATP (median exposure: 3 days per patient) when compared with the OP (median exposure: 57 days per patient).

## **BASIS trial data used to inform the model** 

The Phase 3 BASIS study represents the pivotal clinical trial demonstrating the efficacy and safety of marstacimab prophylaxis compared to factor prophylaxis. Data from the primary and secondary endpoints of the BASIS trial are presented in Section B.2.6. Additional post hoc analyses were conducted to inform the data used in the economic model. The trial patients considered in these post hoc analyses, along with the efficacy inputs for the cost effectiveness model base case, are presented in Document B Section B.2.9. Post hoc data informing scenario analyses are presented below.

bleeding stops. Recombinant factor VIII and factor IX concentrates are made using genetic technology and aren’t made from blood. Treatment will be needed by everyone with haemophilia if they are bleeding. It will also be necessary to prevent bleeding if they need an operation or have an injury where there is a risk of bleeding. Clotting factor concentrate is given intravenously (into a vein) into the bloodstream through a needle. Children can have anaesthetic cream rubbed onto the skin before an injection to reduce any pain. Standard half-life factor concentrates stay in the blood for a relatively short time and require repeat injections for prophylaxis – every 2-3 days for haemophilia A and twice a week for haemophilia B. Extended half-life (EHL) treatments are factor VIII or FIX products that can stay in the bloodstream for longer. They mean people are able to have injections to prevent bleeds (prophylaxis) less often or may stay on the same dose/schedule and have higher trough levels. They are likely to need fewer injections to control any bleeds they have. Half-lives are shorter in children and young people than adults. Emicizumab is a subcutaneous (under the skin) treatment used to prevent or reduce bleeding in people with severe haemophilia A that is given weekly, two weekly or once a month. It is an antibody which mimics the action of factor VIII. Treatment with regular infusions of clotting factor aims to prevent the long-term damage caused by bleeding into joints and muscles. Prophylaxis works by stopping the bleeding that occurs without any obvious injury, often called spontaneous bleeding. It also reduces the risk of bleeding from minor injuries. Most people with severe haemophilia treat themselves or their children with clotting factor at home. Home treatment has many advantages including making regular treatment possible, treatment can be given as soon as possible after bleeding starts, there is less disruption to home, school and working life, greater independence and control for the parent/person with haemophilia, reduced need for hospital attendances and early treatment reduces recovery time and risk of permanent damage. A complication of haemophilia care is the development of an inhibitor. An inhibitor is an antibody that the immune system develops when it recognises the clotting factor being infused as something foreign. The inhibitor removes 

Patient organisation submission Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over [ID6342] 

7 of 20 



<!-- page 480 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

the clotting factor before it can work to stop any bleeding. Inhibitors usually affect people with severe haemophilia A in early childhood, but they can also occur later in life in milder forms of haemophilia. They are much more unusual in people with haemophilia B. People with inhibitors may not respond to treatment with factor products and will need bypassing agents such as FEIBA and rFVIIa to control bleeding. If they have haemophilia A and an inhibitor they will often use emicizumab to prevent bleeding. People with haemophilia can have any surgery they need but careful planning is essential. Good dental education and care is particularly important for people with haemophilia to prevent tooth decay and gum disease and avoid the need for dental surgery. Gum bleeding is caused by gum disease but will be worse for someone with haemophilia. Exercise and sport have many benefits for health and can improve self-esteem, learning and concentration. There are some particular benefits for children and adults with haemophilia as strong muscles, good balance and posture can help to protect joints from bleeding. Maintaining a healthy weight helps to reduce stress on joints that have already been damaged by bleeding. The choice of activity or sport will be individual and can be decided in consultation with a specialist haemophilia physiotherapist. There are risks and benefits of different sports taking account of the person’s condition, treatment and disease severity. In general, sports involving a lot of physical contact and those where head and neck injuries occur carry the highest risk of injury and therefore risk of bleeding. Factor prophylaxis can be tailored around days of highest activity so that there is maximum protection from bleeding at these times. With modern treatment, haemophilia shouldn’t have a serious impact on a child’s education. There may be times when a child has to miss school while they recover after a bleed. Rarely, a child may temporarily need to use a wheelchair or crutches. For children with haemophilia who are on effective treatment, ordinary play activities aren’t usually a problem beyond the occasional bruise. Cuts and grazes can generally be managed with standard first aid. Most young people with haemophilia will go through school much as the rest of their peer group. This means that choosing to go to college or out to work won’t be any different either. If their haemophilia has been wellmanaged, people with severe haemophilia can reach adulthood with limited joint damage and will not be overly restricted in careers and lifestyle choices.

Many older people with haemophilia will have been treated with contaminated blood products in the 70s and 80s and will be living with HIV or liver damage from hepatitis B and C.

**8. Is there an unmet need** The inherited bleeding disorders patient survey first conducted in 2020 and repeated in 2022 showed that the **for patients with this** majority of people with a bleeding disorder feel anxious because of their condition and up to 25% said they felt **condition?** anxious “a lot” in the last 12 months. In both surveys almost half of respondents said that they had felt depressed in the last 12 months because of their condition. 

In the 2022 survey we asked a series of questions on pain which showed that only a third of people with bleeding disorders lived a life free from pain as a result of their condition. Around a quarter said this was chronic long-term pain that they felt every day. The Haemophilia Society provides its members with advice on pain management, and this is a common area of concern for clinicians managing the condition of people with haemophilia. 

Pain is highly prevalent in people with haemophilia with studies reporting acute pain being experienced by 20– 68%. A detailed investigation on what impact pain in people in the UK with haemophilia has on their lives has shown that people make major changes to their life and that their experience of pain is a complex bio-medical and social construct. (P. McLaughlin, M. Hurley, P. Chowdary, D. Stephensen & K. Khair (2022) How does a lifetime of painful experiences influence sensations and beliefs about pain in adults with severe haemophilia? A qualitative study, Disability and Rehabilitation, 44:26, 8412-8419, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/09638288.2021.2018053) 

People with severe haemophilia still have painful bleeds requiring additional treatment and often rehabilitation. These bleeds mean that most people with severe haemophilia still develop joint damage impacting on their quality of life (O’Hara, J., Walsh, S., Camp, C. et al. The impact of severe haemophilia and the presence of target joints on health-related quality-of-life. Health Qual Life Outcomes 16, 84 (2018). https://doi.org/10.1186/s12955-018-0908-9) 

A number of people with haemophilia have spoken to us about how despite their current treatment they do not have full confidence to walk in crowds and will adapt their lives to avoid bumping into people and the risk of bleeds and bruising. For example, they will make changes to their plans to ensure they go to the supermarket at less busy times. People with haemophilia often do not have the confidence to take whatever career path they

want or participate in all sports and social activities they want as they cannot rely on their protection from joint damage and bleeds at all times. 

Some people with haemophilia, particularly those affected by the scandal of contaminated blood products in the 70s and 80s, are put off by frequent attendance at hospital where they or their family members were prescribed or treated with blood products that gave them HIV and Hepatitis C leading to long-term health impacts including liver damage and premature death.

|**9. What do patients or**<br>**carers think are the**<br>**advantages of the**<br>**technology?**|People with haemophilia value convenience of administration of their treatment. ## **Equality** 

**12. Are there any potential equality issues that should be taken into account when considering this condition and the technology?** 

People will need to understand the benefits and disadvantages of this product compared to the current standard of care. NICE should be careful to avoid guidance which does not make clear that some products, particularly with optimised high dosing, are more effective in preventing and managing bleeds and reducing joint damage than others. 

With current products we have seen large regional variation in uptake of new treatments. NICE and NHS England should work to ensure there is equity of access across England and that patients in different centres are able to choose the best treatment option for them in well-informed shared decision-making.

In your view, is there an unmet need for patients** Yes. **and healthcare professionals in severe haemophilia A** There are 3 current strategies for treating severe haemophilia: **or severe haemophilia B?** -replacement therapy with either FVIII or FIX -non-replacement therapy with a monoclonal FVIII mimitic drug for haemophilia A only (emicizumab). -gene therapy in currently very limited numbers in developed countries and only currently in adults (over 18). Around 1 in 3 boys with severe haemophilia A develop antibodies agaisnt FVIII, making this treatment useless. If attempts to get rid of these antibodies (called inhibitors) are either not possible (there is a huge expense and high treatment burden associated) or not desired, this group have access to emicizumab which provides good bleed prevention, effectively converting the severe haemophilia A to a milder form of the condition. A much smaller proportion of boys with severe haemophilia B develop inhibitory antibodies against FIX. These are more difficult to remove and currently the only licensed treatment options (called bypassing agents) do not provide good bleed control. Children and men with this complication of severe haemophilia B typically have recurrent bleeds leading to disability (for example becoming wheelchair dependent in their second decade). Marstacimab therefore offers to meet the currently unmet needs of: 1) a subcutaneous treatment for severe haemophilia B and 2) effective prophylactic treatment for severe haemophilia B patients with inhibitors. **11. ## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

There is no currently licensed and available subcutaneous treatment for severe haemophilia B in the UK. 

Marstacimab would offer a weekly subcutaneous prophylaxis option for severe haemophilia B and A. 

Marstacimab may be the first available effective prophylaxis for severe haemophilia B complicated by antibodies (inhibitors) to FIX 

(this is currently an unmet need, although there are several other potential treatments in the trial pipeline). 

Marstacimab (and any other subcutaneous prophylaxis treatments for severe haemophilia B in the future) would offer a potential reduction in treatment burden for patients and their families in line with that observed when emicizumab was made available for treatment fo haemophilia A. 

Thank you for your time.
