## **Executive Summary** 

This summary provides a brief overview of the key issues identified by the External Assessment Group (EAG) as being potentially important for decision making. It also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental costeffectiveness ratios (ICERs). 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues. Section 1.2 provides an overview of key model outcomes and the modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER. Sections 1.3 to 1.6 explain the key issues in more detail. Background information on the condition, technology and evidence and information on non-key issues are in the main EAG report. 

All issues identified represent the EAG’s view, not the opinion of NICE. 

## **1.1** _**Overview of the EAG’s key issues**_ 

## **Table 1: Summary of key issues** 

|**ID6342**|**Summary of issue**|**Report**<br>**sections**|
|---|---|---|
|1|Generalisability over the BASIS trial and its<br>relevance to UK practice.|2.2.2|
|2|The source of information for baseline annualised<br>bleed rates and treatment efficacy within the<br>economic model.|2.2.2.2,<br>2.5.3|
|3|Dose-escalation of marstacimab|2.2.2.6,<br>5.3.1|
|4|Discontinuation of haemophilia treatments.|5.1.2|
|5|Dosing of factor prophylaxis|2.2.2.7,<br>5.3.2|
|6|Separate or pooled modelling of haemophilia types|2.2.2.3,<br>4.3.1|



The key differences between the company’s preferred assumptions and the EAG’s preferred assumptions are the source of information used for the baseline annualised bleed rates, the estimates of relative efficacy, the mean IU dose for FVIII/FIX, whether clinical effectiveness estimates should be differentiated by 

haemophilia A and haemophilia B and whether marstacimab dose escalation during the open label extension should be included and extrapolated.

## **1.2** _**Overview of key model outcomes**_ 

NICE technology appraisals compare how much a new technology improves length (overall survival) and quality of life in a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- Having a different annualised treated bleed rate to other therapies 

- Being subcutaneous rather than intravenous administration compared to FVIII/FIX, and having a different annual number of administrations compared to FVIII/FIX and emicizumab 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect costs by: 

- Having a different purchase price to other therapies 

- Affecting the mean number of bleeds and so the cost of treating these 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER are: 

- The mean FVIII/FIX dose, whether this should be based upon UKHCDO data or company assumptions, and if the latter whether wastage calculations should take into account some doses being rounded down. 

- Whether marstacimab dose escalations during the open label extension are included and whether there will be further marstacimab dose escalations. 

- Whether the clinical effectiveness estimates should be pooled across or differentiated by haemophilia A and haemophilia B, and within this whether dose escalation rates should be similarly differentiated. 

- Whether clinical effectiveness estimates for the second year and beyond should be based upon the BASIS open label extension or upon the BASIS. 

## **1.3** _**The decision problem: summary of the EAG’s key issues**_ 

The EAG did not identify any key issues relating to the decision problem.

## **External Assessment Group Report** 

## **1 INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND** 

## **1.1** _**Introduction**_ 

## **1.1.1 Remit of this appraisal** 

To appraise the clinical and cost-effectiveness of marstacimab within its marketing authorisation for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over. 

## **1.1.2 Condition, epidemiology and symptoms, and economic burden** 

This section provides a summary and critique of the company overview of haemophilia, including symptoms and effects on quality of life. The CS provides a thorough examination of these factors in Section B.1.3.1 using a large number of citations. The EAG has focused the critique on key elements of relevance to the decision problem and selected references from primary studies only for checking. Overall the EAG considers that the CS provides an accurate summary of these factors. 

Congenital haemophilia is a rare bleeding disease that follows an X-linked inheritance pattern and is characterised by a deficiency in clotting factors.[1] There are two main types of haemophilia: haemophilia A caused by a defect in factor VIII, and haemophilia B by a defect in factor IX (hereafter in the background referred to collectively as ‘haemophilia’ unless there are specific data by type).[2] Haemophilia predominately affects males.[2] Data from 60 UK haemophilia treatment centres show that in 2022-2023, there were 6,609 males living with haemophilia A and 1,305 males with haemophilia B in the UK.[3] Although rarer, females may also be affected by haemophilia. In 2022-2023, 74 females with haemophilia A and 36 with haemophilia B were recorded in the UK.[3] 

The CS describes the severity of haemophilia in Section B.1.3.1.2. Haemophilia can be mild, moderate or severe depending on the clotting factor levels in a patient’s blood, which does not change over time.[4] Clotting factor is either expressed as a 

20 



<!-- page 524 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

percentage relative to normal human plasma or in international units (IU) relative to an international standard for FVIII or FIX in plasma.[5] The normal level of clotting factor in the blood is 1 IU/mL / 100% (range 0.50–1.5 / 50%-150%).[4] The focus of the current appraisal is on severe haemophilia. Patients with severe haemophilia have a clotting factor level of <1 IU/dL (less than 1%) and experience recurrent, often spontaneous, bleeding in muscles and joints.[6] In 2022-2023, UK data show that there were 2,230 people (all ages) with severe haemophilia A and 374 people (all ages) with severe haemophilia B.[3] The CS reports that in 2022/23 in the UK 2,128 people were treated for severe haemophilia A and 329 people were treated for severe haemophilia B;[3] the EAG notes that these data include people of all ages. The EAG is unclear of the reasons why 5-8% of people with severe haemophilia are untreated. The focus of this appraisal is on those aged ≥ 12 years and the CS reports data from a bespoke analysis of the UKHCDO database conducted for Pfizer, which found that in 2022/23 ***** people aged 12 years or more were treated for severe haemophilia A and *** were treated for severe haemophilia B.[7] 

Severe haemophilia has a greater impact on people than mild or moderate haemophilia; repeated bleeding can lead to inflammation and pain, movement can be affected, and additionally people require regular access to treatment and healthcare services which impacts quality of life.[5, 8] People with severe haemophilia can also suffer from other complications, such as increased fracture rates (due to a lower bone mineral density) and joint disease.[9, 10] The CS reports the potential impact of severe haemophilia in Section B.1.3.1.5; much of the focus of this section is from analyses of the Cost of Haemophilia across Europe – a Socioeconomic Survey (CHESS)[11-13] and CHESS II[10, 14] studies. These were real-world studies of people with severe haemophilia from five European countries (France, Germany, Italy, Spain and UK) between 2014 – 2015 and 2019 – 2020 respectively. Participants provided information on quality of life and adherence and also cost information such as work loss and out-of-pocket expenses. The EQ-5D-3L was used to assess health related quality of life. The EAG has checked the information reported in CS Section B.1.3.1.5 with the source data where possible and concurs with the CS that severe haemophilia, and in particular the recurrent bleeding episodes into joints, can lead to more pain and worse HRQoL.[10, 11, 13] There is also the potential for an economic burden on an individual from greater likelihood of 

21 



<!-- page 525 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

unemployment[15] and from the direct and indirect costs of treatments.[11] Clinical advice to the EAG is that many people with haemophilia have significant musculoskeletal comorbidity and this is particularly the case for older people who have not received prophylaxis since childhood. 

Despite improved treatments for haemophilia, the CS makes the case that haemophilia may still be associated with a lower life expectancy compared with the general population, citing data from an epidemiological study undertaken in the Netherlands. This study followed 1066 people with haemophilia between 2001 and 2018 and found mortality was increased compared with the general Dutch male population.[16] The study data also suggested a higher risk of mortality in those with severe haemophilia, but study authors noted limitations including changes in treatments over time and not having data for all potential determinants of mortality and confounding variables which need to be considered.[16] The CS also refers to data reporting the median life expectancy for people with severe haemophilia A and B, which were 77 and 79 years, respectively, in those registered between 1996 and 2023 in the UKHCDO database. The UKHCDO 2023 report states these values are 84 and 85 years, respectively, for individuals with mild haemophilia.[3] The view of the EAG clinical advisers, however, is that life expectancy in the UK is very similar to the general population. 

## **1.1.3 Current treatment pathway** 

The CS provides an overview of current clinical treatment options in Section B.1.3.2.1. Both haemophilia A and haemophilia B require lifelong treatment. Treatment aims to prevent bleeding episodes.[2] 

The traditional standard-of-care for haemophilia A and B involves supplementing clotting factors through factor replacement therapy.[2] This therapy can be administered on-demand (in response to a bleeding episode) or prophylactically (to prevent bleeding episodes), or a combination of both. The EAG clinical advisors agree with the CS that on-demand treatment alone is only used by a minority of patients with severe haemophilia in the UK.[17] Factor replacement is given through intravenous infusions of varying dosing regimens. Factor replacement therapies can 

22 



<!-- page 526 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

be subdivided into standard half-life (SHL) and extended half-life (EHL) therapies, with the latter being longer-acting and therefore administered less frequently.[2] 

Haemophilia A can also be treated with emicizumab, a non-factor replacement treatment which is available in the UK for people with severe haemophilia A following NHS Clinical Commissioning Policy approvals.[18, 19] Emicizumab is used as a prophylaxis and is self-administrated subcutaneously following a weight-based dosing regimen, either once weekly, once every two weeks or once every four weeks.[20] There is currently no equivalent treatment for people with haemophilia B.[3] 

Figure 5 in the CS provides an overview of the available standard of care products for both haemophilia A and B respectively, and CS Tables 5 and 6 report the rates these products are used in the UK based on confidential sales data and data from the UKHCDO, reported as international units and days of therapy.[3] The CS states that these rates are similar to those provided by UK clinical experts; that over 50% of severe haemophilia A patients received emicizumab, and that EHL products are used significantly more than SHL products in both severe haemophilia A and B. Clinical advice to the EAG concurs that generally around half of men with haemophilia A are treated with emicizumab, although in some centres now emicizumab is the standard of care and rates may be higher. Clinical advisers also noted that EHLs in general require less frequent dosing and most people would use an EHL for prophylaxis. One expert noted that SHLs are easier to use for managing breakthrough bleeds and for surgery, but for some minor procedures EHLs would be used to minimise the number of required doses. 

Some people with haemophilia develop antibodies against the factor replacement therapies called inhibitors.[2] About 30% of patients with haemophilia A develop inhibitors to factor VIII, and up to 5% of people with haemophilia B develop inhibitors to factor VIII.[5] Clinical advice to the EAG is that there are several risk factors that contribute to some people developing antibodies while others do not, including genetics, ethnicity, age, intensity of first treatment and environmental factors. Often linked to disease severity, inhibitors are more common among people with severe haemophilia.[5] Inhibitors decrease the effectiveness of factor replacement therapy and pose a challenge in the management of bleeding episodes.[21] Patients with 

23 



<!-- page 527 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

inhibitors need specific monitoring and may require additional treatments called bypassing agents or alternatively treatment with emicizumab.[5, 21] 

Gene therapies are at various stages of development and approval and may offer life-long cures for haemophilia A or B in the near future.[22] Etranacogene dezaparvovec for moderately severe or severe haemophilia B was recommended with managed access by NICE in July 2024.[23] NICE guidance on efanesoctocog alfa for haemophilia A and fidanacogene elaparvovec for haemophilia B are both currently in development (expected publication dates to be confirmed).[24, 25] 

## **1.1.4 Marstacimab mechanism of action** 

Marstacimab is a human monoclonal antibody, specifically immunoglobulin G isotope subtype 1 (IgG1), that targets the Kunitz 2 domain of the protein, tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI).[26] TFPI is an anticoagulant protein that prevents blood clot ‐ formation by inhibiting tissue factor activated FVII (FVIIa) and activated FX (FXa) _(see CS, Figure 2)_ . By binding to and neutralising TPFI, marstacimab alters the extrinsic clotting pathway to promote blood clotting.[26] Marstacimab's regimen involves an initial one-off loading dose followed by a weekly, flat dose, subcutaneous self-infection through a pre-filled syringe (PFS) or pre-filled pen (PFP) device.[27, 28] 

Marstacimab does not currently have marketing authorisation for any indication in the UK. The company has a submitted application for marketing authorisation to the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and a positive CHMP opinion was granted on 19[th] September 2024. The CS anticipates that following EMA review ****************** ************************************************************************************************

## **1.1.5 Proposed placement of marstacimab in treatment pathway** 

The company states that marstacimab differs from factor replacement therapies as it is administered subcutaneously (as opposed to intravenously), which may improve patients' quality of life.[29] CS Section B.1.3.3.1 describes an unmet need for a treatment that is convenient and simple to administer, making the point that there is 

24 



<!-- page 528 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

currently no self-administered subcutaneous treatment for haemophilia B available and that the self-administered subcutaneous treatment available for haemophilia A is complex to administer due to the weight-related dosing. The CS describes how the treatment burden on individuals has an additional emotional impact for individuals who already have a number of day-to-day challenges. The company considers that a more convenient method of administration could improve confidence in selfadministration, adherence, and have a positive effect on patient outcomes, although no direct evidence was provided to support this and the EAG has not been able to identify any. The EAG clinical advisers commented that it is not a significant burden for patients to account for any changes in their dosage of haemophilia treatments due to weight changes as their weight is monitored in clinic and doses are adjusted accordingly. EAG experts also considered that compliance with emicizumab in haemophilia A is very good. 

The CS proposes that in haemophilia A, marstacimab would be considered at the same line in the treatment pathway as emicizumab. The EAG clinical experts consider that while marstacimab would provide another treatment option, it would be unlikely a patient already receiving emicizumab would be switched from emicizumab to marstacimab unless emicizumab was found to be ineffective. If marstacimab is unlikely to displace any usage of emicizumab, then it raises the question of whether emicizumab is a relevant comparator, however the EAG considers this of low importance given that comparisons with FVIII are already provided. In the clinician’s experience there is a very small number of people in whom emicizumab is less effective than FVIII and who have been switched back to FVIII. Clinical advice to the EAG was that for people with haemophilia B, the subcutaneous administration of marstacimab (as opposed to intravenous administration of factor) would be a benefit.

## **2 CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS** 

## **2.1 Critique of the methods of review(s)** 

CS Appendix D reports a systematic literature review (SLR) to identify evidence on the efficacy and safety of marstacimab and relevant comparator therapies. Searches were originally undertaken in August 2020 (“original SLR”), then updates run in August 2023 and May 2024. The company’s response to clarification question A43 explains that the SLR undertaken in 2020 included both clinical and economic evidence, but separate clinical and cost effectiveness searches, screening and reporting were undertaken from 2023 onwards. 

## **2.1.1 Search strategies** 

CS Appendix D.1.1 describes the literature search sources and strategies. A good, appropriate range of databases and other sources were searched, including clinical trials registries and proceedings of recent conferences. Some changes to the searches were made between the 2020 original SLR and the 2023 update (partly reflecting the splitting of clinical and economic SLRs); these are all sensible changes and would not have compromised the quality of the review. 

The EAG has some concerns about the quality of the search strategies (Appendix D.1.1, Tables 1-14), including the use of the same search terms across both Embase and MEDLINE, which is not best practice as the databases have different controlled vocabularies (Emtree vs MesH). Some important Emtree terms such as ‘Controlled clinical trial’ and ‘Double blind procedure’ were missed, and some MeSH terms (‘Randomized controlled trial’, ‘Clinical trial’) should have been exploded to include narrower terms like ‘Clinical Trial, Phase I/II/III/IV’. Additionally, in Embase (Tables 1- 3) a limit to “article or article in press” is used (line 10); this limit did not work when tested by the EAG and, if functioning, would risk missing useful papers not yet indexed or defined as an ‘article’. 

Despite the limitations identified, when the EAG ran a targeted MEDLINE search (see Appendix 7.2) for trials or systematic reviews on marstacimab or emicizumab, no additional studies that should have been included in the company’s SLR were identified. 

33 



<!-- page 537 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

## **2.1.2 SLR Methods** 

The methods of the company SLR were reviewed by the EAG using a modified ROBIS tool.[34] The full assessment can be found in Appendix 7.1. The EAG assessment of the overall risk of bias of the SLR was high concern. The initial SLR applied pre-defined eligibility criteria and the steps taken to select studies minimised the potential for errors. However, limited summary details of the 79 studies initially included in the SLR were reported in CS Appendix Table 17 and there was no synthesis or risk of bias assessment for these studies. 

In addition, to determine eligibility of studies for the ITC the company undertook two feasibility assessments of potential studies. The EAG had concerns that not all eligibility criteria were pre-specified and for some criteria there was no justification reported. The steps taken to assess studies against the eligibility criteria were also not stated. However, the EAG generally agrees with the exclusion of most of these studies from the ITC. The exception is the exclusion of the HAVEN 4 study which the EAG considers relevant, see section 2.3 for more details. 

## **2.2** _**Critique of trials of the technology of interest, the company’s analysis and interpretation (and any standard meta-analyses of these)**_ 

## **2.2.1 Trial design** 

The source of evidence for the assessment of clinical effectiveness of marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or B in people 12 years or over is from a single study, BASIS (NCT03938792), and its open-label extension (OLE) study 

(NCT05145127). A Phase 2, dose-investigation study of marstacimab[35] is also cited by the CS, but results are not presented. The EAG agrees there are no data of relevance in this study. 

BASIS is a Phase 3 open-label multicentre study conducted across 19 countries, including some sites in Europe, but none were in the UK. It is described as a oneway crossover study by the CS. All participants received their current treatment (ondemand therapy or prophylaxis factor replacement therapy) during a 6-month 

34 



<!-- page 538 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

observational phase (OP), then received marstacimab for a 12-month active treatment phase (ATP). The study therefore provides a comparison of marstacimab and factor replacement therapy within the same participants. The population of BASIS is comprised of a number of cohorts of participants, some of which are not relevant to this appraisal, this is discussed further below. The cohort and comparison of relevance in BASIS is people without inhibitors receiving prophylaxis therapy during the OP. 

Participants who did not require early termination in BASIS could enter the OLE and continue treatment for up to 16 additional months. Both BASIS and its OLE are ongoing. The CS presents analysis from the 17[th] April 2023 data-cut for BASIS, and interim analysis from the 10[th] March 2023 for the OLE (with an additional limited 4- month interim data-cut conducted in October 2023 and provided to the EAG at clarification). Results from BASIS[36] and the OLE[37] have been published as abstracts only. In clarification A32 the company confirmed that they are unable to provide a copy of the draft manuscript for the BASIS study but that updates on the status of the publication will be provided during the appraisal. The company also confirmed in clarification A14 that the final CSR of the BASIS OLE is anticipated in quarter four 2030 but that data for another interim analysis is anticipated to be available in October 2024. 

CS Figure 6 summarises the study design of BASIS. A summary of BASIS methodology with cross-references to the relevant sections of the CS where more detail can be found is presented in Table 4. Areas that the EAG has identified for further consideration are described below.

## **2.2.1.1 Population and eligibility** 

Men aged 12 to <75 years with severe haemophilia A (coagulation FVIII activity < 1%) or moderately severe to severe haemophilia B (coagulation FIX activity ≤2%) were eligible for BASIS. However, no patients with moderately severe haemophilia B were enrolled, so the population comprised only those with severe disease. The minimum age and severity of disease criteria in BASIS are in line with the NICE scope and anticipated marketing authorisation (MA), although limits on sex or upper age are not specified by NICE *********************. 

To be eligible for inclusion in BASIS, participants had to demonstrate at least 80% compliance with the scheduled prophylaxis regimen during 6 months prior to enrolment. To enter the ATP, participants had to demonstrate at least 80% compliance during the OP. In clarification A1, the company stated that compliance prior to enrolment was confirmed by the investigator, but did not explain how this was assessed. Compliance during the OP was monitored by sites and study teams and involved the use of an eDiary. The EAG has no concerns regarding the low numbers 

37 



<!-- page 541 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

of participants who did not meet inclusion criteria or discontinued due to compliance (clarification A1). 

People with active hepatitis B or C, or HIV uncontrolled by antiretroviral drugs were excluded from the study. The EAG clinical expert noted that this group of patients tend to be older, so may not have been on effective prophylaxis since childhood and may have more established joint disease and bleed more frequently. 

Results are presented in the CS for a selected subgroup of participants from BASIS based on: 

1. whether or not participants had inhibitors: only those without inhibitors were reported ( _non-inhibitor cohort);_ 

2. whether participants were receiving on-demand therapy or factor prophylaxis therapy at OP entry and during the OP: only those receiving _prophylaxis therapy_ were reported. 

The patient cohorts were specified _a priori_ in the BASIS protocol, see CS Figure 6. The CS and the submitted CSR do not present results for people who had inhibitors at OP entry. Inhibitor testing was conducted in the ATP at day 180 and study completion (day 360) and on days 180 and 360 or study completion of each year of the OLE. There were * participants in the prior prophylaxis cohort of BASIS who were identified as having a change in inhibitor status during the ATP (clarification A6). The EAG does not consider this ************ to be a concern 

The CS also does not present results for people who received on-demand therapy at screening and during the OP (although these are available in the CSR). On-demand therapy is not specified as a comparator by the NICE scope, therefore this omission is appropriate. The cohort of participants without inhibitors is in line with the anticipated MA for marstacimab, and the comparison with routine factor prophylaxis therapy is appropriate. 

## **2.2.1.2 Interventions** 

During the OP, participants continued with their routine factor FVIII or FIX replacement prophylaxis for 6 months. A breakdown of factor therapies used during

the OP was provided by the company in clarification A23 and is presented in Table 5. It appears that none of the participants were receiving emicizumab, which the CS notes is considered standard of care for haemophilia A (CS B.1.3.2). In addition, ***** participants were receiving extended half-life agents than would be seen in the UK. The EAG clinical experts considered it likely that in general, the participants in BASIS were not on prophylaxis comparable to current UK standards of care.

After the OP, participants who met additional criteria (Table 4) progressed to the ATP. Marstacimab was administered as a loading dose of 300 mg subcutaneous (SC) (as 2 x 150 mg injections) followed by 150 mg once weekly in a prefilled syringe for 12 months. After 6 months, participants who met protocol specified dose-escalation criteria could have their dose increased to 300 mg once weekly at the discretion of their clinician. The criteria were: 

1. Weight at least 50kg 

2. Two or more spontaneous bleeds (consisting of joint bleeds or significant soft tissue/muscle or other site bleeds) treated with infusion(s) of coagulation FVIII or FIX over a 6-month period in the absence of a confirmed FVIII or FIX inhibitor, respectively. Significant spontaneous bleeds were defined as those that lead to a transient or persistent loss of function.[27] 

Breakthrough bleeding during the study was stabilized using the participant’s standard haemostatic treatment regimen, which may include FVIII- or FIX replacement therapy. 

The dose of marstacimab and the potential for dose escalation remained the same during the OLE, however the mode of administration changed from prefilled syringe to prefilled pen. This is discussed in section 2.5.4. 

## **2.2.1.3 Outcomes** 

## _**Measures of bleeding**_ 

The BASIS trial protocol adheres to the World Federation of Hemophilia (WFH) guidelines for the classification and documentation of bleeding events. The definitions in the BASIS study are as follows. 

_Bleed:_ a bleed was classified as either "spontaneous" or "traumatic," with specific criteria for each type outlined below. Any indication of a bleed, whether it led to the administration of medication or treatment, was documented as a "bleed" or "bleeding episode", see further definitions below. 

_Spontaneous bleeding episodes:_ a bleeding event without any known contributing factor, such as definite trauma, strenuous activity, or overuse. The determination of 

40 



<!-- page 544 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

what constituted "strenuous" or "overuse" was left to the discretion of the participant, caregiver, or investigator. 

_Traumatic bleeding episodes:_ known or presumed contributing factor or reason for the bleed. For instance, if a participant exercised strenuously and subsequently experienced a bleed without any obvious injury. Bleeding episodes in target joints could be classified as traumatic if a specific action or event was known to have triggered the bleeding into the joint. 

_Treated bleed:_ treatment with factor replacement or bypassing agents within 48 hours of the onset, regardless of whether the treatment is preventive, prophylactic, or administered on-demand. 

_New treated bleed:_ occurred at the same location more than 72 hours after treatment for the initial bleed had stopped, or if it occurred at a different site, regardless of the time since the previous bleed. 

_New untreated bleed:_ occurred more than 48 hours after a previous untreated bleed at the same location, or more than 72 hours after the cessation of treatment for the original bleed for which treatment was initiated. An untreated bleed occurring at a different location was considered a new untreated bleed, regardless of the time since the previous bleed. 

Bleed data were recorded in an electronic handheld device which was provided to each participant at baseline (if not available a paper copy was provided). Participants were given training which included the timing and the nature of information to be entered in the diary, including the location of the bleed. In the final protocol amendment (22[nd] March 2022) Section 6.4 was amended to state that the eDiary data must be reviewed at each study visit (telephone or in-person). This was to reinforce the need for the diary data review at each scheduled contact, to ensure data accuracy (the diary was also used to record dosing details and adverse events). Bleeding episodes from participant diaries were validated with medical records. The investigators also assisted in the classification of the bleed if necessary. Training materials and user guides were provided to study sites and to participants; no further details were available in the CS. All data were time-stamped and automatically uploaded to a database in real time. Investigators were responsible for informing 

41 



<!-- page 545 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

participants of their data entry schedule and monitoring compliance via an electronic portal, with automatic notifications for any missed entries. 

Measuring the ABR is an important indicator of patient outcomes. Bleed data were considered in the BASIS trial as annualised bleeding rates (ABR) according to two definitions. ABRtreat recorded the number of treated bleeding episodes during the 12-month ATP, this was the primary endpoint of the trial. ABRtotal recorded the number of both treated and untreated bleeding during the 12-month ATP and was a secondary endpoint. ABRtotal accounts for all bleeds, including those that, although not treated, still impose a burden on the patient. ABRtreat was also assessed for bleeding by type, such as spontaneous, joint, and target joint bleeds. Bleeding measured as ABR is the gold standard outcome measure in haemophilia, it is a clinically meaningful, valid, and reliable measure, although is partially subjective.[5, 38] The ABRs calculated in the BASIS trial are in-line with the recommendations of the WFH.[5] However, although ABRs are frequently used as a primary endpoint, they are subject to several biases, including the subjective nature of how patients and physicians define and report bleeding events.[39, 40] 

## _**Joint health**_ 

An additional efficacy endpoint in the BASIS trial was the Hemophilia Joint Health Score (HJHS), which assesses joint health in the joints most frequently affected by haemophilia. The HJHS is a valuable tool in haemophilia management as it provides a standardised method to assess joint health, enabling clinicians to identify early signs of joint deterioration and to monitor the effectiveness of treatments over time.[41, ] 42 It evaluates various aspects of joint health across six joints (elbows, knees, ankles), with the following items being scored on scales ranging somewhere between 0-4: swelling, duration of swelling, muscle atrophy, crepitus during movement, flexion loss, extension loss, joint pain, and strength. Each joint can achieve a maximum score of 20. Gait is also assessed with a score ranging from 0−4. The tool has a maximum possible total score of 124 where higher scores indicate poorer joint health. The tool is designed to be used by physiotherapists, in BASIS training of the tool was provided. The HJHS is considered the best studied measure of joint health and has been validated in children and adults with 

42 



<!-- page 546 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

haemophilia.[5, 42] Its use in clinical practice, however, is limited owing to the time taken to administer the tool.[38] 

## _**Patient reported outcomes**_ 

Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) were systematically recorded using an electronic device referred to as a ‘site tablet’ during study visits. Five measures were used: the EuroQoL 5 Dimensions 5 Level (EQ-5D-5L); the Haemophilia Quality of Life Questionnaire for Adults (Haem-A-QoL) and for Children (Haemo-QoL); the Hemophilia Activities List (HAL); the Pediatric Hemophilia Activities List (pedHAL); the Patient Global Impression of change Hemophilia (PGIC-H) and the Hemophilia Life Impacts Questionnaire (HLIQ). Participants were asked to complete these measures at scheduled office visits before any other study activities (OP Baseline and ATP Visits 6, 7, 10, 12, 14, 16, and 20). 

The EAG briefly summarises below the haemophilia specific PROs to provide more context about what they measure, how the scores are interpreted and their validity and reliability. 

## _**Haem-A-QoL and Haemo-QoL**_ 

These are disease-specific measures of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) for haemophilia patients, tailored by age. The Haem-A-QoL is used for participants aged 17 years and older, with 46 items across 10 domains, including physical health, feelings, and treatment. This measure provides insights into how haemophilia affects daily life and overall well-being.[43] The Haemo-QoL is for participants aged 12 to <17 years, comprising 77 items across 12 domains similar to the Haem A QOL. Items are rated as ‘never’, ‘seldom’, ‘sometimes’, ‘often’ or ‘always’ for a 4-week recall period. For both versions the scores can be calculated by domain and as a total, the CS presented data for the physical health domain and the total score only. Scores range from 0 to 100 with lower scores indicating better HRQoL. There is a risk of recall bias with these tools due to the need to remember events that occurred over an extended period in the past. It's also important to consider that cultural differences can influence how questions are interpreted, which may affect the accuracy of the 

43 



<!-- page 547 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

results.[44] Nevertheless, this tool is generally regarded as reliable, consistently producing similar results when administered multiple times to the same individual.[45] 

## _**HAL (version 2) and pedHAL**_ 

These are also disease-specific HRQoL measures for haemophilia, based on age. Both tools help in evaluating the physical impact of haemophilia on daily activities and can guide rehabilitation and physical therapy.[46] The HAL assesses the functional abilities of adults (aged 17 and older) with haemophilia by focusing on physical activities potentially limited due to joint damage or bleeding episodes. HAL evaluates functional impact through 42 items across seven domains: 

Lying/Sitting/Kneeling/Standing, Lower Leg Functioning, Upper Arm Functioning, Self-care, and Sports/Leisure. Similar to HAL, pedHAL is for children (aged 12 to <17 years), focusing on age-appropriate activities, and assesses 53 items across the same seven domains.[47] Scoring can be by domain or total, additionally for HAL scores can be by components such as activities involving the upper extremities only. The CS only reported these measures total scores in BASIS. Scores range from 0 to 100 in both instruments, higher scores indicate better status. As discussed above, it's important to account for recall bias when evaluating these measures.[44] 

## _**PGIC-H**_ 

This tool captures the patient’s subjective assessment of overall change in health status due to treatment, providing a patient-centred outcome that is simple and quick to administer.[48] It is an assessment of the participant’s overall impression of change in their life with haemophilia. This was used to measure the participant’s impression during the two phases of the BASIS study (OP and ATP). The PGIC-H asks participants to reflect on changes "since the start of the study" or "since the infusion," using a 7-point categorical scale with three grades of improvement, three of worsening, and a central ‘no change’ option. It is noteworthy, that subjectivity can introduce variability in responses, as patients' perceptions may be influenced by factors unrelated to the treatment.[49] Additionally, as mentioned previously, recall bias may impact accuracy, particularly if patients are asked to remember how they felt before starting treatment.[44] 

## _**HLIQ**_ 

44 



<!-- page 548 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

This tool is designed to evaluate the impact of haemophilia across various aspects of life, including physical, emotional, and social dimensions. By providing a comprehensive view of how haemophilia influences daily living, it helps researchers identify specific areas where intervention may be needed.[50] This is a 9-item measure evaluating the impacts of living with and being treated for haemophilia, with a recall period of the past week. It was an exploratory endpoint in BASIS. It includes four items rated on a 5-point ordinal verbal rating scale (VRS) from 0 to 4; four items that use a branching format where a ‘yes’ response leads to a 5-point VRS and where a ‘no’ response specifies reasons for not participating in the activity (due to haemophilia or other reasons), and one item rated on a 4-point ordinal VRS from 0 to 3. Questions include items such as ‘how much was haemophilia on your mind’, ‘how much did haemophilia interfere with your ability to perform day to day activities’ and ‘did you participate in any social activities’. Higher scores on the VRS indicate a greater impact of haemophilia on daily life or treatment. 

Each of these tools provides unique insights into the lives of individuals with haemophilia, focusing on quality of life, functional abilities, and perceived health changes. Although all are validated and reliable, potential issues such as recall bias, cultural differences, and subjectivity must be considered in the interpretation of results. 

## **2.2.1.4 Risk of Bias** 

BASIS is described by the company as a one-way crossover study; the design is justified in the study protocol by a sample size advantage and to allow assessment of potential confounding factors in a rare disease. The company conducted a quality assessment of BASIS using a modified version of the Downs and Black checklist. The EAG agrees that this checklist is appropriate for the design of BASIS and that the modifications are acceptable. However, the company has focused on the overall summary score and has not discussed any of their responses that suggest a source of bias. The use of summary scores is no longer recommended.[51] The EAG conducted an independent assessment of quality; a comparison of the company’s and EAG’s judgements is presented in Appendix 7.3. The first section of the tool 

45 



<!-- page 549 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

focuses on reporting of the study, and as BASIS has not been published as a full article the EAG has based their judgements on the reporting of the study in the CS. 

In contrast to the company, the EAG considers the external validity of BASIS (questions 11 to 13) to be unclear, because the CS does not identify the population that the participants were sourced from or describe how the patients were selected. It is unclear whether the population is representative of the target population in the UK and thus whether outcomes for the study population can be generalised to the UK population. The CS reports the number of participants screened but not the number of participants who were asked to participate, and does not demonstrate that the distribution of the main confounding factors was the same in the study sample and the source population. Additionally, the CS does not clearly demonstrate that location and delivery of the intervention was representative of that in use in the source population. The protocol states ‘when necessary, the site staff may administer study intervention to the participant’, but the impact of this is not clear. Question 21 also asks if all participants were recruited from the same source population, so this was also considered to be unclear by the EAG. 

The EAG agrees with the company’s judgement that principal confounders were not clearly described or adjusted for in the analysis, and that there was no blinding of outcome assessment, which is possible even in an open-label study. The bleed data outcomes were self-reported, and untreated bleeds are subjective. The EAG clinical expert considered that it is possible that not all recorded untreated bleeding episodes are bleeding events (for example, they may be musculoskeletal pain without bleeding). 

The design of BASIS meant that patients receiving marstacimab were compared with the same patients who had previously been receiving factor prophylaxis and therefore each patient acts as their own control, with the potential for known and unknown factors changing between the time-periods. It is unclear whether there were any differences in the care participants received, either intentionally or unintentionally, during the OP and ATP. The company notes in section CS B.2.12.1 that many participants entered the ATP in early 2022 as COVID-19 rates were rising, and that 21.7% of participants experienced COVID-19 during the ATP. COVID-19 was designated as an adverse events of special interest (AESI) due to its potential to 

46 



<!-- page 550 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

increase the risk of thrombotic events. Changes in activity levels during lockdown may also have had an impact on real-world haemophilia care; the EAG clinical expert considered that bleeds may have been less well treated, as patients may not have attended hospital for review. The EAG notes, however, that in TA989,[23] the committee concluded that the pandemic did not have a substantial impact on the magnitude of clinical benefits in the trial of etranacogene dezaparvovec for treating moderately severe or severe haemophilia. The company provided additional details of the impact of COVID-19 on the conduct of BASIS in clarification A24; the EAG has no concerns regarding this. 

There was no washout-period between the OP and ATP, however sensitivity analyses were available in the CSR to assess the impact of a carryover effect from the OP. 

## **2.2.1.5 Participant flow and analysis sets** 

Participant flow for the cohort without inhibitors through BASIS is presented in CS Appendix D.2, Figure 3. Of 179 patients, 47 (26.3%) failed screening and another four did not enter the OP (due to adverse event, withdrawn, or assignment after data cut off). The EAG considered this to be a high proportion of screening failures and requested reasons for failing screening in clarification A7. In response, the company stated that there was a typo in CS Appendix D.2, Figure 3 and that the wording “patients without inhibitors” was incorrect (i.e. the participant flow was for all patients entering BASIS). The company also stated that the 47 participants who failed screening includes both inhibitor and non-inhibitor cohort participants. A listing of screen failures and reasons was provided by the company in clarification A7, but the number of participants did not total 47 (only ** unique Participant IDs were included). The EAG was unable to determine whether there is a generalisability issue due to the high proportion of screening failures. 

Of the 128 patients without inhibitors entering the OP, 37 were receiving on-demand therapy and were not considered further in the CS. A total of 91 participants without inhibitors and with prior routine prophylaxis therapy entered the OP (all safety-set), and 83 of these entered the ATP (mITT and marstacimab safety set). Of the eight participants not entering the ATP, seven did not complete the OP (5 no longer met the eligibility criteria, 2 had protocol deviations), and one completed the OP but did

## **2.2.2.1 Baseline characteristics** 

The baseline participant and disease characteristics of BASIS are shown in Table 6. A total of 83 male participants treated with prior factor prophylaxis in the OP entered the ATP of BASIS. The mean age was 32.6 years, and the study population was composed of 54.2% White and 43.4% Asian individuals. The participants had an average weight of 69.1 kg and mean body mass index (BMI) was 23.6. The company’s clinical advisors considered that the population in BASIS was younger and lower weight compared with those in the UKHCDO dataset,[3] with the latter being more reflective of patients in the UK. They also noted that patients in BASIS had more severe disease and that Asian patients were overrepresented, but they did not consider this to be a prognostic variable or treatment effect modifier. As noted above (2.2.1.2), it is likely that participants were not receiving optimal prophylaxis at enrolment and during the OP, therefore the appearance of more severe disease could relate to treatment rather than underlying phenotype. Only ***% of the safety set (data not available for the mITT set) were aged 65 years or older, with ****% aged 45 to 64 years. The EAG clinical expert noted that older participants are less likely to have had routine prophylaxis since childhood and as a result have more complications and are harder to treat.

## **2.2.2.3 Subgroup analyses** 

Subgroup analyses are presented by the company in Figure 10 of the company submission. Whilst these results should be treated with caution due to the small number of people contributing information and lack of statistical power, the relative efficacy of marstacimab appeared worse for people with haemophilia B compared to the efficacy in the haemophilia A population. Hence, the EAG considers it reasonable to use haemophilia type-specific inputs for the economic model as they may be of interest to committee. The EAG is not aware that any models including interaction terms for treatment and haemophilia type have been fitted, or of any biological rationale for this difference.

## **2.3** _**Critique of trials identified and included in the indirect comparison and/or multiple treatment comparison**_ 

The CS considered studies for an indirect treatment comparison (ITC) to the BASIS study. Two potential comparator studies were identified in the CS SLR, HAVEN 3[53] and HAVEN 4.[54] The CS assessed the similarity of the study populations between the two HAVEN studies and the BASIS study in Section B.2.11.1, focusing on comparing with the subgroup of BASIS with haemophilia A, since HAVEN 3 and HAVEN 4 included only haemophilia A. The CS included data from Cohort D of the HAVEN 3 study in the indirect comparison; the population in this Cohort were without inhibitors and had received prior prophylaxis treatment, and were deemed similar enough for comparison to BASIS. 

The HAVEN 4 study included both people with inhibitors and those without inhibitors at baseline; the CS excluded this study from the ITC as there were no baseline characteristics available for the relevant subgroup without inhibitors. Since submission there has been a publication of HAVEN 4 that includes details of participants without inhibitors.[55] HAVEN 4 included both prior episodic (on-demand) 

59 



<!-- page 563 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

and prophylactic regimens, however the majority had prior prophylaxis (Table 17). The EAG has compared the core study characteristics of BASIS, HAVEN 3 and HAVEN 4 in Table 16, and the baseline characteristics in Table 17. All studies included participants aged 12 years or older with severe haemophilia. All were multicentre studies and data of relevance to an ITC were all from non-randomised cohorts. The duration of treatment varied between the three studies, with BASIS treating for 12 months, HAVEN 3 for at least 24 weeks and HAVEN 4 for 24 weeks. Similar to BASIS, the HAVEN trials followed the WFH guidelines for defining and categorizing bleeding episodes, ensuring consistency and standardization across studies. This includes the categorization of bleeds as either spontaneous or traumainduced, and further classification into joint, muscle, or other types of bleeding.

## **2.3.1 Baseline characteristics** 

Table 17 presents the baseline characteristics of participants of relevance to the ITC from the BASIS, HAVEN 3 and HAVEN 4 studies. Comparisons are difficult to make for some characteristics because of reporting differences. The proportion of white participants was lower in the BASIS study compared with both of the HAVEN studies, and the participants in BASIS were slightly younger with a lower BMI than those in HAVEN 3 (not reported in HAVEN 4). The proportion with a target joint at baseline was higher in BASIS compared with HAVEN 3, but lower than in HAVEN 4, and prior total ABR was also higher in BASIS than HAVEN 3 (not reported in HAVEN 4). These factors lead the CS to commenting in Section B.2.11.3 that relative to the HAVEN 3 study, participants in BASIS had more severe disease. The treatment regimen at baseline was 100% prophylactic in BASIS and in HAVEN 3, but in HAVEN 4, 32.5% had only received prior episodic treatment. The EAG has concerns as to whether BASIS is similar enough to either of the HAVEN studies to be compared in an ITC.

## **2.3.2 Quality assessment** 

The company’s quality assessment of HAVEN 3 using the Downs and Black checklist is reported in CS Appendix D.1.8. HAVEN 4 was excluded by the company therefore they did not assess it for quality. The company focuses on the overall summary score 

63 



<!-- page 567 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

and does not discuss any of their responses that suggest a source of bias. The summary score is described as falling within the “poor” category. There is no explicit use of the quality assessment in the evidence synthesis. The EAG has conducted an independent quality assessment of both HAVEN 3 (the relevant non-interventional Cohort D only) and HAVEN 4, and presents this alongside the company’s judgements of HAVEN 3 in Appendix 7.4. 

There are several differences between the company’s and EAG’s judgements of HAVEN 3; in most of these cases the company has responded with a ‘No’ or ‘Unclear’ response and the EAG has responded with a ‘Yes’ (Appendix 7.4). While the EAG has concerns regarding a number of items on the checklist, these are fewer than the company’s. 

The EAG’s responses for HAVEN 4 are identical to those for HAVEN 3 (noninterventional Cohort D), reflecting the similarity in study design and reporting. The HAVEN studies do not describe the source population or how patients were selected, therefore the external validity of the studies is unclear. The principal confounding factors were not clearly described or adjusted for in the analysis, and there was no blinding of outcome assessment. It is unclear whether there are any differences in care between the treatment periods. Compliance was not reported in the HAVEN studies. The EAG considers the overall quality of HAVEN 3 and 4 to be similar to that of BASIS, with similar limitations of study design (section 2.2.1.4). 

## **2.4** _**Critique of the indirect comparison and/or multiple treatment comparison**_ 

## **2.4.1 Overview** 

In the absence of a head-to-head comparison between marstacimab and emicizumab, an unanchored simulated treatment comparison (STC) was conducted. The STC compared the control of bleeding events among adult and adolescent patients with severe haemophilia A without inhibitors who had previously received routine prophylaxis therapy. The company compared five efficacy outcomes between the haemophilia A subpopulation of the marstacimab BASIS trial and a subgroup of group D of the emicizumab HAVEN 3 trial. The STC accounted for a range of effect 

64 



<!-- page 568 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

modifiers and prognostic variables between the two studies. Overall, emicizumab is favoured numerically across the five efficacy outcomes, however the STC found none of these differences between marstacimab and emicizumab to be statistically significant. 

## **2.4.2 Methods** 

The company ruled out conducting an anchored ITC such as a network metaanalysis due to the single-arm crossover design of the BASIS study. Additionally, the company deemed it infeasible to conduct an anchored ITC using the intrapatient comparison data between the lead-in observational phase and active trial phases due to the differences in disease management, differences in sample size between HAVEN 3 subgroup of group D (N=48) and BASIS haemophilia A subgroup (N=65) and an absence of baseline characteristics data for the HAVEN 3 group D subgroup intrapatient comparison population. Hence, the company opt for an unanchored approach. 

Note that HAVEN 3 recruited 4 groups of patients, but only group D (n=63) is of interest as they received previous prophylactic factor therapy. This unanchored STC uses baseline characteristics and efficacy estimates for the entire group D population. For the BASIS clinical trial, the STC used data from the haemophilia A patient subgroup only, since emicizumab is used in haemophilia A patients only. The EAG notes the company uses rate ratios to compare efficacy of emicizumab and marstacimab, and not rate differences as it has reported in the company submission for the BASIS trial. 

The STC used individual-level patient data (IPD) from the BASIS trial and aggregatelevel data from the HAVEN 3 trial. Analyses are based on bleed rates for all participants, and do not distinguish between people who do and not experience bleeds. The effect modifiers and prognostic variables accounted for were: prior ABRtotal (rate), target joints (yes/no), age (years), body mass index (BMI; kg/m[2] ), percent white, and percent Hispanic/Latino. 

The EAG requested additional analyses based on those published by Astermark et al.[57] who included covariates for age, % white, BMI, baseline ABR, proportion with <9 bleeds in prior 24 weeks, and proportion receiving SHL FVIII (clarification question A35). The company conducted this analysis also including target joints in 

65 



<!-- page 569 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

their STC adjustment. Note this analysis used only the first 33 weeks of follow-up from BASIS for consistency with the reported follow-up available for HAVEN 3. The EAG considers this analysis to be an improvement over the company’s preferred analysis based on the choice of covariates. 

The EAG also asked for a MAIC analysis to be run, to compare to the STC analyses (A36), however the company declined this opportunity for reasons based on anchored comparisons, which do not necessarily apply to unanchored analyses as presented by the company. 

Within group D, results are reported for the subgroup who received prior prophylaxis as part of a non-interventional study (n=48) by Mahlangu (2018).[53] The EAG notes that an anchored comparison is possible using this information. 

The EAG also requested that the company perform an indirect comparison to the HAVEN 4 study, to avoid reliance on comparisons of a single pair of studies (clarification question A34). The main limitation of this approach is that the information available for the HAVEN 4 study and used in the indirect comparison includes groups of people who did and did not receive prior prophylaxis, reducing the generalisability to UK patients. To reduce potential bias within the comparison, the company included information from the patients who did not receive prior prophylaxis from the BASIS study. These analyses included adjustments for age (% <18), race (% white), number of bleeds in prior 24 weeks, target joints (%), record of ≥1 CV risk factor (%) and prior on demand therapy (%). 

## **2.4.3 STC Results** 

Overall, the STC found no statistically significant differences between marstacimab and emicizumab at a p = 0.05 threshold. Emicizumab has numerical improvements in ABRs (total, treated and joint treated) and numerically lower proportions of patients experiencing bleeds (total and treated) when compared to marstacimab (Table 18). For the STC using covariates based on Astermark et al. the bleed rate ratios is closer to one, however the proportion with zero bleeds is further from one. The EAG considers that neither study was designed to be compared this way, and it is possible that differences in treatment effect may exist that have not been detected in these analyses.

## **2.5.4 Marstacimab Administration** 

In the BASIS Clinical Trial, marstacimab was administered using a prefilled syringe (PFS).[58] In the BASIS OLE, marstacimab was administered using a prefilled pen (PFP).[59] The company's economic model was informed by administration-related utility decrements based on the PFP.[58] 

The company conducted a phase 1, randomised, cross-over study (NCT04832139) to investigate bioequivalence.[60] The company established bioequivalence between the PFS and PFP devices for 300 mg marstacimab administered as two single injections of 150 mg marstacimab subcutaneously in a cohort of 22 healthy adult male participants.[59, 60] 

The EAG questions the generalisability of this cohort to the UK haemophilia population and whether PFP and PFS have equal efficacy among haemophilia patients. The EAG raises the concern that the BASIS trial used an administrative device that was not the intended administrative device for marstacimab in real-world use and that PFP and PFS could differ in safety/adverse event frequency, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, frequency of dosing/administration errors and impact on quality of life.[61] 

There is the potential that PFPs could be preferable and medically equivalent, among haemophilia patients compared to syringes – and literature comparing the two among different biological medicines suggests that to be the case.[61-63] However, the EAG would prefer to err on the side of caution and suggest further investigation into the efficacy and safety profile of marstacimab administrated through the PFP. 

The clinical expert consulted by the EAG suggests they have little/no concern over this generalisability of PFS to PFP and that the pen form may be preferable to patients - highlighting the recent research in a similar medicine, concizumab, that is also administrated as a PFP.[62] 

## **2.5.5 Immunogenicity** 

Biologics, such as monoclonal antibody-based therapies like marstacimab and emicizumab, are immunogenic.[64] Drug immunogenicity occurs when a patient’s immune system produces anti-drug antibodies (ADAs).[64] ADAs can be neutralising 

73 



<!-- page 577 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

(NAb) – whereby they inhibit the biological activity of the drug by blocking or altering the active part; or non-neutralising (non-NAb) – whereby they bind to the drug but do not affect the drug-target interaction.[64] Both NAb and non-NAb form antibody-drug complexes that the immune system clears and therefore may affect the efficacy, safety, pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of a medicine.[65] 

The company conducted immunogenicity testing during the BASIS clinical trial to evaluate the incidence and effect of ADAs against marstacimab. Of the 116 ADAevaluable participants, 23 (19.8% incidence) were positive for treatment-induced ADAs. Of the 23 treatment-induced ADA-positive participants, 6 produced NAbs. The company states that immunogenicity testing results showed ADA were of “low incidence”, low titre with a relatively early onset, and mostly transient.[58] A concern of the EAG is that patients with haemophilia A who produce ADAs against emicizumab – a patient subgroup of potentially good candidates for marstacimab – could be at greater risk of developing ADAs against marstacimab. Scientific literature, to the knowledge of the EAG, does not support or oppose this suggestion. Additionally, the link between emicizumab inefficacy among patients and ADAs remains under investigation; with most evidence being individual case study data.[66-69] Indeed, emicizumab discontinuation due to lack of efficacy with a proven ADA is a very rare event.[70] 

## **2.5.6 Review of recent relevant appraisals** 

The EAG examined the key issues raised in the recent NICE technology appraisals of efanesoctog alfa for treating and preventing bleeding episodes in haemophilia A and etranacogene dezaparvovec for moderately severe or severe haemophilia B, to investigate their relevance to the appraisal of marstacimab. Only issues already raised by the current EAG were identified, including uncertainties around the indirect comparisons, the source of ABR information and the treatment of bleeding events.

## **2.6** _**Conclusions of the clinical effectiveness section**_ 

The BASIS trial demonstrates that marstacimab is non-inferior to routine prophylaxis for people with severe haemophilia. However, the BASIS trial has limited generalisability to NHS practice given the differences in baseline bleed rates, in the proportion of people receiving EHL factor prophylaxis, and potentially the dosing of factor prophylaxis. These may also effect estimates of relative efficacy coming from BASIS, in addition to the dose-escalation of marstacimab. 

The EAG is concerned about the potential for marstacimab to be inferior to routine prophylaxis for people with severe haemophilia B. The relative efficacy of marstacimab to emicizumab for haemophilia A comes from indirect comparisons which have very high uncertainty but consistently suggest that marstacimab is 

*********************** to emicizumab. The EAG considers UKHCDO to be a valuable source for informing efficacy of current NHS treatments.

## **3 COST EFFECTIVENESS** 

## **3.1** _**EAG comment on company’s review of cost-effectiveness**_ 

## _**evidence**_ 

The company’s SLR “to identify economic evidence in the field of haemophilia” (CS Document B.3.1) comprised three “evidence streams”; economic evaluations, utilities/health-related quality of life and healthcare costs/resource use (reported in CS Appendices G, H and I respectively). The original SLR undertaken in August 2020 included both clinical and economic evidence, then in May 2024 update searches and screening for the three economic evidence streams were undertaken separately to the clinical SLR. As a result, 123 publications from the original SLR were excluded from the SLR in 2024 because they did not report relevant economic outcomes (Company clarification responses A45 and A46). 

Due to a large number of included studies, a process of evidence prioritisation for each evidence stream was undertaken. The prioritisation criteria are described in CS Appendices G.1.2, H.1.2 and I.1.2, and deprioritised studies are listed in CS Appendices Tables 75, 81 and 86. The prioritisation criteria include UK relevance and recent publication. However, as stated in CS Appendix G.1.3: “included records were prioritised for extraction if they were key studies informing the structure of the economic model in this submission, or informed utilities or costs in the economic model”, which leads the EAG to conclude that some studies may have been selected for the SLR based on prior use to build the economic model, rather than the literature review informing the building of the model in an unbiased manner based on _a priori_ eligibility criteria. 

## **3.1.1 Search strategies** 

CS Appendix G.1.1 describes the various literature search sources and strategies for the economic SLR’s three evidence streams. A good, appropriate range of databases and other sources were searched, including recent conference proceedings, HTA agency websites and the CEA Registry and EQ-5D Publications databases. The electronic database search strategies (Appendix G.1.1, Tables 2668) are good and comprehensive. The 2024 update searches (Tables 52-68) are limited by publication year (2020-current), however use of the date a record is _added_ to the database is best practice, as sometimes database records can be added, or 

76 



<!-- page 580 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

significantly changed, long after an article is published. The same search terms were used across Embase and MEDLINE, which can mean useful terms are missed, as the databases have different controlled vocabularies (Emtree vs MesH), however the EAG does not consider this to have affected the sensitivity of the searches for this review. 

Due to the SLR not identifying any cost effectiveness analyses of marstacimab the company developed a de novo model. This model is informed by the previous NICE assessments in the area. The EAG critique of the company modelling tries to bring in the evidence and ACD/FAD conclusions of the previous NICE assessments. The EAG review of the company identified cost effectiveness literature is limited, and may require further work depending upon which elements Committee identifies as key model drivers.

## **3.2.2 Model structure** 

The company model structure is most easily thought of as a partitioned health state model 1F[2] with an annual cycle, a 64 year time horizon and 3.5% discounting of costs and benefits. 

Individual treatments are modelled, marstacimab, emicizumab, 7 FVIIIs and 4 FIXs. The outcomes for the 7 FVIIIs and 4 FIXs can be subsequently pooled weighted by UK market shares. 

For each cycle patients are split into three categories, those with: 

- No bleeds 

- Joint bleeds requiring treatment 

- Non-joint bleeds requiring treatment 

A 6.02% discontinuation rate from marstacimab to a pooled FVIII basket for those with haemophilia A and to a pooled FIX basket for those with haemophilia B is applied during the first cycle for the company base case. The model contains the facility to apply marstacimab discontinuations in every model cycle. 

Mortality is applied through standard UK life table estimates. A scenario analysis applies an SMR of 2.4 for those with bleeds requiring treatment. 

The BASIS baseline EQ-5D quality of life is applied to all patients. 

QALY decrements specific to joint bleeds and to non-joint bleeds are applied. 

> 2 There is one transition probability, that of discontinuing from marstacimab to FVIII 

79 



<!-- page 583 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

QALY decrements per administration for subcutaneous treatments, marstacimab and emicizumab, and for intravenous treatments, FVIII and FIX, are applied. These QALY decrements are the main source of the estimated QALY gains from marstacimab over FVIII and to a lesser extent over FIX. 

All routine treatments, marstacimab, emicizumab, FVIII and FIX are assumed to be home administered and incur no administration costs. 

A one-off dose escalation of 13.25% from 150mg to 300mg marstacimab is applied based upon the BASIS ATP. 

Emicizumab is assumed to be dosed fortnightly as 3.0 IU/kg. There are no discontinuations from emicizumab to FVIII. 

Dosing for FVIII/FIX is based upon the centre of the ranges of the dose and frequency specified in each FVIII/FIX SmPC. 

There is no vial sharing and wastage is assumed for emicizumab and FVIII/FIX. 

The base case assumes that bleeds require one additional FVIII/FIX treatment at the same dose as routine prophylaxis. The large majority of treated bleeds also require a haematology outpatient visit, and an A&E visit or something similar with some patients being admitted as inpatients. 

The company presents a range of scenario and sensitivity analyses. The two main company scenario analyses split the bleed rate estimates by: 

- Scenario 1: haemophilia A and haemophilia B 

- Scenario 2: SHL and EHL FVIII/FIX. 

Note that the company presents estimates for analyses that censor marstacimab estimates for dose escalation and analyses that do not. Throughout this chapter all inputs and results are from the analyses that do not censor marstacimab estimates for dose escalation.

## **3.2.5 Perspective, time horizon and discounting** 

These are largely aligned with the NICE reference case, though the time horizon of 64 year can be argued as being less than lifetime for any younger patients being modelled. 

After the first model cycle the company base case is essentially static, making the time horizon relatively unimportant 2F[3] . Only the scenarios of an ongoing annual discontinuation from marstacimab and an SMR for those with bleeds change this. 

## **3.2.6 Treatment effectiveness and extrapolation** 

The main effect estimates are the proportion of patients with bleeds that require treatment, and the treated ABR (ABRT) and treated joint ABR (AJBRT) conditional upon having a treated bleed. The treated non-joint ABR is the residual: AnJBRT = ABRT - AJBRT. 

The estimates for emicizumab are derived by applying the ITC odds ratio of no bleeding of **** to the marstacimab odds of no bleeding, and the rate ratios of **** for ABRT and **** for AJBRT. 

The EAG presents the implied unconditional ABRs in the last two columns of Table 27 for ease of comparison with the clinical effectiveness section. These are all that are needed for the company base case and most analyses, the proportion with

## **3.2.7 Marstacimab dose escalation** 

A one-off dose escalation rate for 13.25% from 150mg to 300mg marstacimab is applied in the first cycle of the model, based upon the ATP of BASIS. 

## **3.2.8 Treatment discontinuations** 

A one-off treatment discontinuation rate of 6.02% for marstacimab is applied in the first cycle of the model, based upon the ATP of BASIS. The company presents a scenario analysis that applies this for each annual model cycle. 

Haemophilia A patients discontinuing from marstacimab are assumed to have the costs and efficacy of the market weighted FVIII basket. It is assumed that none discontinue to emicizumab. 

Haemophilia B patients discontinuing from marstacimab are assumed to have the costs and efficacy of the market weighted FIX basket. 

It is assumed that there are no discontinuations from emicizumab. 

## **3.2.9 Adverse events** 

Adverse events have minimal effects upon model outputs and are not included in the company base case. If included, they occur during each model cycle for marstacimab and emicizumab, rates being taken from BASIS for marstacimab and from HAVEN 3 for emicizumab. The rates for marstacimab are a constant 1.2% across all adverse events, but with there being no epistaxis as shown in Table 28.

## **3.2.10 Mortality** 

The company base case applies standard UK life table values. 

The model also contains the facility to apply an SMR for those with bleeds. The 

company uses the relatively recent study of 1,031 Dutch patients with data between 2001 and 2018,[16] of whom 421 had severe haemophilia with a reported SMR of 2.4 (1.8-3.0).

## **3.2.12.2 Administration and monitoring costs** 

All routine prophylaxis is assumed to be patient administered and there are no administration costs.

treatment these would net out between the arms. For scenarios which model a difference in overall survival monitoring costs would not net out between the arms. 

## **3.2.12.3 Bleed FVIII/FIX costs** 

Bleeds are assumed to be treated with an FVIII basket or a FIX basket depending upon whether the patient has haemophilia A or haemophilia B. This applies not only to bleeds among patients on marstacimab or emicizumab prophylaxis. It also applies to bleeds for those receiving a specific FVIII or FIX; e.g. patients using BeneFIX for prophylaxis do not have their bleeds treated with BeneFIX but with a weighted average of FIX treatments. 

The dosing required for treating bleeds is assumed to be the same as a routine prophylactic dose, hence FVIII and FIX costs per bleed are as per Table 32 and Table 33, ****** and ****** respectively with wastage and ****** and ****** without wastage. The model also allows for a doubling in the dose and hence the cost per bleed for joint bleeds.
