## **4.4** _**Company sensitivity analyses**_ 

The company presents a wide range of sensitivity analyses in Document B, Section B.3.10.2 (Page 134) of the effects of various inputs upon the estimated net health benefits. The four inputs that the company reports the model being most sensitive to for the comparison with the FVIII basket, across the ranges explored, are: 

- Baseline weight 

- Baseline age 

- The proportion of marstacimab patients who dose escalate 

- The proportion of marstacimab patients who discontinue to FVIII 

The estimated proportions with bleeds also have some effect. 

The results for the baseline age need to be interpreted with some caution as the analyses are reporting net health benefits. A given annual net health benefit will result in a lager total net health benefit for a younger patient. 

As would be expected, for the comparison with emicizumab results are also sensitive to the odds ratio of bleeds and the rate ratio of bleeds. 

The pattern for the comparison with the FIX basket is similar to that for the FVIII basket, but the proportions with bleeds for marstacimab and the individual FIX treatments matter more. This is due at least in part due to the lesser importance of administration route for the QALY gains for the comparison with the FIX basket due to less frequent administrations within the FIX basket, whereas as summarised in Section 3.2.11.3 above these are more important for the comparison with the FVIII basket. 

Further scenario analyses, as reported in Document B, Table 74 (Page 138) suggest a reasonable sensitivity as to whether: 

- The UKHCDO market shares should be applied or the iQVIA estimates 

- The UKHCDO emicizumab dosing should be applied 

- Wastage is applied 

- Double FVIII/FIX dosing for joint bleeds is applied 

97 



<!-- page 601 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

Results are also sensitivity as to whether a 2.4 SMR is applied for those with bleeds. Applying this worsens the net health benefits for marstacimab compared to both the FVIII basket and the FIX basket, but improves them for marstacimab compared to emicizumab. This apparently perverse result is due to annual treatment costs being substantially more than the £30,000 per QALY willingness to pay threshold for all treatments, meaning that a superior net survival worsens the cost effectiveness estimate. 

## **4.5** _**Model validation and face validity check**_ 

## **4.5.1 EAG cross check model rebuild** 

The EAG has fully rebuilt the company model and gets good agreement with it. There are minor disagreements in terms of the total discounted bleeds that are modelled. The largest discrepancy for the discounted sum of any outcome is 0.2%, with the discrepancies for the discounted total costs and QALYs being 0.004% and 0.002% respectively. 

Based upon the EAG model rebuild the EAG provides a simplified model cross check within the EAG revised company model to highlight the main structural errors. 

- The marstacimab versus emicizumab rate ratios for ABRT and AJBRT are for the entire population. They are applied to the ABRT and AJBRT of those who have had a bleed. This causes the modelled ABRT and AJBRT risk ratios to be overstated by the relative risk of having a bleed, ***, which in turn causes the bleed rates of emicizumab to be understated by a similar amount. 

- The FVIII/FIX costs for treatment of bleeds are double counted. This error favours the more effective treatment. 

- The weekly loading doses for the first 4 weeks of emicizumab are assumed to be in addition to the Q2W dosing. 

- Those who dose escalate with marstacimab require two subcutaneous administrations. The model assumes only one disutility for these administrations. The EAG thinks that the most reasonable interpretation of the administrative disutilities paper is that dose escalation should involve two administration disutilities. 

98 



<!-- page 602 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

- Wastage calculations are based upon the smallest vial available. The cost per IU is identical across all vial sizes for the factor VIII/FIX and for emicizumab. Given this, if the smallest vial is a factor of all other larger vials the company wastage calculation is correct, but not if not. Emicizumab is available as 30 IU, 60 IU, 105 IU and 150 IU so the company wastage calculations for it are incorrect. Basing wastage on the 30 IU vial means that for doses between 90 IU and 120 IU four 30 IU vials and so 120 IU are required. But the 105 IU vial is available which saves 15 IU for doses between 90 IU and 105 IU. This 15 IU saving recurs at various higher doses. For the company base case weight distribution the company method estimates an annual cost for emicizumab with wastage of ********. Correcting this results in an annual cost for emicizumab of ********, an annual ******* less. 

- For the modelling of haemophilia B to estimate the FIX direct drug costs the proportion surviving during the first cycle is applied to the annual direct drug cost for both the first cycle and the second cycle. The proportion surviving during the second cycle is applied to the annual direct drug cost for the third cycle, the third cycle proportion to the fourth cycle, and so on. This inflates the FIX direct drug costs by a little over 1%.

It can be argued that the effect of bleeds upon quality of life is transient. Some patients in BASIS will not have had a bleed within the EQ-5D recall period, but will have had prior to it. The effect of bleeds on these patients may not be reflected in their EQ-5D. But others will have had a bleed during the recall period and the effect of their bleeds will be reflected in their EQ-5D. Given a large enough sample these effects would be expected to cancel out, with the correct overall effect of bleeds on quality of life being reflected in the EQ-5D responses. But the relatively small sample size of BASIS increases the uncertainty around this. 

The model simulates a loss from baseline due to bleeds and administration effects upon QoL, in contrast to a gain from baseline during BASIS. The EAG thinks that this could argue for adjusting the baseline value within the model, but this would be inconsequential for the net effect estimates. 

The main result appears to be that the net quality of life gains are not particularly large. The modelled absolute net gains are reasonably aligned with the modelled net gain being only 0.0045 larger than the company reported BASIS net gain, but this small absolute value is an increase of 20% compared to the medians. Assessing this is complicated by the company reporting medians rather than means. If nothing else it illustrates that small absolute changes in the quality of life inputs to the model may cause large changes in the ICERs. 

## **5 EXTERNAL ASSESSMENT GROUP’S ADDITIONAL ANALYSES** 

## **5.1** _**EAG critique of elements of the company model**_ 

## **5.1.1 FVIII/FIX treatment of bleeds** 

The company model assumes that those requiring additional FVIII for the treatment of a bleed have the average cost of the market share weighted FVIII basket. The parallel assumption applies for FIX. 

100 



<!-- page 604 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

It may be more reasonable to assume that those requiring additional FVIII for the treatment of a bleed have the same FVIII as their routine prophylaxis, and likewise for FIX. 

## **5.1.2 Discontinuations** 

The model applies an annual discontinuation rate from marstacimab to a basket of FVIII/FIX of 6.02% for the first cycle of the company base case, and for all cycles in a sensitivity analyses. The model assumes no discontinuations from emicizumab. 

The effect of this is most obvious for the comparison with emicizumab. Emicizumab is in effect being compared with a basket of marstacimab and FVIII. If the cost effectiveness of emicizumab against marstacimab is worse than the cost effectiveness of emicizumab against the FVIII basket a higher discontinuation rate for marstacimab improves the cost effectiveness of emicizumab against the basket of marstacimab and FVIII. 

The estimates of the company base case of a discontinuation from marstacimab during the first cycle of 6.02% can be compared with this discontinuation rate being applied every cycle and set to 0.00% for marstacimab. 

## **Table 55: The effect of marstacimab discontinuation rates upon the NHB @ £30k/QALY vs main comparators** 

||Emicizumab|FVIII Basket|FIX Basket|
|---|---|---|---|
|Base case: One off 6.02%|***<br>***<br>***|**<br>**<br>***|***<br>**<br>***|
|6.02% each cycle||||
|0.00%||||



A lower discontinuation rate improves the estimated cost effectiveness of marstacimab. This also suggests that at comparator list prices the model structure may be biased against marstacimab due to it assuming that emicizumab has in effect a 0.00% discontinuation rate. 

101 



<!-- page 605 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

## **5.1.3 Longer term effects of bleeds: Complications and Mortality** 

## **5.1.3.1 Complications** 

In common with other NICE STAs in the area, the downstream complications of bleeds such as a higher likelihood of joint replacement are not modelled. 

The EAG undertook a literature search of the relationship between bleeds and joint arthropathy and possible replacement. The initial search found 9 possibly relevant papers. Kubes et al. analysed time to arthropathy and joint replacement by age but with no other contributory factors such as bleed rates or treatment.[74] Lin et al. provide some estimates of joint replacement and associated clotting factor frequency among on demand US patients but it is difficult to see how this data could be used for modelling purposes.[75] 

Tobase et al. estimated the risks of arthrodesis or arthroplasty to be 40% less with continuous prophylaxis.[76] They also reported the odds ratio of arthrodesis or arthroplasty by the number of joint bleeds in the previous 6 months compared to none: 1.1 for 1 joint bleed, 2.9 for 2 to 3 joint bleeds and 4.4 for 4 or more joint bleeds, the latter two odds ratios being statistically significant. 

The most promising paper for modelling purposes is Fischer et al[77] who analysed the data of 117 Dutch patients with severe haemophilia A or B and found that the Petterson score, a measure of arthropathy, increased slowly over time even in the absence of joint bleeds, but that it increased by 1 point per 13.5 joint bleeds over a mean period of 10.3 years between first and last Petterson score. This relationship was used by Zhou et al. in the cost effectiveness modelling of emicizumab, with an assumption of joint replacement when the Petterson score reached 28.[78] 

In short, it may be possible to explore the effects of joint bleeds on the likelihood of joint replacement surgery. This might be quite speculative and would require a fair number of additional assumptions which may not be uncontroversial. It would also require an entirely new modelling approach. Also note that the EAG exploratory base case applies rather lower baseline bleed rates than the company base case which would reduce the impact of any modelling of joint replacement. Nevertheless, not including it biases the model against the more effective treatment. 

102 



<!-- page 606 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

## **5.1.3.2 Mortality** 

EAG expert opinion suggests that with better modern treatments haemophilia patients may in time have similar life expectancy as the general population. Issues that may affect this for the currently prevalent population are adherence to older therapies such as SHLs. New patients are more likely to use the more modern treatments so this is becoming less of an issue over time. 

As the company notes, within Hassan et al.[16] most bleed related deaths were due to intracranial bleeds with a crude death rate of 2.33 per 1,000 patient years. But it can also be noted that non-hepatic cancers had a non-trivial crude death rate within this data as well. Not all the mortality within Hassan et al. was directly bleed related and the SMR may similarly not be directly attributable to differences in treated bleeds. 

It is credible that reducing treated bleeds will improve life expectancy. It can be argued that the base case should include this. But due to the high direct drug costs of treating haemophilia the situation could arise where a treatment that is less effective with a higher cost is estimated to be cost effective due to the shorter survival and the shorter duration of expensive treatment. The EAG thinks that this may mean it is better not to differentiate haemophilia treatments by mortality for the assessment of cost effectiveness. 

## **5.2** _**EAG critique of the handling of quality of life within the model**_ 

## **5.2.1 Baseline quality of life value and age weighting** 

The baseline quality of life value and age weighting have no effect upon net effects or the base case ICERs due to all utility decrements being absolute rather than proportional and there being no mortality effects. 

It does affect the scenario with mortality effects but as reviewed in Section 5.1.3.2 the EAG questions the desirability of this scenario for decision making purposes. It also affects the severity calculation as reviewed in Section 6 but the baseline quality of life would need to be hugely lower for the severity multipliers to be applicable. For these reasons the EAG does not further consider the baseline quality of life value. 

103 



<!-- page 607 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

## **5.2.2 Disutilities per administration** 

The disutilities of 0.0003 QALYs per IV administration and 0.0002 QALYs per subcutaneous (SC) administration are central to the company cost effectiveness estimates. For the company base case and as outlined in greater detail in section 3.2.11.3 above, they provide around 75% of the modelled QALY gain over FVIII and 50% of the modelled QALY gain over FIX. Due to the EAG exploratory base case reducing the baseline number of bleeds for FVIII/FIX it is likely to be even more central to the modelled QALY gains. 

The company draws these disutilities from Johnston et al.,[72] a paper sponsored by Hoffman-La Roche, the manufacturer of emicizumab which is administered subcutaneously. 

Johnston et al. performed a time trade-off (TTO) study among 82 members of the Canadian general public. Vignettes were presented for six possible health states: 

- On demand routine treatment with an ABR of 36 

- IV prophylaxis 2-3 times per weeks with an ABR of 4 to 5 

- IV prophylaxis 2-3 times per weeks with an ABR of 10 

- IV prophylaxis 7 times per weeks with an ABR of 4 to 5 

- SC prophylaxis weekly with an ABR of 1 to 2 

- SC prophylaxis 4 weekly with an ABR of 1 to 2 

The vignettes summarise an IV administration as you “ _have to go to a clinic/hospital to receive an intravenous infusion of medication. Over time you may be able to do this yourself_ ” which is “ _administered through vein in arm, wait up to 30 minutes for full dose_ ”. This is augmented with “ _Challenges: pain, burning or scarring may be experienced at the injection site, making it difficult to find a suitable vein, infusion may take several tries to complete_ ”, and “ _Risks: Significant risk of complications, including injury, infections and internal bleeding_ ”. For child patients the vignettes note “ _Challenges: Parents administering painful treatment to their children can be a difficult experience. Pain or scarring may occur at the injection site so infusion may take several tries to complete_ ”. 

104 



<!-- page 608 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

The vignettes describe SC administration as “ _This involves inserting a needle under your skin and administering a dose_ ” and that “ _the process is completed in less than two minutes_ ”. This is augmented with “ _Challenges: You might experience a burning sensation while the medication is injected_ ”. There are no risks. 

The TTO study was among members of the general public so the EAG thinks that their awareness of what is involved with haemophilia and its treatment is likely to be very limited and no better than that of the EAG economist. Due to this the EAG has a number of concerns around the vignettes. 

- IV administration is initially at a clinic or hospital. Admittedly the vignette says you may in time be able to do this yourself, but given the significant risks of injury, infection and internal bleeding it is an open question how many respondents thought they would be likely to be able to or want to do IV administrations by themselves at home. This is not aligned with usual UK practice where EAG expert opinion is that after a few administrations, perhaps 1-2, almost all patients will perform IV administrations themselves or have their parents/carers do it at home, significantly lessening the treatment burden. 

- The significant risks including of internal bleeding with IV administration are not quantified or placed in any real context. Where is the internal bleeding, how serious is it, how often does this occur, etc? Members of the Committee may be more familiar with the IV administration associated with haemophilia, but the EAG economist would have been quite concerned by the significant risk of internal bleeding and that this might seemingly occur in e.g. the chest cavity. EAG expert opinion is that internal bleeding from IV administration does not happen, with the worst that is seen being bruising or haematoma at the infusion site 

- SC administration has no risks. 

The EAG thinks that the design of the TTO study may be biased against IV administrations. 

The disutilities are based upon a random-intercept analysis of the TTO data but very little further explanation or data is provided. There are no confidence intervals 

105 



<!-- page 609 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

around the estimates or any indication of the statistical separation between the two estimates. 

The estimates are provided at 4 decimal places. This means that the actual mean for the IV administration disutility could have been anything from 0.00025 to 0.00035, while the mean for the SC administration disutility could have been anything from 0.00015 to 0.00025. There may have been little to no actual difference between the two central estimates, the apparent difference simply being a function of rounding. 

During FAC the company has pointed out that the paper estimates a statistically significant preference for subcutaneous treatment. To the EAG it is unclear whether this preference arises in part or in whole due to the subcutaneous vignettes having ABRs of 1-2 compared to intravenous ABRs of 4-5 and 10. Given the health state descriptors the EAG cannot see how a preference for subcutaneous administration can be estimated without other unwritten assumptions; e.g. a constant disutility per administration and a constant disutility per bleed. The study might have been more reliable if there were common dimensions; e.g. a vignette for IV with ABRs of 1-2 and perhaps also weekly administration, as per some EHLs, and a vignette for subcutaneous with ABRs of 4-5, and again perhaps with an administration frequency of 2-3 times per week to square the circle. By construction the data will have a high degree of collinearity between administration frequency and ABRs. 

This also does not address the main point in terms of rounding and the point estimates for the disutilities per administration only being reported at one significant figure, which the EAG finds unusual. It can also be noted that the p-values for the disutilities per administration are 0.22 for subcutaneous and < 0.001 for intravenous. This suggests that the disutility per administration for subcutaneous may be zero, or it may be somewhat greater than zero. The EAG thinks that this means that the point estimates per administration are probably not statistically significantly different from one another; i.e. the confidence interval for the subcutaneous estimate is likely to encompass -0.0003. 

EAG expert opinion is that SC administration compared to IV administration provides a patient benefit in and of itself, with less frequent administration at least compared to SHL providing a further benefit. 

106 



<!-- page 610 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

Due to the apparent bias of Johnston et al[72] and the uncertainty around the estimated mean disutilities, the EAG will supply scenarios which (a) halve the disutilities and (b) do not apply them. 

## **5.2.3 Disutilities per bleed** 

The company sources disutilities of 0.16 for a non-joint bleed from Neufeld et al[71] and 0.28 for a joint bleed from O’Hara et al.[13] 

Neufeld et al., funded by Novo Nordisk, surveyed 52 US haemophilia patients with inhibitors who had frequent bleeds, at least 4 bleeds requiring treatment with factor in the previous quarter. Patients or their caregivers were asked to complete daily diaries for at least 90 days or until 4 bleeding episodes had been experienced. The EQ-5D was also completed daily, this being valued using the US dataset. Daily diary completion rates were around 80%. Across 36 patients who did complete daily EQ5D diaries the mean (s.e.) EQ-5D index was 0.82 (0.03) during non-bleed days and 0.66 (0.04) during bleed days, yielding a net effect of 0.16. There may be some concerns that this analysis may not capture any overall effect of the patients’ high bleed rates upon their quality of life such as fear of bleeding, but rather captures how the patients’ day to day quality of life varies with bleeds. That said, the average quality of life on non-bleed days of 0.82 is above the baseline quality of life of BASIS so this may not be a concern. The more immediate point is that Neufeld et al. was not limited to non-joint bleeds. 

O’Hara et al., funded by Novo Nordisk, explored the effect of target joints on quality of life among 515 European patients with severe haemophilia including 37 UK patients, the 515 being the 42% of the sample who returned EQ-5D responses in the CHESS study. They used a general linear model to estimate the effect of the presence of one or more target joints, defined as chronic synovitis: 30% with 0, 30% with 1, 25% with 2, 8% with 3, 3% with 4 and a few patients with more than this. The EAG has not been able to source the 0.28 utility decrement, which may be due to incorrect referencing. But regardless of this the key point is that O’Hara et al. is a study of target joints, not of joint bleeds. The two will be linked but there is not an obviously linear 1:1 relationship with the number of joint bleeds and the number of joints with chronic synovitis. 

107 



<!-- page 611 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

The EAG will apply the disutility of Neufeld et al. to both joint and non-joint bleeds. This is not to say that they have the same disutility, only that the data from Neufeld et al. encompasses both types of bleeds so it should be a reasonable average value for them. 

The direct effects of bleeds from Neufeld et al. were specifically estimated for bleed days and non-bleed days, additional information on bleeds being recorded both during the bleed and during any treatment follow-up period after the bleed had ended. Of the 52 patients enrolled 39 completed diaries and 38 of these experienced bleeds with a total of 194 bleeds being reported. Among the 37 patients who complied with daily diary entries, these having a 99.8% completion rate, 472 days were bleed days. While the N=38 and N=37 are not perfectly aligned this suggests an average bleed duration of 2.4 days. 

It can be argued that the quality of life effects of bleeds might extend beyond the post bleed treatment period. If this applied this data would be available to Neufeld et al. and it would be strongly in the interests of the sponsor, Novo Nordisk, to have this aspect of the data also investigated and reported. The EAG thinks that the most likely explanation is that the data showed that this did not apply or at least not to the extent that it was worth reporting. The alternative explanation is that the authors were incompetent. 

The company assumes that the bleed disutilities apply in full for 2 days and at 50% for a further 5 days, so in effect for 4.5 days. The EAG will apply the 2.4 day duration implied by the Neufeld data and provide a scenario of the company assumed 4.5 days.

## **5.3.2 FVIII/FIX dosing compared to BASIS and UKHDCO data** 

At clarification the company supplied dosing data that showed a mean total of ***** IU/kg/year for routine prophylaxis during the BASIS OP. 

The model applies a mean total of ***** IU/kg/year for routine prophylaxis when the company base case iQVIA market shares are applied, 15% higher than that of BASIS. 

The EAG asked the company to provide data on the proportions of patients receiving the individual FVIII/FIX during the OP of BASIS. Unfortunately only the proportions receiving SHL and EHL split by haemophilia A and haemophilia B were provided. Applying these weights while retaining the iQVIA market shares balance within these categories results in a mean total of ***** IU/kg/year for routine prophylaxis, 17% higher than that of BASIS. 

This raises two possibilities. 

- Dosing during BASIS was less than would occur in the NHS which may imply suboptimal treatment during the OP and that BASIS is biased in favour of marstacimab within the NHS context. 

- The FVIII/FIX dosing for routine prophylaxis in the model is too high. 

The first bullet cannot be formally addressed by the EAG, the second can be explored by adjusting the dosing within the model. 

The 2023 UKHCDO annual report Tables 8a and 8b note that among 483 with severe haemophilia A and without inhibitors receiving FVIII SHL a total of 259,574 IU per person during 2022/23 was issued, and 271,697 IU per person among those receiving FVIII EHL. Adolescents were around 28% of those contributing data and

This appears to include both routine prophylaxis and IU issued for the treatment of bleeds, but excludes those not registered for the full treatment period, those issued with emicizumab and those using gene therapy. The company base case assumes 

routine prophylaxis requires an annual ******* IU of FVIII SHL and an annual ******** IU of FVIII EHL, *** and *** more than the UKHCDO data. Figure 10 of the report also suggests a mean of around 3,500 IU/kg/year which is reasonably aligned with BASIS.

## **5.3.3 Emicizumab dosing: maximum weight applied** 

The company assumes that as patients’ weight increases beyond 100kg, their dose of emicizumab continues to increase. EAG expert opinion is that the emicizumab dose is capped at that for a weight of 100kg: i.e. 300 IU Q2W. The EAG will apply this cap in its exploratory base case. 

## **5.3.4 FVIII/FIX dosing: vial rounding** 

The company assumes that all patients whose calculated optimal dose fall above a given number of vials round up the number of vials required, resulting in wastage. 

EAG expert opinion is that no product is unused due to patient doses being rounded up or rounded down to whole vials. This rounding is more often up than down, but there is rounding down. The ACD of ID6170 for efanesoctocog alfa for severe haemophilia A reports Committee notes much the same.

The EAG will explore vial rounding down for FVIII/FIX at 50%, 40% and 30% cuts for rounding down. 

## **5.3.5 Hospital visits per bleed** 

The company base case assumes the same hospital visit resource use per bleed as the company submission for the ID6170 efanesoctocog alfa STA: an average of 2.12 non-IP visits and 0.29 IP admissions, based upon O’Hara et al.[8] yielding an average cost of £545 per bleed. This is the same source as cited in the company submission for ID3812 etranagogene for moderate or severe haemophilia B with the same resource use being reported in Table 37 of the company submission, though with a somewhat higher cost per bleed of £1,384 due mainly to a higher inpatient unit cost of £3,081 compared to the current £157 being assumed. 

O’Hara et al. reported results from the Novartis funded CHESS study of resource use among those with severe haemophilia A, with resource use and EQ-5D data gathered from a range of European countries through patient completed questionnaires.[13] Another publication with O’Hara as lead author suggests very different PCS completion rates by country, this ranging from a high of 73% in France to a low of 12% in the UK, the UK contributing only 37 responses out of the overall CHESS PCS responses of 552 and its average 43% response rate.[12] 

As previously noted, O’Hara et al. explore the relationship between the presence or absence of joints with chronic synovitis, target joints, and resource use.[13] O’Hara et al. estimate higher costs for those with target joints compared to those without target joints. But the EAG has not been able to source the company reported resource use from O’Hara et al., and also notes that this paper explores target joints’ effects upon resource use and not bleeds. The company may be able to address this during FAC. 

O’Hara et al. appear to report non-drug direct costs and drug related direct costs of major and minor bleeds.[11] CHESS defined major bleeds as moderate to severe pain, effusion, limitation of motion and failure to improve within 24 hours, while minor bleeds were associated with minor pain, minimal joint selling, minimal restriction of movement and resolution within 24 hours. 

The paper is poorly documented and provides minimal information on input data. After controlling for age and number of target joints they report an additional annual non-drug direct cost per bleed of €2,489 (± €671) for major bleeds and a non- 

113 



<!-- page 617 -->

EAG Report Marstacimab for treating severe haemophilia A or severe haemophilia B in people 12 years and over 

statistically significant €145 (± €114) for minor bleeds. The drug costs are reported as being in 2015 prices. Assuming that non-drug costs are also in 2015 prices these can be converted to sterling using the mid-year exchange rate of €1.40/£ and inflated to 2021/22 prices using the PSSRU NHS Cost Inflation Index uplift of 12.8% so as to be aligned with model inputs results. This results in estimates for non-drug annual direct costs of bleeds of £2,005 (± £472) for major bleeds and £117 (± £80) for minor bleeds. 

Drug related direct cost estimates of €8,092 for major bleeds and €11,944 for minor bleeds were based upon an average cost per IU of €0.61, suggesting a mean dose of 13,266 IU per major bleed and 19,580 IU per minor bleed. These are both somewhat larger than the company base case mean dose per bleed of 3,474 IU, 3.8 times as large for major bleeds and 5.6 times as large for minor bleeds. 

Unfortunately, the EAG has not been able to find the balance between major and minor bleeds within O’Hara et al. PCS completion rates are a concern, particularly the UK 12% reporting rate. All reported bleeds seem likely to classify as treated bleeds given the estimated mean IU per minor bleed. The markedly higher mean IU for minor bleeds is also a concern, even though this does not appear to be limited to the treatment of bleeds but may include changes to routine prophylaxis. 

The ACD of ID6170 efanesoctocog alfa for bleeding episodes in haemophilia A noted that mild to moderate bleeds would be managed over the phone, often by specialist nurses instead of doctors. 

EAG expert opinion is that most bleeds are managed at home without the need for a hospital visit, and that very few bleeds now require hospital admission or inpatient treatment. 

In the absence of other data, the EAG base case will assume that 20% of treated bleeds require the resource use outlined in Table 34 above. It will present scenarios of 10% and 100%.

The EAG exploratory base cases are sensitive to: 

- Whether marstacimab dose escalation increases beyond that which occurred during the ATP and the OLE October 2023 data cut and what is the final maximum proportion of marstacimab patients dose escalating. 

- The mean FVIII/FIX dosing that is most reasonable to apply, and if based upon company estimates what the cut-off is for rounding down doses. 

- Whether it is reasonable to differentiate clinical effect estimates by haemophilia A and haemophilia B, and if so whether it is reasonable to differentiate dose escalation rates between haemophilia A and haemophilia B. 

- Whether the UKHCDO or BASIS should provide the ABR estimates for emicizumab and FVIII/FIX. 

Unfortunately, due to the nature of the revised clinical effectiveness data, the available data and time constraints the EAG has been unable to characterise the uncertainty around these parameters and so does not provide probabilistic scenario analyses. The EAG is unable to adequately capture the uncertainty around the estimates derived from BASIS and UKHCDO, however the company may be able to provide the former.

## **6 SEVERITY MODIFIERS** 

While there are arguments for not including (a) long term complications due to the probably speculative nature of such modelling or (b) mortality effects due to possible perverse results for the assessment of cost effectiveness, this is less warranted for the assessment of severity modifiers. 

The EAG presents the results of the company base case severity modelling that does not include the 2.4 SMR for those with bleeds, and modelling that does include it in Table 62. The EAG estimates are based upon the inputs to the model, including the mortality and general population quality of life values, in order to ensure consistency between the various estimates. The reasons for the discrepancy between the EAG estimated 18.7 discounted QALYs and the company 19.4 discounted QALYs for the general population is unclear but may be due to alternative inputs being used by the company or to EAG errors 6F[7] . 

**Table 62: EAG severity modelling using Company model: QALYs** 

||QALYs|Shortfall|% Shortfall|
|---|---|---|---|
|Population|18.704|-|-|
|No SMR for those with bleeds||||
|FVIII basket<br>Emicizumab<br>FIX basket|******<br>******<br>******|*****<br>*****<br>*****|***<br>***<br>***|

|FVIII basket<br>Emicizumab<br>FIX basket|******<br>******<br>******|*****<br>*****<br>*****|***<br>***<br>***|



The inclusion of the 2.4 SMR for those with bleeds increases the shortfall, but the absolute shortfall remains well below 12 QALYs and the proportionate shortfall 

remains well below 85%. Even with the 2.4 SMR for those with bleeds the long term effects of complications such as joint replacement would have to more than double the absolute QALY shortfall for severity multipliers to apply.

Additionally, there are considerable limitations to consider when comparing clinical trials to UK registry data. Since bleed rates are self-reported by patients, the different conditions, definitions and reporting requirements between the BASIS trial dataset and a real-world dataset may prevent a fair comparison being made. Participants in the BASIS trial were closely monitored and sent regular reminders to complete their eDiary. In contrast, bleeding data reported from the UK registry is reliant on the Haemtrack system and patient compliance with reporting.
